articles.title: September's CPI Came in Hotter Than Expected and Geopolitical Tensions Climbed. Stocks Fell. - International Business Times
articles.summary: September's CPI Came in Hotter Than Expected and Geopolitical Tensions Climbed. Stocks Fell.  International Business TimesStock market today: Hot inflation report drops tech, drives S&P 500, Dow and Nasdaq down  Yahoo FinanceAI stocks drop after hot inflation report bolsters bets for Fed rate hikes  CNNTrading Day: Tech melt  ReutersDollar Strengthens on Hot Inflation Data, Higher Treasury Yields  WSJ
articles.full_text:
Stocks fell on Wednesday after September's inflation reading came in hotter than expected and geopolitical tensions, particularly between the U.S. and Iran, remain high.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.09%, while the S&P 500 did so 1.10%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite underperformed, plunging 1.88% as AI-related stocks continued to drag the index.
Traders believe there are higher chances that the Federal Reserve will hike rates in October's meeting after the inflation report, although they moderated their expectations throughout the day.
Chances now stand at almost 35%, compared to 22.1% before the figures were released, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. However, they touched 49% during the session.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics noted that inflation gained 0.6% last month. The annual figure stood at 3.7%, compared to the 3.6% expected by analysts.
More than half of the increase was explained by gas prices, which rose more than 9% last month.
"The energy index increased 5.2 percent over the month following a 2.1-percent increase in August. The shelter index rose 0.4 percent in September after rising 0.3 percent in August. The index for food was unchanged in September, as the index for food away from home increased 0.2 percent and the index for food at home fell 0.1 percent," BLS detailed.
Fed officials expected to hike rates again before the latest reading, according to the most recent minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC).
"Most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end," reads a passage of the document.
There are no signs that energy markets will get a reprieve soon. Two ships sunk in the Strait of Hormuz over the past day as Iran escalates attacks against ships it does not allow to transit through the waterway.
The ships in question are a container ship and a dry bulk carrier. They were hit by projectiles in separate incidents.
The development follows a report detailing that Tehran is resorting to new tactics to disrupt traffic in the waterway.
The tactics in question were not revealed by senior Iranian officials who talked to Reuters, but they seek to prevent the U.S. from bringing down oil prices ahead of the midterms.
They did say that the pace and type of attacks have changed and are targeting more vessels seeking to transit through the waterway.
A U.S. official told the outlet that Tehran has begun using unarmed spotters in small boats to find potential targets.
Iran had announced on Friday it would escalate hostilities, with the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps saying in a statement that it will now pursue vessels that don't transit the routes it has approved even outside the waterway and "throughout the entire region," and that "its punishment will be definitive."

articles.title: US Inflation Latest News: September CPI Rises 3.7% as Core Inflation Beats Forecasts, S&P 500 Futures Fall and Treasury Yields Jump – Check Fed Rate Decision Outlook - The Sunday Guardian
articles.summary: US Inflation Latest News: September CPI Rises 3.7% as Core Inflation Beats Forecasts, S&P 500 Futures Fall and Treasury Yields Jump – Check Fed Rate Decision Outlook  The Sunday Guardian
articles.full_text:
US Inflation Latest News: American consumers are facing renewed pressure from rising prices, while financial markets are reassessing what the latest inflation figures mean for interest rates. September’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) report showed that overall inflation accelerated to 3.7% year over year, while core inflation also came in above economists’ expectations.
The figures, released by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, put the Federal Reserve’s next policy decision under fresh scrutiny as officials weigh persistent price pressures against the wider economic outlook.
Markets reacted quickly to the report. S&P 500 futures reversed earlier gains, Treasury yields moved higher and the US dollar strengthened as traders considered whether the Federal Reserve might keep interest rates elevated for longer or raise them again. Rising energy costs, particularly gasoline prices, played a major role in the latest increase, adding another complication to the inflation outlook amid continuing US-Iran tensions.
US Inflation Latest News: Gasoline Prices Drive September Inflation Higher
Energy costs were the biggest factor behind the monthly increase in consumer prices. The energy index jumped 5.2% in September, while gasoline prices climbed 9.1%, accounting for about half of the increase in headline CPI, according to the figures in the report.
Other categories also contributed to the rise in living costs:
- Shelter: Prices increased 0.4% during the month.
- Used cars and trucks: Prices rose 0.7%.
- Food: Prices remained unchanged from August but were 2.5% higher than a year earlier.
- Core CPI: Prices excluding food and energy rose 0.3% in September, above the 0.2% forecast.
The jump in gasoline prices reflects the impact of rising energy costs amid the continuing US-Iran conflict. Higher fuel prices can also increase transportation and production costs, potentially putting additional pressure on prices across the economy.
The core CPI reading is particularly important for policymakers because it helps them assess inflation trends beyond the more volatile food and energy categories. Its stronger-than-expected monthly increase suggests that underlying price pressures have not disappeared.
September CPI Report: How Did Wall Street React to the CPI Inflation Report?
The September inflation figures prompted an immediate reaction in financial markets as traders reassessed the outlook for Federal Reserve policy.
Market reaction after the CPI report
- S&P 500 futures: Fell 0.3%, reversing an earlier gain of 0.2%.
- 10-year Treasury yield: Rose to 5.29%, from 5.19% before the release.
- 2-year Treasury yield: Jumped 13 basis points to 4.92%, reflecting its sensitivity to Fed policy expectations.
- US dollar: The dollar strengthened as Treasury yields moved higher.
Market figures reported immediately after the September CPI release; prices and yields can change throughout the trading session.
Higher Treasury yields can make borrowing more expensive for households, businesses and the federal government. They can also put pressure on stock valuations because investors may demand stronger returns from equities when safer assets offer higher yields.
The market reaction showed that investors were particularly concerned about the core inflation figures and what they could mean for the Federal Reserve’s next decision.
US Inflation Latest News: Will the Federal Reserve Raise Interest Rates on October 28?
The hotter-than-expected core CPI reading has kept the possibility of another Federal Reserve rate hike in focus. Before the inflation report, markets priced in a 22% chance of a 25-basis-point increase at the October 28 policy meeting, according to the supplied market data.
The Fed faces a difficult choice. Raising interest rates could help cool demand and reduce inflationary pressure, but it could also increase borrowing costs for consumers and businesses. Holding rates steady would give policymakers more time to assess whether the latest price increases reflect temporary energy shocks or more persistent inflation.
The Federal Reserve’s reported benchmark interest-rate target range stands at 3.75% to 4%. Several officials have signalled support for another increase this year while remaining flexible about its timing.
Market expectations also point to the December 9 meeting as another important date for monetary policy. The latest CPI report could influence those expectations, although the Fed will consider additional economic data before making its decision.
September CPI Report: Why the Producer Price Index Could Change the Fed’s Outlook
The next major inflation indicator is the Producer Price Index (PPI), scheduled for release on Thursday, October 15, at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time, according to the supplied report.
Unlike CPI, which measures prices paid by consumers, PPI tracks changes in prices received by producers. The data can provide further insight into business costs and inflation pressures that may eventually reach consumers.
The PPI report will also provide additional inputs used to estimate the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index. Healthcare services inflation is one of the components investors and economists will watch.
Economists at Pantheon Macroeconomics had expected the Fed to avoid an October rate hike if CPI and PPI data pointed to a monthly core PCE increase above 0.30%. The firm’s earlier forecast anticipated a 0.2% monthly rise in core PCE.
The PPI figures could therefore change the market’s interpretation of the CPI report and influence expectations for the October 28 meeting.
US Inflation Latest News: What Does the September CPI Report Mean for the S&P 500?
The S&P 500 had finished Tuesday’s session just 0.2% below its October 6 record closing high, despite slipping in the previous two sessions. Futures initially rose 0.2% on Wednesday before reversing direction after the CPI release.
The inflation report creates a fresh challenge for equities. If inflation remains elevated, the Federal Reserve may keep interest rates higher for longer or consider another increase. Higher yields can make stocks less attractive relative to bonds and raise the cost of financing for companies.
However, the CPI report does not determine the market’s direction on its own. Corporate earnings, economic growth, oil prices and the upcoming PPI release will also influence trading.
For investors, the key question is whether the September increase marks another temporary energy-driven jump or signals that inflation is becoming harder to control. The answer could shape expectations for both the Federal Reserve’s next decision and Wall Street’s performance in the weeks ahead.

articles.summary: Gold, silver rebound as Treasury yields tumble despite hot PPI - Kitco AM Report  KitcoGold approaches $4,170, silver gains 3% as bond rally lifts precious metals - Kitco PM Report  KitcoGold rebounds on weaker dollar, yield drop; October Fed hike bets subdued  ReutersGold Silver Rate Today Live Updates: Gold slips as Fed rate hike bets rise on inflation concerns  The Times of IndiaGold eases after climbing over 1% in previous session  TradingVie...
articles.full_text:
(Kitco NewsWire) – Spot gold and silver prices are solidly higher in early U.S. trading Thursday, rebounding from Wednesday's sharp losses as falling Treasury yields, a weaker U.S. dollar and renewed safe-haven demand outweighed another upside U.S. inflation surprise. A technology-led global equity selloff pushed investors toward government bonds and bullion, even as September producer prices rose much faster than expected. At the time of writing, spot gold was trading near $4,147.50 an ounce, up $43.00, or 1.05%, while spot silver was trading near $56.620, up $1.10, or 1.99%.
Market positioning remains caught between persistent inflation and growing concerns about the sustainability of the AI-driven equity rally. September producer prices surged 1.3% on the month and 6.3% from a year earlier, the largest monthly advance since March 2022. Producer energy prices jumped 10.8%, including a 20.3% increase in gasoline. The report followed Wednesday's stronger-than-expected CPI, which showed headline inflation rising 0.6% on the month and 3.7% annually. September retail sales increased 0.8%, exceeding forecasts, although sales excluding autos and gasoline rose just 0.2%. Initial jobless claims edged up to 199,000, reinforcing the picture of limited layoffs despite slower hiring.
Fed funds pricing put the probability of an October rate hike near 29% following the morning data, leaving a pause as the base case but keeping additional tightening by December heavily priced. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield fell toward 5.08%, its lowest level in about three weeks, as selling in heavily indebted AI-linked technology companies fueled demand for Treasuries. The dollar index retreated toward 102.1 from Wednesday's 18-month high. The next tests include Friday's import and export prices, industrial production and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's appearance at the IMF annual meetings in Bangkok. The sharp yield decline provides immediate support for gold, but persistent producer inflation and resilient consumer spending leave the Fed's tightening bias intact.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remains a significant source of geopolitical and energy-market risk, although crude prices retreated Thursday. Washington is considering easing sanctions on certain oil tankers to lower shipping costs, while signs of recovering Middle Eastern exports have reduced some immediate supply concerns. The security picture remains volatile. A container ship and a dry bulk carrier sank near the strait following separate projectile attacks, and Tehran has indicated it is intensifying strikes in response to the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. Brent crude fell toward $104.39 a barrel, while WTI traded near $92.91. Lower crude prices offer some relief from inflation pressure, but shipping disruptions, elevated freight costs and the unresolved U.S.-Iran confrontation continue to support defensive demand for gold. Silver is benefiting from the precious-metals rebound but remains more exposed to weakening industrial demand and broader risk-asset liquidation.
Global equity markets remained under pressure before the U.S. open. S&P 500 futures were down about 0.3%, Nasdaq futures fell 1.2% and Dow futures were modestly higher as concerns about AI-sector financing and stretched valuations extended Wednesday's technology selloff. South Korea's Kospi dropped about 7.6%, Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 4.9% and Taiwan's Taiex declined 3.4%. European equities were mixed, with defensive sectors outperforming technology shares. The flight toward government bonds provided the clearest cross-market support for gold.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil prices lower and trading near $92.91 a barrel, while Brent crude was near $104.39. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note is trading near the 5.08% area. The U.S. dollar index is softer and trading near 102.1. (Kitco Global Index shows how much of today's gold move is the dollar versus the gold market itself.)
Technically, spot gold bulls' next upside price objective is to push prices back above the $4,161.46 to $4,181.44 resistance zone, with a sustained move targeting $4,216.96 and then $4,267.20. Bears' next near-term downside price objective is a break below $4,127.56, with deeper downside targets at $4,107.28 and then $4,088.10. First resistance is seen at $4,161.46 and then at $4,181.44. articles.title: US September CPI Preview: High Oil Prices Expected to Push Up Overall Inflation, Moderate Core Inflation May Ease Urgency for Rate Hikes - Bitget
articles.summary: US September CPI Preview: High Oil Prices Expected to Push Up Overall Inflation, Moderate Core Inflation May Ease Urgency for Rate Hikes  Bitget
articles.full_text:
Driven by rising gasoline and food prices, U.S. consumer prices are likely to surge significantly in September.
According to Zhitong Finance APP, driven by rising gasoline and food prices, U.S. consumer prices in September may have risen significantly, adding more bad news for President Trump and the Republican Party ahead of the key midterm elections on November 3. The U.S. Department of Labor will release the Consumer Price Index (CPI) report at 20:30 Beijing time on Wednesday. Economists predict that the CPI for September may rise by 0.6% month-on-month, compared to a 0.4% increase in August. The year-on-year CPI for September is expected to rise 3.6%, higher than August's 3.4%. The Federal Reserve tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index and takes it as a reference indicator for its 2% inflation target.
Previous surveys have shown that as dissatisfaction with the rising cost of living grows, consumer confidence has deteriorated and Trump’s approval ratings have fallen. Polls show about 78% of Americans blame rising prices on Trump's policies, including import tariffs and the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran; the rise in prices is outpacing wages.
However, the September CPI report is expected to show that excluding the more volatile food and energy prices, other goods will show a moderate increase in prices, which will further reduce the urgency for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again this month.
Rising Food and Energy Prices
Economists say that the slowdown in core CPI monthly inflation brings little comfort to most consumers, especially those at the so-called "bottom" of the K-shaped economy.
“People care about food and energy. These are what they feel every day,” said Sung Won Sohn, Professor of Finance and Economics at Loyola Marymount University. “Many voters are at the bottom of the K-shaped economy. They are suffering from rising energy and food prices, and I think this will affect the election results—as do a lot of other people.”
Some economists estimate that gasoline may contribute about 0.3 percentage points to September's CPI. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, gasoline prices surged 7.1% in September. Food prices are expected to rise at least 0.2% after two consecutive months of 0.1% increases.
The September CPI report will be closely watched by millions of retirees and other Social Security beneficiaries, who are trying to estimate how much their benefits will increase next year. The U.S. Social Security Administration uses CPI data for urban wage earners and clerical workers from the third quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026 to determine the annual Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA) for Social Security and Supplemental Security Income benefits in 2027. These programs benefit retired American seniors, as well as the disabled, certain widows, widowers, and children. The Senior Citizens League, one of the largest organizations for older Americans, expects the COLA to increase by 3.5% in 2027, up from 2.8% in 2026, which would increase the average monthly benefits for retirees by $67.90 to $2,007.
The impact of the shock in energy prices is closely monitored for signs it may spill over beyond the transportation sector. Some economists argue that higher energy prices have yet to be embedded in inflation, given the moderate rise in core CPI. Others warn that diesel prices at record highs, plus no end in sight to the Middle East conflict, will soon be reflected in supermarket prices. They point out that price indices in business surveys remain high.
Core Inflation Expected to Moderate
Excluding the volatile food and energy prices, the September CPI is expected to increase by 0.2% month-on-month, compared with a 0.3% increase in August. Core CPI inflation is expected to slow down in September, reflecting the waning impact of the jump in mobile phone prices caused by changes in AT&T service, although a higher-than-expected increase cannot be ruled out. Other service providers also raised fees in September.
Airfare prices may rise further due to higher jet fuel costs. Rents are expected to rise moderately. As the impact of tariffs fades, goods prices may edge up slightly. For the 12 months ending in September, core CPI inflation is expected to rise 2.5%, compared with 2.4% in August. This indicator lags core PCE inflation, which rose 3.0% in August, as the composition weights differ in the index basket.
Federal Reserve Rate Hike Expectations Cool in October
Last month, the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark overnight interest rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75%-4.00%, the first increase in three years, and signaled it would further raise borrowing costs in the coming months. CME’s FedWatch tool shows financial markets see about a 22% chance of an interest rate hike at the October 27-28 policy meeting.
Disappointing nonfarm payroll growth in September and lower-than-expected PCE inflation in July and August have reduced the likelihood of a rate hike this month. Economists expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates in December.
“If the September core CPI monthly increase can stay in the 0.2% range, the Federal Reserve should be able to keep rates unchanged in October. However, this does not end the debate about whether further hikes will be needed in the future,” said Scott Anderson, Chief U.S. Economist at BMO Capital Markets.

Kalshi traders raised their expectations of an October Federal Reserve rate hike after a new inflation report showed consumer prices rising faster than anticipated.
Kalshi's October Federal Reserve decision market shows a 33% chance of a 25-basis-point rate hike, up from 16% before the report. The probability of the Fed holding rates steady fell from 84% to 66%.
For informational purposes only. Not financial advice. See full disclaimer below.
The latest inflation numbers
The New York Times reported that the Consumer Price Index Report shows prices rose by 0.6%. The increase is the largest monthly increase in the last five months.
Rising energy costs drove September's inflation increase, with gasoline prices accounting for more than half of the monthly rise in the Consumer Price Index.
“The bulk of the increase stemmed directly from energy prices, which have shot higher this year because of the war with Iran,” The Times wrote. “Gasoline prices, which in late September rose to the highest level in four months at nearly $4.50 a gallon, surged 9.1% for the month. That accounted for more than half of the overall monthly increase in prices. They are up 34.2% over the past year.”
Other financial markets also showed a sharp increase in expectations for an October rate hike.
Reuters reported that "traders had priced interest-rate futures about a 22% chance of an October rate hike. After the report, which also showed faster underlying inflation than economists had anticipated, the implied probability of a rate hike at the Fed's October 27-28 meeting rose to around 40%."
Federal Reserve officials have also expressed concerns about persistent inflation, although the timing of additional interest rate increases remains uncertain.
The Associated Press reported earlier this week that officials "unanimously agreed" at last week's meeting that interest rates would need to be raised to combat inflation.
"The officials unanimously agreed that inflation was still elevated and had not made much progress towards their 2% target in recent months, the minutes said," The AP reported. "The Fed increased its key interest rate at the Sept. 15-16 meeting by a quarter-point to about 3.9%, its first increase in three years."
Trump criticizing Kevin Warsh
The inflation report also coincided with higher market expectations that President Donald Trump will publicly criticize Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh.
The probability of Trump publicly criticizing Warsh before April 2027 rose from 33% to 48%. The price for criticism before January 2027 increased from 35% to 37%, while the price for criticism before December rose from 21% to 27%.
The Motley Fool reported that President Trump "hasn't been shy about voicing his displeasure with the [Federal Open Market Committee's] stance on interest rates." He regularly criticized former Fed Chair Jerome Powell. Following the September meeting, "President Trump took a very subtle jab at Fed Chair Warsh for not voting against what he refers to as a 'very hostile' board. But according to the head of the central bank, rate hikes were completely justified."
With inflation moving further above the Fed's 2% target, traders will be watching whether Warsh and other policymakers favor another rate increase at their October meeting.

articles.title: Inflation heats up in September; Fed rate hike this month back on table - KSL News
articles.summary: Inflation heats up in September; Fed rate hike this month back on table  KSL News
articles.full_text:
- Consumer prices rose in September due to a 9.1% surge in gasoline prices.
- The consumer price index increased 0.6% in September, complicating the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision.
- Core CPI inflation rose 2.6% annually, raising rate hike odds to 52% for October
WASHINGTON — Consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged, dealing another blow to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections and putting an interest rate increase later this month back on the radar.
The consumer price index report from the Labor Department on Wednesday showed a broadening of price pressures beyond energy, raising concerns among economists that underlying inflation could be getting sticky. Financial markets now see the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision this month as a closer call than before the data was released.
The report added to surveys this month that showed a further deterioration in consumer sentiment and a plunge in Trump's approval rating, driven by angst over the rising cost of living. A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed about 78% of Americans blamed Trump's policies, including tariffs on imports and the Middle East conflict, for rising prices, which are outpacing wages.
"The last mile back to target could remain bumpy and keep interest rates elevated," said Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial. "The report complicates the Fed's decision this month, as the road back to price stability is looking increasingly difficult to navigate."
The CPI rose 0.6% last month after climbing 0.4% in August, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said. The increase in the CPI was in line with economists' expectations.
A 9.1% surge in gasoline prices accounted for more than half of the increase in the CPI over the month. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran is driving up energy prices. Diesel prices have vaulted to record highs and there are fears that those costs will soon feed through to higher prices at the supermarket.
Food prices were unchanged after gaining 0.1% in both July and August. Grocery store prices dipped 0.1% over the month, but rose 1.8% on a year-over-year basis. Beef prices dropped 1.0% in September and the cost of dairy and related products eased 0.9%. But prices for nonalcoholic beverages surged 0.9%, while fruits and vegetables cost 0.5% more.
In the 12 months through September, the CPI advanced 3.7% after rising 3.4% in August.
Core inflation above expectations
Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI gained 0.3% in September, matching the gain in August. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the so-called core CPI would rise 0.2%. The core CPI was lifted by a 0.4% increase in the cost of shelter, including hotel and motel rooms. Owners' equivalent rent rose 0.3%.
There were increases in the costs of recreation and education. Prices for used cars and trucks increased 0.7%, while airline fares rose 1.2% amid higher jet fuel prices. Apparel prices climbed 0.3%.
In the 12 months through September, core CPI inflation increased 2.6% after advancing 2.4% in August. The central bank tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index for its 2% inflation target.
The core CPI measure is lagging core PCE inflation, which increased 3.0% in August, because of the different weights assigned to the components in the baskets.
Financial markets raised the chances of a rate hike at the Fed's Oct. 27-28 policy meeting to roughly 52% from about 22% prior to the CPI report, CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed. The odds of a rate increase this month had diminished following underwhelming payroll gains in September as well as cooler-than-expected PCE inflation readings for July and August.
Treasury yields were mostly higher while the dollar advanced versus a basket of currencies. U.S. stocks opened lower.
The Fed in September raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range, its first hike in three years, and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the months ahead. Economists had expected the Fed to raise rates in December.
The September CPI inflation report was keenly awaited by millions of retirees and other Social Security recipients trying to figure out how much their benefits will increase next year.
The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security and Supplemental Security Income benefits for 2027. The programs benefit older Americans who have retired as well as the disabled and certain widows, widowers and children.

articles.summary: Fed rate hike call seen tight as inflation heats up  WTVB
articles.full_text:
Oct 14 (Reuters) – A Federal Reserve interest-rate decision later this month may be a closer call than previously thought, traders bet on Wednesday, after Labor Department data showed consumer prices were up 3.7% last month from a year earlier, well above the Fed’s 2% target and moving in the wrong direction.
Higher gasoline prices from the Middle East war were a main driver. Excluding volatile food and energy prices, the core consumer price index (CPI) was up 2.6%, more than the 2.5% economists polled by Reuters had projected.
Fed officials have said they are looking closely for signs of broadening price pressures that could keep inflation high even if gas prices fall, even as they have signaled they have time to weigh more data before following last month’s interest-rate increase with another one.
“The surprise was not concentrated in any one item, like it was with wireless in the August report, but instead reflected a number of components showing strength, i.e., it was broad-based,” wrote Omair Sharif, founder of Inflation Insights.
Traders had priced interest-rate futures for about a 22% chance of an October rate hike. After the report, the implied probability of a rate hike at the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting rose to around 45%, pointing to unusual uncertainty around the outcome just two weeks before the decision.
Fed policymakers will also have to weigh the risk of tightening too fast and unduly slowing the labor market.
“September CPI keeps inflation concerns alive, with core inflation still sticky, but weaker jobs data and fragile consumer sentiment mean the Fed still has room to hold in October,” PPHC Chief Economist Martin Beck said.
(Reporting by Ann Saphir; Editing by Mark Potter and Andrea Ricci )

Pill, who voted in favour of raising interest rates at the central bank's September meeting, said it was not yet clear whether borrowing costs would need to rise by as much as financial markets anticipate. He made the remarks at an event organised by Citi on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund's semi-annual meetings in Bangkok, Reuters reported.
Read more: Global Market: China’s yuan firms as investors await US CPI data, assess inflation
Pill said the central bank needed to ensure monetary policy was positioned appropriately to address inflationary pressures, while questioning whether four rate increases would be warranted over the coming 12 months.
The comments highlight divisions within the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee over the appropriate response to the energy shock stemming from the Iran war. Pill and two other MPC members voted for a rate increase in September, while the majority, including Governor Andrew Bailey, favoured keeping rates unchanged until there was greater clarity on the conflict's economic impact, Reuters reported.
Bailey reiterated on Tuesday that the energy shock had so far had a limited effect on broader inflationary pressures in the UK. However, he warned that the longer the disruption continued, the greater the risk that its effects would spread more widely through the economy.
Read more: Global Market: Japan's Nikkei rebounds as chip stocks rise, Topix slips on bank losses
While financial markets have priced in a series of rate increases over the coming year, Pill's remarks suggest policymakers remain divided over the scale and timing of any further tightening, with the outlook likely to depend on how the energy shock evolves and whether it generates more persistent inflationary pressures.

articles.title: Euro-to-Dollar Pressure Builds as U.S. Core Inflation Pressures Fed Into Action - Pound Sterling Live
articles.summary: Euro-to-Dollar Pressure Builds as U.S. Core Inflation Pressures Fed Into Action  Pound Sterling Live
articles.full_text:
Image © Adobe Images
Hotter underlying US price growth has pushed the single currency to a fresh 17-month low, and strategists see the dollar's rate support strengthening.
The Euro to Dollar exchange rate fell to a fresh 17-month low after US core inflation beat expectations, reviving bets on another Federal Reserve rate hike this month.
Core consumer prices, which strip out food and energy, rose 0.3% in September against a consensus of 0.2%, lifting the annual core rate to 2.6%.
Headline inflation rose 0.6% on the month, in line with forecasts, taking the annual rate to 3.7% as gasoline prices climbed.
Hotter core inflation matters more for the Fed than the energy-driven headline, because it shows price pressures spreading into the wider economy; a Fed that hikes again widens the US interest rate advantage and pulls capital towards the dollar.
"Underlying consumer prices rose more quickly than expected in the United States last month, strengthening the case for more rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, and lifting the dollar," says Karl Schamotta, Chief Market Strategist at Corpay.
EUR/USD fell from 1.1199 before the release to 1.1138 within 15 minutes, a drop of 0.5% that broke through Monday's 1.1154 low.
Schamotta says traders are sharply raising the odds of an October hike, and Treasury yields are rising at the policy-sensitive end of the curve.
New York Fed President John Williams had argued only on Tuesday that one more hike this year would be enough, a view that sent the odds of an October move down to around 20%.
"A stronger-than-expected core inflation reading adds to mounting evidence that domestic price pressures are becoming more entrenched, rather than easing," says George Brown, Senior Economist at Schroders.
Brown says markets are right to expect much tighter policy, and the open question is whether the Fed will deliver it.
Richard Carter, Head of Fixed Interest Research at Quilter Cheviot, says another hike this year cannot be ruled out and ten-year Treasury yields could keep rising.
What's Next for EUR/USD
The case for a limited move rests on how much Fed tightening was already priced before the data.
Societe Generale's Kit Juckes said in a recent update that market pricing for the Fed Funds rate stood just below 5%, already above the highest forecast in the Bloomberg survey, and that only a core reading well above consensus would lift it further.
Corpay expects some of today's dollar gains to fade, though Schamotta says the Fed's calculus has shifted.
"We suspect this knee-jerk reaction could fade somewhat, but there's no question that the monetary tightening calculus has shifted," he says.
Positioning adds to the case for a bounce, with Societe Generale reporting euro short positions at their highest since December 2024, but the technical targets sit lower:
• Support at 1.1115, UOB's one-to-three-week target
• Support at 1.11, the area ING and KBC both flag
• Resistance at 1.1154, Monday's low, now overhead
• Resistance at 1.1220, the level UOB says would confirm the decline has stabilised
"A test of 1.110 remains the risk for EUR/USD," says Francesco Pesole, FX Strategist at ING.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks at the IMF on Friday, the next chance for policymakers to confirm or push back on the October hike pricing that today's data rebuilt.
A daily close back above 1.1154 would mark today's break as a false one; failing that, 1.1115 and then 1.11 are the next stops.

articles.title: US inflation to hit 3.6% in September? Why CPI data matters for Fed rate decision | Hindustan Times - Hindustan Times
articles.summary: US inflation to hit 3.6% in September? Why CPI data matters for Fed rate decision | Hindustan Times  Hindustan Times
articles.full_text:
US inflation may rise to 3.6% in September as gas prices climb. The CPI report could shape the Fed's October rate decision and rate hike outlook.
The US Consumer Price Index (CPI) report, due on Wednesday, October 15, is expected to show that inflation increased in September as energy prices rose. The data will help investors understand how prices are changing and what the Federal Reserve may do with interest rates.
Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect annual US inflation to increase to 3.6% in September, up from 3.4% in August. This would mean that consumer prices are rising faster than they did a year earlier. Consumer prices are forecast to rise 0.6% in September compared with August. This would be faster than the 0.4% monthly increase recorded in August.
US inflation rises as gas prices hit record high
Gasoline prices are expected to be a major reason for the rise in US inflation in September. When fuel prices go up, travelling becomes more expensive. It also costs more to make and deliver goods.
According to the American Automobile Association (AAA), the average price of gasoline in the US reached a record $4.33 per gallon last month. This was nearly 50 cents higher than the previous monthly record set in 2023.
US core inflation rate expected to rise to 2.5%
Core inflation does not include food and energy prices because they can change quickly. It is expected to rise slightly in September.
Also read: US Treasury yields today: 10-year yield falls as oil prices drop ahead of inflation data
Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expect the annual core inflation rate to increase to 2.5% in September, up from 2.4% in August. Core consumer prices are also expected to rise by 0.2% from August to September. This would be lower than the higher-than-expected 0.3% increase recorded in August.
Core inflation is an important measure for Federal Reserve officials because it excludes food and energy prices, which can be volatile. The September reading will help policymakers assess whether underlying price pressures are easing or remaining high.
Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said the September CPI report is expected to be relatively straightforward. However, he warned that the absence of a major surprise does not mean the inflation problem has been solved, as price pressures remain elevated, according to Yahoo Finance.
Fed rate decision: Will interest rates stay unchanged?
If core inflation comes in around economists' expectations, the Federal Reserve may have enough reason to leave interest rates unchanged at its October 28 meeting. Policymakers will also consider other economic data before making their decision.
The September jobs report showed that the US added only 29,000 jobs, while the unemployment rate increased. This relatively weak employment data is another factor that could influence the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision.
Recent comments from Federal Reserve officials have been mixed, particularly over when rates might need to change again. Their comments reflect the challenge of bringing inflation down without putting too much pressure on the economy.
Traders currently see a 76% chance that the Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its October meeting. This expectation reflects the latest economic data and comments from central bank officials.
Also read: US bank earnings: JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and Citi show consumers remain resilient despite high rates
US inflation risks: Airfares, hotels and diesel prices
Economists warn that core inflation could rise more than expected. Higher costs for services and other goods could prevent inflation from slowing, making it harder for the Federal Reserve to bring price increases under control.
Rising costs for air travel, hotels and auto parts are among the factors economists are watching. If these costs increase faster than expected, they could push core inflation higher in September. Diesel fuel is widely used to transport goods. A sharp increase in diesel prices can make shipping and distribution more expensive, potentially pushing up prices for businesses and consumers.
October Fed rate hike back in focus as inflation stays high
Economists at RBC, led by Mike Reid, said there is still a limited chance of a major slowdown in core inflation. They also warned that September's CPI report may not fully reflect the risks that could push inflation higher in the coming months, according to Yahoo Finance.
If core inflation remains elevated for a second consecutive month, an interest rate hike in October could become a possibility again. This would depend on the inflation figures and the Federal Reserve's wider assessment of the economy.
Bank of America economist Stephen Juneau said a monthly core CPI increase of 0.3% would likely bring back speculation that the Federal Reserve may need to continue raising interest rates in October. Such a reading would be higher than the 0.2% increase currently expected, according to Yahoo Finance.
Why inflation data matters for the Fed
The report will help show whether inflation is moving closer to the Federal Reserve's goal or remains too high. If core inflation matches expectations, the Fed may keep rates unchanged. However, a stronger-than-expected reading could increase pressure on policymakers to consider another rate hike.

articles.title: BOE Hawk Pill Skeptical of Market Pricing Four UK Rate Hikes - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: BOE Hawk Pill Skeptical of Market Pricing Four UK Rate Hikes  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
(Bloomberg) -- One of the Bank of England's most hawkish officials cast doubt on market pricing that suggests the UK central bank will hike interest rates four times by next summer.
Most Read from Bloomberg
- Epic Games Delays Disney Project, Asks Developers to Use More AI
- Apple Unveils $299 HomeView Hub as Part of New Smart Home Push
- PepsiCo Cuts Estimates for Poppi Payout While Soda Sales Slump
- Billionaire Birla Plans $30 Billion Push Undeterred by Crises
- Stocks Bounce From Lows on Williams' Rate Remarks: Markets Wrap
While Chief Economist Huw Pill said on Wednesday that the BOE should have acted sooner to tackle the energy shock caused by the Iran war, he added that more concrete evidence was needed before a bigger rise in rates.
"Is it obvious that we will need to follow market pricing to four 25 basis point hikes and so forth? There I would be a little bit more skeptical," he said at an event in Bangkok, where he's attending annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. "To get to 100 basis points, then I do think we probably need to see some more concrete manifestation of these risks."
Pill has been in the minority on the Monetary Policy Committee backing an immediate rate hike since April, shortly after the US and Israeli attacks on Iran rattled energy markets. Most BOE officials have held off action so far, believing that a tepid labor market and sharp tightening in financial conditions since the Middle Eastern conflict broke out have bought them time to assess the risk of high inflation persisting.
However, more UK officials are now edging toward support for an increase in borrowing costs.
In an interview with CNN late on Tuesday, Governor Andrew Bailey reiterated that it is becoming harder to avoid a rate hike, the longer the energy shock drags on.
Markets are pricing in a near-100% chance of the MPC voting for their first increase in bank rate in over three years at their November meeting. Traders then expect the BOE to back a further three quarter-point hikes by next summer. But Pill suggested he is reluctant to support a series of rate rises yet, given scant evidence on whether the energy shock is spreading widely across the economy.
"We will get more evidence, I think, over the next six-nine months around, for example, second round effects, which I would emphasize in my thinking are key to whether a shock to inflation becomes a more self-sustaining, persistent dynamic in inflation," he said.
Pill pointed to a more resilient UK economy and labor market as important factors, arguing that holding off action in response to uncertainty is a "little bit misguided."

articles.title: Gold Recovers as Dollar and Bond Yields Retreat; Markets Await US Inflation Test - اقتصاد آنلاین
articles.summary: Gold Recovers as Dollar and Bond Yields Retreat; Markets Await US Inflation Test  اقتصاد آنلاین
articles.full_text:
Gold Recovers as Dollar and Bond Yields Retreat; Markets Await US Inflation Test
EghtesadOnline :Global markets reversed part of Monday’s moves ahead of Wednesday’s US inflation report. Oil prices fell on expectations of increased Russian diesel supplies and Saudi Arabia’s pipeline expansion, while investors turned their attention to bank earnings, inflation and the outlook for monetary policy.
Spot gold rose approximately 0.24% from the previous close to around $4,181.60 per ounce. The weaker dollar, lower oil prices and declining bond yields supported gold. Lower bond yields reduce the opportunity cost of holding gold, making the precious metal more attractive to investors.
However, inflation figures above expectations could revive the possibility of interest-rate increases and weaken this support.
Oil: Expectations of Higher Supply Counter Risks to Exports
Oil prices retreated after Monday’s surge. Reuters and The Wall Street Journal identified the prospect of increased Russian diesel supplies as a factor easing concerns about fuel shortages. However, damage to Russian refineries has cast doubt on whether those additional supplies can materialize as promised.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has announced plans to increase the export capacity of its pipeline network. Temporarily converting a gas pipeline could increase oil transportation capacity by 1.2 million barrels per day within seven to eight weeks. The plan matters for the outlook for exports, but the additional capacity has not yet translated into actual oil supplies reaching the market and has so far had only a temporary effect on prices.
The Dollar and Foreign Exchange Markets
The US Dollar Index fell approximately 0.24% on Tuesday to 102.33, retreating from the 18-month high it reached on Monday. Safe-haven demand and concerns about the Middle East had supported the dollar’s gains on Monday. Lower oil prices and renewed attention to the interest-rate outlook shifted its direction on Tuesday.
The euro rose approximately 0.24% to $1.11818, although concerns over France’s debt and budget outlook continue to weigh on its prospects.
In its analysis published on Tuesday, ING said markets had almost fully priced in a European Central Bank rate hike in December, leaving limited room for further support for the euro from that prospect.
The bank lowered its EUR/USD forecast for the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027 to 1.13. It also continued to identify a possible test of the 1.11 level in the short term.
ING also expects EUR/GBP to trade within a range of 0.84 to 0.85 over the coming months. France’s difficulties and the possibility of further UK interest-rate increases are factors supporting the pound.
However, the bank considers market expectations for the scale of rate increases in 2027 to be excessive. The UK budget on October 28 is another risk on the horizon, although ING does not currently expect it to have a lasting negative effect on the pound.
Japan: October Rate Hike Pause Becomes More Likely
According to Bloomberg, Bank of Japan officials are reluctant to raise interest rates at two consecutive meetings and are therefore likely to pause at their October 30 meeting.
Policymakers want to assess the effects of September’s rate increase before making another move. A further increase in December remains possible, however, and the final decision has not yet been made.
Concerns Over US Equities
US cash markets had not yet opened on Tuesday. On Monday, the S&P 500 closed down 0.06% at 7,807.24, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.44% to 27,245.90.
Reports of progress by Chinese company CXMT have heightened concerns about competition and pressure on the profits of US chipmakers. Selling pressure has also spread to Asian markets, as investors worry that heavy investment in artificial intelligence may fail to generate sufficient returns in an environment of elevated interest rates.
Treasury Yields and the Federal Reserve
The US Treasury market has followed two different paths over the past week. Between October 6 and October 13, the yield on one-month Treasury bills rose from 3.943% to 4.042%, an increase of 9.9 basis points. Yields on three-month, six-month and one-year securities also increased by 3.9, 4.4 and 2.1 basis points, respectively.
From the two-year maturity onward, however, yields declined. The two-year Treasury yield fell 2.8 basis points to 4.77%, while the three-year yield dropped 3.2 basis points to 4.892%. The declines were greater for five-year and seven-year Treasuries, at 5.8 and 7.2 basis points, respectively.
The largest pullbacks occurred in longer-dated bonds. The 10-year Treasury yield fell 9.2 basis points to 5.194%, the 20-year yield declined 10 basis points to 5.602%, and the 30-year yield dropped 10.3 basis points to 5.558%.
As a result, the spread between the 10-year and two-year Treasury yields narrowed from 48.8 to 42.4 basis points, indicating a flattening of the yield curve.
In Tuesday’s trading, The Wall Street Journal identified lower oil prices and declines in AI-related stocks as factors boosting demand for Treasuries and pushing yields down.
Reuters, citing Saxo Bank, reported that elevated yields in recent weeks had attracted buyers back into the bond market. However, persistent inflation, high oil prices and heavy government borrowing continue to stand in the way of a sustained recovery.
Wednesday’s inflation report will be an important test of whether the decline in yields can continue.
FedWatch puts the probability of the Federal Reserve holding rates steady at its October 28 meeting at 80.6%, compared with a 19.4% probability of a rate increase. The probability of a hike is 1.6 percentage points lower than on Monday.
What Are Markets Waiting For?
Earnings reports from major banks on Tuesday and the US Consumer Price Index (CPI) report on Wednesday are the most important tests ahead.
On Thursday, markets will receive the Producer Price Index (PPI), retail sales figures and oil inventory data. On Friday, remarks by Kevin Warsh could provide further clarity on how investors interpret the outlook for monetary policy.

articles.title: US inflation rises before midterm elections, fuelling rate hike fears - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: US inflation rises before midterm elections, fuelling rate hike fears  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
United States consumer prices jumped in September in the final inflation report before the midterm elections, increasing chances of an interest rate hike later this month.
Annual inflation accelerated to 3.7 percent, up from 3.4 percent in August. On a monthly basis, prices rose by 0.6 percent, according to the Consumer Price Index report released by the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Wednesday.
Petrol prices led the surge as tensions between the US and Iran, as well as Russia and Ukraine, weighed on global energy prices. Petrol prices rose 9.1 percent in September, accounting for more than half of the CPI monthly increase, according to the BLS. They were up 34.2 percent from the same time a year ago.
“The directionless war in Iran continues to disrupt global supply chains, driving up the prices of food and fuel,” Kyle Moore, chief economist at The Century Foundation, an economic think tank, said in a statement provided to Al Jazeera.
Petrol prices have continued to climb. The average price for a gallon of petrol is $4.33 ($1.14 per litre), compared with $4.31 a month ago, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. Diesel prices are higher, at $6.29 per gallon (1.66 per litre), compared with $6.23 a month ago.
In a post on X, Patrick DeHaan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, said, “2026 has now seen more days with average gas prices over $4/gal than any year before: 158 days.”
Shelter costs also jumped 0.4 percent from the previous month, following a 0.3 percent increase in August. Food costs were a bright spot in the report, remaining unchanged overall.
Food away from home, including restaurant meals, rose 0.2 percent, but that increase was offset by a 0.1 percent decline in food-at-home prices, which track grocery costs.
At the grocery store, poultry prices jumped 0.7 percent, fruit and vegetable prices rose 0.5 percent, and juice prices increased 1.1 percent. However, milk prices dropped 2.1 percent and beef prices fell 0.9 percent.
Amid heavy investment in AI infrastructure, prices for computer software and accessories have jumped 28 percent from the same time last year.
“The AI boom is playing a huge part, and we have all read about the hundreds of billions being poured into data centers, AI firms, and models,” Rami Cassis, principal of Parabellum Investment, said in comments provided to Al Jazeera.
Fed pressures
The inflation data comes days before the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision later this month. Last month, the US central bank raised rates by 25 basis points, bringing the target range to 3.75–4.00 percent, the first hike in three years.
Economists are divided over whether the Fed will raise rates again or hold them steady. According to CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, there is a 52.9 percent chance that rates will remain in the 3.75–4.00 percent range, while a 47.1 percent chance of a quarter of a percentage point hike that would bring them to 4.00–4.25 percent.
The inflation data puts pressure on Republicans before the midterm elections on November 3. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that about 78 percent of Americans blamed US President Donald Trump’s policies for price increases.
US markets trended downward following the inflation report. The Nasdaq fell 0.8 percent and the S&P 500 dropped 0.6 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was roughly flat in midday trading.

articles.title: Euro Breaks to 1.1135 as 5.278% Treasury Yields and $106 Brent Widen the Gap — 1.1000 Next if 1.1135 Fails - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: Euro Breaks to 1.1135 as 5.278% Treasury Yields and $106 Brent Widen the Gap — 1.1000 Next if 1.1135 Fails  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- EUR/USD dropped 0.55% to 1.1135, its weakest level since May 2025, after US core CPI hit 2.6%.
- The US-German 10-year yield spread widened to 182 basis points as Treasuries rose to 5.278% and Bunds eased to 3.45%.
- A daily close below 1.1135 targets 1.1000, while a reclaim of 1.1250 opens a path to 1.1312.
The euro spent the European morning trying to build a base and lost it inside an hour of the US inflation release. EUR/USD dropped 0.55% to 1.1135, its lowest level since May 2025, and the one-hour chart showed the pair at 1.1139 shortly after, pinned under both its 100-period moving average at 1.1194 and its 200-period average at 1.1209.
The session had started constructively. The pair climbed above 1.1200 in the European morning, and it pushed toward 1.1210 as the dollar retreated and Treasury yields eased ahead of the data. By the time New York walked in, the euro had slipped to 1.1192, down just 0.05% on the day. Then the inflation print landed at 8:30 a.m. ET and the pair fell almost 60 pips in a straight line.
The level matters. Earlier this week, EUR/USD set a 17-month low around 1.1150, with the intraday floor at 1.1152. Wednesday’s slide broke through that low and printed a new one at 1.1135. A break of the weekly low on the day of a major data release is a classic continuation signal, and the pair is now trading 15 pips below the floor that held on Monday and Tuesday.
The thesis for this forecast is straightforward. EUR/USD is being driven by three forces pointing the same way: a widening interest-rate gap after a hot US CPI, an energy shock that damages the eurozone’s terms of trade far more than America’s, and fiscal stress in France that adds a risk premium to euro assets. The ECB is hiking too, but from a lower base and into a weaker economy. Until one of those three forces turns, rallies in the euro are corrections inside a downtrend.
The trend has been running since January. At the end of that month, the euro hit a 4½-year high above $1.20. From that level to 1.1135, the single currency has lost more than 7% against the dollar. The decline accelerated through the summer as the Fed moved toward hikes and oil climbed, and it extended in October as French borrowing costs jumped.
There is a counterpoint. Before the release, the dollar rally looked stretched, EUR/USD appeared oversold, and bearish momentum was fading. Some of the hot inflation was arguably priced in. That setup is why the pair recovered toward 1.1210 earlier in the session. The CPI details were strong enough to override the oversold condition. The question now is whether 1.1135 marks a final flush or the start of the next leg toward 1.1100 and 1.1000.
The CPI Print That Flipped the Dollar Pullback
The euro’s European-session bounce rested on one assumption: that US inflation would disappoint or match forecasts and give the stretched dollar an excuse to correct. The Bureau of Labor Statistics delivered the opposite.
Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September, matching the monthly forecast, and the annual rate accelerated to 3.7% from 3.4% in August, above the 3.6% consensus. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% on the month against a 0.2% estimate and climbed to 2.6% year over year from 2.4%, also above the 2.5% forecast. US inflation has now been above the Fed’s 2% target for 67 straight months.
Energy drove the headline: gasoline jumped 9.1% in September and accounted for more than half of the monthly increase, and the broader energy index rose 5.2%. The core surprise came from shelter, up 0.4%, used vehicles, up 0.7%, plus airfares, recreation, education and medical services. Shelter alone added 0.15 percentage point to core.
For currency markets, the core number is what moved prices. A headline surprise driven by gasoline can be dismissed as a supply shock the Fed will look through. A core surprise forces a policy response. The rate market reacted at once. The probability of a 25-basis-point Fed hike in October jumped to 47% from 22% the day before, according to one measure of futures pricing. Other readings of fed funds futures still showed 78% odds of a hold, while one prediction market moved the October hike probability to 55% from 21%. Across every measure, the direction was the same: more Fed tightening priced in.
That repricing hit the euro through the most direct channel in FX: relative yields. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped more than 6 basis points to 5.278%. Higher US yields make dollar-denominated assets more attractive and pull capital out of lower-yielding currencies. The euro, with its larger yield discount to the dollar and its exposure to energy, took the hit.
Before the data, the risk being flagged across European trading desks was that US CPI would accelerate on both headline and core, sparking higher yields and a firmer dollar and pushing the euro below this week’s low at 1.1152. That is precisely what happened. The scenario some euro bulls had treated as a tail risk turned into the base case in one release.
The Yield Gap: 5.278% Against 3.45% Is a 182-Basis-Point Wall
The core driver of EUR/USD is the spread between what investors earn in dollars and what they earn in euros. That spread widened sharply on Wednesday.
The 10-year Treasury yield climbed more than 6 basis points to 5.278% after the CPI release. Germany’s 10-year Bund yield, the eurozone’s benchmark, eased to 3.45% on the same day, its lowest since September 9, as German bonds drew safe-haven demand during a global equity selloff. That puts the US-German 10-year spread at 182 basis points.
The direction of travel is as important as the level. In early October, Bunds were yielding near 3.5% and the 10-year Treasury was moving toward its October 7 high of 5.364%, the highest since 2002. Since then, Bund yields have drifted lower on safe-haven buying while Treasury yields have bounced back toward that peak. The gap has widened in the dollar’s favor on both sides.
The 2-year sector tells a similar story. Germany’s 2-year yield stood near 3.10% in early October, reflecting expectations for further ECB tightening. US 2-year yields sit well above that level with the Fed’s upper bound at 4% and markets now pricing a higher chance of an October hike. The short-end spread is the purest measure of relative policy expectations, and it moved against the euro on Wednesday.
Rate differentials matter more than ever in this environment because the dollar is also delivering positive real yields. A 10-year Treasury at 5.278% against US core inflation at 2.6% offers a real return of 2.68%. A 10-year Bund at 3.45% against eurozone headline inflation at 3.8% offers a negative real return. A global investor choosing between the two can lock in more than 2.5 percentage points of real yield in Treasuries and lose purchasing power in Bunds. That gap pulls capital toward the dollar steadily, not just on data days.
The spread also explains why the euro has struggled even as the ECB hikes. The ECB has raised rates twice this year, but Bund yields have not kept pace with Treasuries because markets see eurozone growth as weaker and the ECB as more constrained. The Fed is hiking into an economy with 3.7% inflation and still-positive growth. The ECB is hiking into stagflation risk.
For the forecast, the 182-basis-point 10-year spread is the line to watch. A move above 190 basis points, driven by Treasuries breaking 5.364%, would likely push EUR/USD toward 1.1000. A narrowing toward 170 basis points would give the euro room to retest 1.1250.
Fed vs ECB: A 4% Ceiling Against a 2.50% Deposit Rate
Both central banks are hiking. The Fed is doing it from higher ground, and that keeps the policy gap firmly in the dollar’s favor.
The Fed raised its target range by 25 basis points in September to 3.75% to 4%, its first increase since 2023, and 16 of 18 officials projected another hike. The October 27–28 meeting now carries real risk of a second move after Wednesday’s CPI, with futures-implied odds jumping to 47% on one measure. New York Fed President John Williams had said one more hike this year looks appropriate, with no further tightening needed in 2027. Boston Fed President Susan Collins wants another increase before year-end. Even the dovish read points to at least one more Fed hike in 2026.
The ECB has been tightening too. It held its main refinancing rate at 2.15% and its deposit rate at 2% in March, then hiked in June and again in September. The deposit facility rate has stood at 2.50% since September 16, the main refinancing rate at 2.65%, and the marginal lending rate at 2.90%. The ECB said the Middle East war was generating inflation pressures and that energy price inflation, then 10.9%, was broadening throughout the economy.
The arithmetic leaves the Fed’s upper bound 150 basis points above the ECB deposit rate. More important is the real-rate comparison. With US headline CPI at 3.7% and the Fed’s upper bound at 4%, US real policy rates are slightly positive. With eurozone flash inflation at 3.8% in September and the deposit rate at 2.50%, ECB real policy rates are 1.3 percentage points below zero. The Fed is restrictive. The ECB is still accommodative in real terms.
The meeting sequence sharpens the comparison. The Fed decides on October 28, and the ECB announces its decision exactly 24 hours later, on October 29 at 14:15 CET, followed by Lagarde’s press conference at 14:45 CET. The ECB will set policy knowing what the Fed has done. If the Fed hikes and the ECB holds, the policy gap widens to 175 basis points and EUR/USD likely breaks lower. If both hike, the gap is unchanged. If the Fed holds and the ECB hikes, the euro has its best chance of a sustained rebound.

articles.title: Oil Price Forecast — WTI ($95.30) Brent ($106.50) Aramco Strike and Hormuz Attacks Lift Crude — $109.96 Brent Target Above $106.65 - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: Oil Price Forecast — WTI ($95.30) Brent ($106.50) Aramco Strike and Hormuz Attacks Lift Crude — $109.96 Brent Target Above $106.65  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- WTI gained $1.16, or 1.23%, to $95.30 after a Houthi missile struck an Aramco building in Dhahran.
- Saudi crude output jumped more than 2 million barrels a day in September to 8.372 million barrels a day.
- A Brent close above $106.65 targets $109.96, while a break below $102 opens a path to $97.06.
Crude pushed higher on Wednesday as the war premium returned to the tape. West Texas Intermediate traded at $95.30 a barrel by late morning in New York, up $1.16, or 1.23%, after touching $95.41 earlier, a gain of $1.27. Brent, the global benchmark, gained 0.79% to $106.50, holding above $105 through the session after trading as high as $106.58 in early Asian hours.
The move recovered most of Tuesday’s damage. Brent settled at $106.65 on Monday, its highest close since September 15, then lost ground on Tuesday as traders weighed Gulf supply risks against the prospect of more Russian diesel reaching world markets. Overnight, the risk side won. A Houthi missile struck an administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Dhahran, and the UK Maritime Trade Operations center reported two more ships hit near the Strait of Hormuz.
The intraday path was choppy. Brent rose 63 cents to $106.32 by 03:45 GMT, eased toward $105.95 later in Asia, and slipped below $106 in early New York trading before recovering. WTI outperformed through the session, gaining 1.3% as US crude caught a bid on supply worries and a tight domestic inventory picture.
The bigger picture shows a market that has already priced a lot of risk. Brent is down 2.06% over the past month but still 72% higher than a year ago. WTI is down 10.24% over the past month and up 63% year over year. Brent bottomed near $70 in July and climbed to a September high of $109.96. The spread between Brent and WTI stands at $11.20, reflecting how much more exposed seaborne crude is to Gulf disruption than landlocked US barrels.
The thesis for this forecast is direct: crude is a risk-premium market sitting on a growing supply buffer. Every attack in the Gulf adds premium, and every barrel of extra Saudi output, every cut to OPEC’s demand forecast and every hawkish turn at the Fed takes some away. Nothing has yet removed physical barrels from the market. The Dhahran strike hit an office, not a processing plant. Tankers are still moving through Hormuz. That keeps Brent in a range rather than a breakout.
The levels that define the range are clear. Above sits $106.65, Monday’s close, and then $109.96, the September high. Below sits $102, the floor of the October trading range, and then $97.06, the October 6 low. With Brent at $106.50, the market sits at the top of its recent range, where the next headline decides the direction.
Dhahran: An Office Fire, Not a Lost Barrel
The attack that lifted crude overnight was symbolic more than physical, and that distinction explains why Brent rose less than 1%.
Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked an administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Dhahran, causing a limited fire. The Saudi Press Agency reported no injuries. Separate reporting described the building as Aramco’s executive headquarters, though neither Aramco nor Saudi authorities have confirmed which structure was hit.
The broader barrage was wider. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Dhahran and other missiles toward Haradh and Riyadh, where falling fragments injured four people. Explosions were heard over Riyadh on Wednesday morning, and a Saudi military spokesman confirmed a Houthi ballistic missile was intercepted over the capital. The Houthis vowed to keep targeting Saudi Arabia’s international airport and oil infrastructure in the coming days in response to coalition strikes on Sanaa.
The escalation is running in both directions. The coalition struck Houthi fuel storage and loading berths in Sanaa, Hodeidah and Dhamar late on Tuesday, which makes another Houthi response likely. Within one week, the Houthis have now hit Saudi airports and the national oil company’s headquarters. The group’s spokesman had named the Aramco headquarters as a target before the strike, and the attack made good on that threat.
Oil markets price attacks on Saudi Arabia by the barrels at risk. An office fire with no injuries removes none directly. It is unclear whether the incidents could affect production, refining or exports, and no effect on operations has been reported. That is why Brent recovered Tuesday’s losses but did not break Monday’s high.
The risk is in the next target. The Houthis have shown they can reach Dhahran, the heart of Aramco’s operations. The Abqaiq processing complex, the Ras Tanura export terminal and the East-West pipeline all sit within the same broad region. A successful hit on any of those would be a fundamentally different event, putting millions of barrels a day at risk. The 2019 strike on Abqaiq briefly knocked out more than half of Saudi output.
Washington’s posture adds another variable. President Trump has said he is considering joining attacks on the Houthis as the group targets Saudi Arabia and threatens global energy supplies, and the Houthis have threatened US personnel and interests across the region if he does. Direct US involvement would widen the conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran seven and a half months ago. For crude, the Dhahran strike lifted the risk premium. A strike on Saudi energy infrastructure would turn premium into lost supply.
Hormuz: More Strikes, More Mines, and Oil Still Moving
The Strait of Hormuz remains the market’s most important chokepoint, and the attack rate is rising even as crude continues to flow.
UKMTO reported on October 13 that a container ship and a tanker were each struck by an unknown projectile north of the Musandam Peninsula. On Wednesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said a container ship sank south of the strait after striking a naval mine and catching fire. These incidents add to a run of attacks that began on October 10, when an outbound tanker caught fire after a strike on its port side. The Guards also claimed a strike on a third supertanker on October 12, which has not been independently confirmed.
The intent is now explicit. Iranian officials said they were deploying new tactics against shipping in an effort to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, with one official saying the new offensive approach started ten days ago. Iran did not disclose details. US Central Command rejected Iran’s claim that the strait is under Tehran’s control and that any approaching US Navy warships would be sunk.
The physical flow data tells a more measured story. As of late September, crude transiting Hormuz reached a seven-day average of 13.5 million barrels a day, matching the prewar baseline, as US military escorts boosted shipments and pipelines redirected flows. Refined products told a different story. Product shipments through the strait averaged 677,000 barrels a day, compared with 3.6 million before the war. Crude and products combined averaged 14.2 million barrels a day, 80% of the prewar baseline of 17 million.
That split matters for the forecast. Crude supply through Hormuz has recovered. Refined fuel supply has not. The disruption is concentrated in diesel, jet fuel and gasoline, which is why product cracks and pump prices have climbed faster than crude and why September CPI showed gasoline up 9.1%.
The cost of moving oil has exploded. OPEC and non-OPEC ministers said shipping and insurance costs have surged to unprecedented levels, exceeding one-third of the commodity’s value. Those costs act as a tax on every barrel moving out of the Gulf and keep delivered prices elevated even when supply volumes look normal.
Tankers are still transiting. Freight and insurance costs are rising, but there is no measurable loss of crude supply yet. A sustained drop in transit counts would turn today’s risk premium into a supply loss and push Brent through its September high quickly. Until that shows up in the tanker data, the strait is a source of volatility, not of shortage.
The Diesel Squeeze: IEA Warns Constraints Could Run Well Into 2027
The tightest part of the oil market is not crude. It is diesel, and the International Energy Agency’s latest report says that will not end soon.
The IEA’s October Oil Market Report, published Wednesday, warned that constraints on diesel markets could continue well into 2027, with fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia threatening to derail a recovery on the supply side. Its September report estimated that Iran’s near-closure of the strait had cut Gulf diesel exports to a quarter of prewar levels. That shortfall is visible in the product shipment data: 677,000 barrels a day through Hormuz against 3.6 million before the war.
Russia, normally one of the world’s largest diesel exporters, has made the problem worse. Ukrainian drone strikes have forced half of Russia’s top diesel refineries to cut output, and six large refineries produce roughly 50% of Russian diesel. Moscow responded by banning diesel exports by producers until October 31, 2026, extending the restriction on September 30.
Washington is trying to ease the pressure. President Trump said Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel. That announcement pulled crude lower on Tuesday as traders priced additional supply. Kyiv’s relationship with Washington has deteriorated sharply since the sanctions relief and the president’s public turn against President Zelenskiy.
The offset may be smaller than the headlines suggest. Russian refinery capacity has been damaged, the producer export ban remains in place through month-end, and extra Russian diesel is unlikely to ease global fuel prices much. The market is treating Russian supply as sentiment relief more than physical relief.
The US domestic picture is tight but not critical. EIA data for the week end
