articles.summary: US Inflation Preview: Eight Banks Set Out The Dollar And Fed Risks  Exchange Rates UK
articles.full_text:
US Dollar Outlook: Core CPI Tests the Case for an October Fed Pause
Banks expect an energy-led US inflation jump, but softer underlying prices could limit the case for an October Fed hike and further US Dollar gains.
A sharp rise in US headline inflation on Wednesday may still leave the Federal Reserve with room to pause this month, as eight banks' forecasts point to a much smaller increase in prices excluding food and energy.
The distinction could determine whether the US Dollar gains fresh support from the September consumer price report, due at 13:30 BST on 14 October.
Headline forecasts cluster around a 0.6% monthly increase, while core estimates generally round to 0.2%.
Yet similar inflation forecasts conceal a disagreement over how urgently the Fed should respond, with BofA and Citi taking different views of what a stronger core result would mean for October.
At the time of writing, EUR/USD was around $1.1195, with the Dollar up roughly 1.2% against the Euro this month.
Petrol drives the headline, phone bills help the core
UniCredit's economists write: "We expect energy to have fuelled a 0.6% mom increase in headline CPI, half of which was probably driven by the price of petrol at the pump, which rose by a further 7% mom. The core CPI gauge that excludes food and energy is likely to have been relatively well-behaved, rising by 0.2% mom."
Higher fuel costs can eventually reach other prices through transport and production, making evidence of wider increases more consequential than an anticipated jump at the pump.
Wells Fargo's forecast relies partly on August's unusual phone-bill increase fading:
"Last month's upside surprise stemmed from an outsized increase in wireless telephone services as major providers implemented price hikes. That dynamic is unlikely to be repeated in September and should help core services inflation ease back toward a 0.2% monthly gain after rising 0.3% previously."
That would represent relief from a specific price adjustment, rather than proof that every source of inflation has weakened.
Deutsche Bank's 0.16% core forecast is below the 0.24% expected by both Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, although all three round to 0.2%.
Morgan Stanley sees pockets of pressure from the artificial-intelligence boom: "We forecast still positive core goods inflation, driven by higher vehicle prices and ongoing, albeit modest, pressure from AI-related demand."
UniCredit sees a more persistent concern in services outside housing: "Housing inflation is likely to remain on a downward trajectory, following with a lag the deceleration in market rents, while the stickiness in core services (ex. housing) will probably remain the main source of concern for the Fed."
A pause would leave further tightening possible
Deutsche Bank's economists write: "Recent Fedspeak, including from Vice Chair Jefferson, NY Fed President Williams, and Governor Waller has sent a relatively consistent message: while additional tightening is likely to be needed, the timing around rate hikes is flexible and not urgent. This communication has set up a strong base case for skipping October and raising rates again in December, consistent with our expectations."
That distinction between delaying an increase and ending the cycle also underpinned Exchange Rates UK's earlier assessment of the Dollar and gold ahead of CPI.
Crédit Agricole also expects a pause rather than an end to tightening, citing downward revisions to PCE inflation and softer September jobs data.
"We still expect additional tightening of 50bp, but only at a gradual, every-other-meeting cadence that in the near-term involves a skip in October followed by another hike in December, and do not think a CPI report in line with expectations would change this."
PCE is the separate inflation measure the Fed targets, so Wednesday's CPI figures will also be assessed for what they imply about that later release.
Since these forecasts were published, Boston Fed president Susan Collins has reiterated support for further tightening before year-end, conditional on incoming data.
She will watch whether price pressures remain concentrated in energy and AI-related categories or spread more widely.
For the Dollar, a core surprise that brings tightening forward could lift US yields and strengthen its interest-rate appeal.
An expected energy-led headline jump offers less new information on that policy path.
BofA's standing forecast includes an October increase.
It writes: "However, risks are tilted modestly to the upside from airfares, wireless service pricing, and AI-related demand for electronics. A stronger 0.3% m/m core CPI print would put an Oct hike back in play".
Citi's rates strategists draw a different conclusion: "Our economists expect a 0.18% MoM core CPI print and see the August wireless services spike as a one-off. In our view, even a 0.3% MoM core CPI print would not justify an October hike."
October US inflation FAQs
When is the US CPI release?
September's report is due on 14 October at 13:30 BST, or 08:30 US Eastern time.
What are banks forecasting for US inflation?
Their monthly forecasts centre on roughly 0.6% for headline CPI and 0.2% for core, which excludes food and energy.
Would stronger inflation guarantee a Dollar rise?
No. The surprise relative to expectations and its effect on the expected Fed rate path matter, particularly whether price pressure extends beyond energy.

articles.title: More Fed chairmen are leaning toward another interest rate hike this year. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: More Fed chairmen are leaning toward another interest rate hike this year.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| New York Fed President John Williams. Photo: Federal Reserve Bank of New York | 
 The Fed may not be finished with its interest rate hike cycle yet.
 On October 13, Boston Fed President Susan Collins stated that she currently believes "a slight further interest rate hike before the end of the year is appropriate." However, she stressed that the final decision will depend significantly on the overall upcoming economic data and its impact on the outlook and the risk balance.
 Collins's view suggests that the Fed may not have finished its monetary tightening cycle after the September move. At that time, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) unanimously agreed to raise interest rates by 0.25 percentage points, bringing the federal funds rate range to 3.75-4.00%. The September 16 decision was approved with a 12-0 vote, as the Fed assessed that economic activity continued to grow strongly, while inflation remained high.
 On the same day, New York Fed President John Williams also reaffirmed his view that another interest rate hike this year is appropriate. In an interview with Bloomberg, quoted by Reuters, Williams suggested that the Fed may need to raise interest rates once more in 2026 to continue bringing inflation back to its target.
 According to the President of the New York Fed, there are signs that inflation will fall significantly and move closer to the 2% target in 2027. He said that at present there is no reason to believe that the Fed will need to continue raising interest rates next year, although he left open the possibility that new economic data could change this outlook.
 Collins and Williams' latest statements don't necessarily indicate disagreement on the Fed's next move. Both lean toward the possibility of one more rate hike this year. More noteworthy is how the two officials assess the persistence of price pressures and when the rate hike cycle might end.
 The Fed's September forecast also aligns with the possibility of another interest rate hike. The median forecast among officials for the federal funds rate at the end of 2026 is 4.1%, higher than the 3.75-4.00% range after the September meeting. The median forecast for personal consumption expenditure inflation this year is 3.7%, while core inflation is at 3.4%, both above the 2% target. 
|  | 
| Boston Fed President Susan Collins. Photo: Federal Reserve/Wikimedia Commons | 
 AI, tariffs, and energy make the problem more difficult.
 The Boston Fed president said the U.S. economy and labor market remain relatively strong, allowing the Fed to focus on its mission to bring inflation back to target. However, she noted that three sources of pressure on prices—a wave of infrastructure investment for AI, the impact of tariffs, and rising fuel prices—could complicate efforts to cool inflation. “I expect both overall and core inflation to remain above the Fed’s 2% target in the coming months,” Collins said.
 Investing in AI can support productivity in the long term, but the surge in infrastructure development to support this technology is also creating additional demand in the economy, complicating the process of cooling inflation.
 Tariffs, in turn, put pressure on costs. When import costs increase, businesses must choose between absorbing the increase into profits or passing some of it on to selling prices. The impact on inflation will therefore depend on demand as well as the pricing ability of businesses.
 Meanwhile, energy prices are a more difficult variable to control. Tensions in the Middle East have kept oil prices high, increasing fuel and transportation costs, and the market continues to worry that high energy prices could prolong inflationary pressures.
 These factors make it more difficult to predict when the Fed might end its interest rate hike cycle. While Collins stressed the risks that could prolong the process of reducing inflation, Williams was more optimistic about price trends in the coming year. However, Williams' view still leaves open the possibility that the Fed may need to take further action before the end of 2026.
 The Fed currently has two policy meetings remaining this year, on October 27-28 and December 8-9. The December meeting also includes new economic forecasts from Fed officials. If the US central bank keeps interest rates unchanged at the end of October, December will be the last opportunity to implement another rate hike in 2026.
 The market is currently leaning towards a scenario where the Fed does not act immediately in October. According to CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders now assess a 77% probability that the Fed will keep interest rates unchanged at the October 27-28 meeting, up from 51% a month ago. At the same time, the market is pricing in the possibility of the Fed tightening policy by approximately 75 basis points by the end of 2027. Attention may therefore gradually shift to the December meeting, especially the inflation data released before that time.
 Some large investment funds also do not believe the tightening cycle is over. Dan Ivascyn, chief investment officer of PIMCO – the world's largest bond manager – stated on October 13th that the Fed may raise interest rates one or two more times before the current cycle closes, amid continued high oil prices fueling concerns about inflation.
 “The Fed will likely keep interest rates unchanged for now, and then more likely raise them again later this year,” said Dan Ivascyn, adding, “Our view is that, given the current outlook, the Fed could have one or two more tightening cycles.”

articles.title: The ECB Governing Council signals the possibility of further interest rate hikes. - Moomoo
articles.summary: The ECB Governing Council signals the possibility of further interest rate hikes.  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
On Wednesday, October 14, the euro/dollar exchange rate is hovering around 1.120, remaining in a low‑range trading band. Meanwhile, members of the European Central Bank's Governing Council signaled further rate hikes at the IMF's annual meeting in Bangkok. In September, the Eurozone's HICP inflation rose to 3.8%, with energy prices surging 18.8% year on year, core inflation at 2.5%, and services inflation at 3.2%. The deposit facility rate currently stands at 2.50%, and market pricing suggests the possibility of additional rate increases before year‑end. However, uncertainties related to energy and artificial intelligence keep the policy path data‑dependent.
Policy Signals and Interest Rate Path Observations
Belgian central bank governor Pierre Wunsch stated that the European Central Bank "will very likely need to raise interest rates again." He noted that inflation remains too high and that market expectations have adjusted, no longer factoring in a move in October, but emphasized that the ECB's decisions remain data-dependent and that no specific timing is ruled out. Governing Council members unanimously stressed that two rate hikes have already been implemented this year; if another increase is added, the deposit facility rate would rise to 2.75%, a level deemed to begin exerting restrictive effects on economic activity. On the same day, ECB President Lagarde pointed out that inflation driven by high energy prices has yet to spread to the broader economy and that, for now, there are no signs of second-round effects, though indirect impacts and indicators such as wages must be closely monitored. French central bank governor Villeroy de Galhau added that rising yields have already put pressure on financial conditions, potentially partially offsetting the impact of policy tightening, while noting that medium-term inflation expectations remain well anchored and that the reaction function has been understood by the market.
This statement relegates the timing of a rate hike—whether in October or December—to a secondary consideration, with the key emphasis on affirming the need for further action. Economists broadly expect the final move to occur in December, consistent with Wunsch's assessment that "market pricing points to the need for additional policy steps, which is a reasonable baseline scenario." Uncertainty surrounding energy‑related developments and AI has been explicitly cited as a reason not to place bets on a specific outcome, underscoring that policy decisions remain firmly anchored to incoming data rather than pre‑set paths.
Inflation Composition and Characteristics of Energy Pressures
In September, the euro area's HICP rose to 3.8% from 3.2% in August, with energy making the largest contribution, as its year-on-year rate jumped from 14.3% to 18.8%. Service-sector inflation edged up to 3.2%, while food, alcohol, and tobacco increased by 1.4% and non-energy industrial goods by 1.1%. Core inflation—excluding energy and food—remained steady at 2.5%, indicating that price pressures are currently concentrated in the energy sector and that broad second-round effects have yet to materialize. Governing Council members have repeatedly stressed that there is no evidence of a significant spread in wage growth or firms' pricing behavior, and medium-term inflation expectations among businesses and households remain anchored near the target.
Energy prices driven by Middle East conflicts are the main external driver, but growth has proven resilient to this shock. Lagarde warned that rising yields could weigh on activity more than previously expected; Mullen, meanwhile, argued that higher yields are already helping to achieve part of the policy mandate, potentially leading to a more moderate response to inflationary pressures. Wunsch added that market pressures, to some extent, help enforce fiscal discipline, as higher debt‑service costs underscore the need to reduce deficits—though achieving this politically is no easy task. Policymakers are currently focused on assessing the extent to which spillover effects are transmitted through the economy and on determining whether there are early signs of second‑round effects.
Financial Conditions and the Boundaries of Policy Instruments
French government bond yields have risen sharply recently, with the 10-year yield hovering around 4.8%, tightening financial conditions across the eurozone. This development has prompted market attention to the European Central Bank's crisis‑response tools, including the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), designed in 2022. Wunsch stated that he does not wish to speculate on whether or when the ECB might intervene; the tool exists and can be deployed in response to excessive market volatility, though gray areas remain. Meanwhile, Müller made clear that the ECB is not tasked with addressing individual countries' fiscal issues. At present, the conditions for activating the TPI are considered difficult to meet, as investor reactions stem at least in part from budgetary political gridlock.
Rising yields have become widespread across advanced economies, emerging as a key topic at the Bangkok meeting. The Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund has previously urged policymakers to take urgent action to bring down high levels of debt and budget deficits. Within the euro area, rising yields both raise financing costs and, through financial conditions, damp demand, thereby partially substituting for policy interest rates. This dynamic means that, in assessing the extent of further rate hikes, the European Central Bank must also factor in the tightening effects already embedded in market pricing.
Daily Chart Analysis of the EUR/USD Pair
The daily chart shows that EUR/USD has remained below the Bollinger Bands' middle band at 1.1369, with the upper band at 1.1664 and the lower band at 1.1074. Prices have retraced from their September highs, with the most recent low marked near 1.1151, and the pair is currently trading around 1.120, maintaining an overall downward trend. The MACD indicates a DIFF of -0.0090, a DEA of -0.0084, and a MACD histogram of -0.0011, with the indicator positioned below the zero axis. The price's deviation from the middle band and the MACD's movement in negative territory suggest that recent price momentum remains weak.
Frequently Asked Questions
Question 1: Why does Powell emphasize that "another rate hike may be needed" while declining to specify a precise timing?
A: He explicitly stated that inflation is too high and that market pricing has already taken further action as the baseline scenario. However, given the high degree of uncertainty surrounding energy and AI, he remains committed to a data‑dependent approach, with policy decisions assessed meeting by meeting; the specific timing—October or December—is not the central focus.
Question 2: After Eurozone inflation rose to 3.8%, why do policymakers still emphasize that no second-round effects have emerged?
A: Price pressures are currently concentrated primarily in the energy component (year-on-year 18.8%), with core inflation at 2.5% and services inflation at 3.2%. Medium-term inflation expectations among firms and households remain anchored, and the Monetary Policy Committee has yet to observe any signs of spillover, such as accelerating wage growth; therefore, indirect transmission channels warrant continued monitoring.
Question 3: What are the boundaries between the rise in French yields and the TPI instrument?
A: Rising yields have put pressure on financial conditions, partly due to budgetary politics. The TPI is designed to address unwarranted market volatility rather than fiscal imbalances; current conditions do not meet its criteria, and the instrument remains available as a backstop but does not trigger automatic intervention.

articles.full_text:
October 12, 2026
The gold price has climbed toward the US$4,200 mark ahead of Wednesday's US Consumer Price Index (CPI) release, while silver is consolidating at around US$61. This inflation report could become a key catalyst: The data will determine whether the US Federal Reserve pauses its rate decisions for the time being following its latest rate hike, or whether valuation pressure on non-yielding precious metals persists.
US inflation will determine whether the Fed pauses rate cuts
The September CPI marks the start of an important series of data releases, followed by producer prices and retail sales. Most recently, a weaker US dollar and declining oil prices provided relief to the precious metals markets. Lower crude oil prices are curbing inflationary pressures and reducing the central bank’s need to raise interest rates further - an essential prerequisite for sustained gains in gold and silver prices.
Analyst firm Natixis expects September consumer prices to be in line with consensus estimates and the previous month's rate hike to remain the final move in the current tightening cycle. For investors, this points to three clear response patterns:
Data in line with consensus: Supports the case for a pause in rate hikes, reduces market uncertainty and provides relief, particularly for gold.
Surprise rise in inflation: A high core rate revives speculation about further interest rate moves and weighs particularly on more volatile silver.
Unexpectedly weak data: Further pressure on the US dollar could create upside potential for gold, but also raises economic concerns about industrial silver demand.
US consumer confidence and energy market signal a directional decision
Alongside the CPI, deteriorating consumer sentiment is influencing the markets. US consumer confidence recently fell to 46.3 points, while inflation expectations edged higher. This combination is a double-edged sword: While persistent inflation concerns underscore gold’s appeal as a tangible asset, weaker consumer data support expectations of reduced Fed activity.
For silver, a hybrid precious and industrial metal, falling energy prices provide some relief for processors, but its near-term direction will be determined primarily by inflation signals from Washington on Wednesday.

articles.summary: BOE’s Greene Says UK Growth Upgrade Is Proof Rate Hike Needed  Yahoo Finance UK
articles.full_text:
(Bloomberg) -- Faster-than-expected economic growth in the UK and a resilient jobs market are evidence that the Bank of England isn't doing enough to bear down on inflation, rate-setter Megan Greene said.
Most Read from Bloomberg
- Epic Games Delays Disney Project, Asks Developers to Use More AI
- Ford Killed Its Electric Truck. Then Demand Surged
- Kroger Plans to Slash 37% of Corporate Jobs in Next Three Years
- Meta Says New Muse Model Hits AI Frontier After Aggressive Push
- US Stocks Waver on Slowest Trading Day in 2026: Markets Wrap
Speaking to the Atlantic Council at the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok, the external member of the Monetary Policy Committee said interest rates should be higher than the current level of 3.75% and warned her colleagues against relying on financial markets to do the hard work. She was speaking after the IMF upgraded UK growth this year to 1.3% from 1%.
"The GDP data that we've gotten suggests that we're not that restrictive, that there's not that much slack in the economy," she said. "There's more recently been some labor market data that has also suggested that maybe slack in the labor market has peaked, so the labor market is loose."
Greene, who is one of the more hawkish members of the committee, has been voting for a quarter-point hike to 4% to stave off a wage price spiral for the last few months but has so far been in the minority on the nine-strong MPC.
UK inflation is 3.1% and forecast to reach around 4%, double the 2% target, due to rising energy prices caused by the conflict in Iran. Markets expect the committee to raise rates at the next meeting in November.
Some MPC members have argued that tighter financial conditions and rising borrowing costs for households are bearing down on inflation, but Greene cautioned that taking a hands-off approach was too complacent.
"At some point a central bank has to put its money where its mouth is. If the markets are pricing in a hike and you don't end up hiking then the curve inevitably moves," she said. "I don't believe in this notion a strategy can be to rely on premia to do your work for you. I think the central bank actually needs to develop a strategy," she said.
Greene said she fears that the longer inflation remains above target, the more it will feed through to people's price and wage expectations, causing a longer lasting problem.
"What we've learned over the past couple of supply shocks is that when you have successive bouts of inflation it does change people's behavior," she said. "My worry is that we have had successive supply shocks and we are facing yet another one."

UBS Global Wealth Management expects the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again in December and March 2027 as persistent inflation pressures strengthen expectations that monetary policy will remain restrictive into next year.
The firm forecasts a 25-basis-point increase in December, followed by another quarter-point hike in March 2027. The projections suggest that the central bank may continue raising borrowing costs as it seeks to contain inflation and maintain price stability.
The outlook follows the Federal Reserve’s decision to increase interest rates by 25 basis points in September, marking its first rate hike since 2023. Stronger-than-expected inflation in September has reinforced concerns that price pressures may take longer to ease, potentially requiring policymakers to keep interest rates elevated for an extended period.
UBS economist Andrew Dubinsky said the combination of rising goods prices and persistent inflation in the services sector supports expectations of higher interest rates for longer.
The assessment reflects broader concerns that inflation has remained more persistent than anticipated, complicating efforts by central banks to ease monetary policy. Several central banks have indicated that restrictive financial conditions may need to remain in place as they respond to ongoing price pressures and economic uncertainty.
UBS identified several factors that could influence the Federal Reserve’s decisions in the coming months. These include demand associated with artificial intelligence, supply disruptions linked to tensions in the Middle East and uncertainty surrounding international trade policies.
According to the firm, extending the tightening cycle could help keep inflation expectations anchored while inflation remains close to 3% amid multiple economic shocks.
The Federal Reserve is scheduled to hold its next monetary policy meeting on October 27 and 28. Investors will be watching for signals about the central bank’s future decisions as policymakers assess inflation and other economic indicators.
Market expectations for further interest rate increases have also strengthened following the latest consumer price index report. According to CME FedWatch data, interest rate futures indicate a 27% probability of a rate hike at the October meeting, compared with 21.6% before the inflation figures were released.
The probability of a December rate increase stands at 89.5%, suggesting that investors increasingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise borrowing costs again before the end of the year.
UBS’s forecast points to the possibility of continued monetary tightening into 2027 if inflation remains elevated. However, the Federal Reserve’s actual decisions will depend on incoming economic data and how inflation develops in the coming months.

articles.title: Will the Fed raise interest rates this month? A Kevin Warsh speech could offer clues - NBC News
articles.summary: Will the Fed raise interest rates this month? A Kevin Warsh speech could offer clues  NBC NewsFed’s Warsh to Get Final Word in Bangkok as Inflation Roars Back  Bloomberg.comWarsh Speech, Schwab Earnings: What to Watch the Rest of the Week  WSJWarsh speaks in Bangkok after hot CPI: is a second Fed hike coming in October?  investingLiveFed chair to join IMF’s “Managing Director’s Fireside Chat with Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh” in Bangkok at 10.30am ...
articles.full_text:
When Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh strides onstage in Bangkok on Friday morning, it will be after 11 p.m. on Thursday in New York. But investors, economists and politicians in the United States will be awake and hanging on his every word.
Any speech by a Fed chair is closely scrutinized. This week’s talk has an extra dose of urgency, though, after two government reports showed inflation heating up for consumers and businesses — spurring speculation about how soon the Fed will raise interest rates to handle soaring prices.
Warsh will be speaking at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, where he will be interviewed by IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. The Fed chairman has repeatedly said he will not use public speaking engagements to intentionally steer the expectations of investors and markets, but his comments could nevertheless signal whether the central bank will hike rates before, or after, the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
It will also be the last speech from a Fed official before policymakers enter a “blackout” period on Saturday that lasts through their next interest rate meeting, which is scheduled for Oct. 27 and 28.
“Broad based” inflation “strengthens the case for an October hike,” Bank of America analysts wrote on Wednesday. “The data continue to underscore two key sources of inflation pressure: AI and Iran.”
Those two factors aren’t likely to be going anywhere soon, either.
The price of politics
Already hammered by soaring interest rates, rising energy prices and stagnant wage growth, American consumers could get an extra dose of financial strain if the Fed raises rates again this month.
Voters are already dissatisfied with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, polls show, so another rate hike could add to Republicans’ headaches as they face potentially losing their congressional majorities in the midterms.
In recent weeks, Trump has tried to pull multiple policy levers to lower gas and diesel prices, which have pushed inflation higher in recent months. But none of them have yet slowed prices meaningfully.
“Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again,” Trump said on the campaign trail in 2024. Inflation as measured by the consumer price index declined to as low as 2.3% four months into Trump’s term.
But that same month, Trump unleashed a wave of tariffs across the globe, dramatically changing the economic story.
By September, inflation breached the 3% threshold again. In February, Trump launched the war against Iran, causing one of the worst energy supply shocks in history. Inflation jumped as high as 4.1% in May, and looks to be headed back in that direction again.
Another Fed rate hike would also further undermine Trump’s yearslong pressure campaign to push the central bank to cut rates. Since Warsh took his post in May, the central bank has either held rates steady or increased them.
Trump hasn’t attacked Warsh after years of hammering former Chair Jerome Powell. But the president has started saying that the other members of the Fed’s board are “very hostile.”
“I’m relying on Kevin,” Trump told reporters in September, “but he’s got, you know, a very tough board. He’s got a board that was put there by a lot of other people, and the interest rates are too high.”
“They’re very political,” Trump said. Four of the Fed’s seven board members were appointed by Trump.
Asked what the president’s expectations are for Warsh’s appearance, the White House pointed to a Truth Social post from September in which Trump had written, “Interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less.”
Diesel and the damage done
Economists and investors are paying close attention to so-called core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices. Both reports this week showed that even this adjusted measure of price growth is running hotter than hoped for.
“Core CPI was the more significant surprise,” wrote analysts at Bank of America.
The core readings showed that skyrocketing fuel prices, particularly diesel, are trickling down. Farmers, truckers and others who keep commerce humming in the United States have to raise their prices in order to digest higher diesel costs. That, in turn, leads to price increases for consumer goods.
“The cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk told NBC News in an August interview. “Everything from … running a farm … cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped gets that extra fee tacked onto it.” At the time, she described the surge in diesel fuel prices as likely “an inflationary problem for the next several months.”
Her warning came to fruition in September, according to the consumer price index and producer price index reports this week. With diesel prices remaining solidly above $6 per gallon so far in October, and with no sign that the Iran war is near an end or that attacks on energy assets in the Ukraine-Russia war will be paused, it could keep fueling overall inflation for months.
Big Tech is also fueling inflation. Trillion-dollar companies are spending, and borrowing, big sums for servers, memory and other components that will be used in data centers. That’s caused price spikes across the economy.
Companies including Apple and Nintendo have raised prices as a result. “We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly,” Apple told NBC News in June.
Companies are also tapping the public debt markets in an unprecedented way. Data center companies and associated utility firms, chipmakers and cloud providers are expected to raise between $300 billion and $570 billion from the debt market this year, according to Vanguard. Those firms are also offering highly attractive interest rates, sometimes better than U.S. Treasury bonds.
A consequence of that, Warsh noted recently, is that there’s a “competition for capital” driving up interest rates on government debt, too.
“This is a complicated set of things that are affecting the most important asset anywhere in the world, the 10-year Treasury,” Warsh said. “It’s the risk-free asset upon which every price of virtually every asset in the world is related to.”
Without referencing the Iran war, he also said yields were being driven by “geopolitics” and the strength of the economy.

articles.title: USD/JPY Price Forecast — USD/JPY (158.87) Hot CPI Breaks the 200-Day as BoJ Pause Bets Grow — 160 Target - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: USD/JPY Price Forecast — USD/JPY (158.87) Hot CPI Breaks the 200-Day as BoJ Pause Bets Grow — 160 Target  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Dollar Clears the 200-Day at 158.87 as a 218-Basis-Point Yield Gap Meets a BoJ Pause — 160 Is the Line Tokyo Defends
Japan bought ¥11.74 trillion of yen in spring and joined the US in a July intervention at a 40-year low | That's TradingNEWS
Key Points
- USD/JPY rose 0.36% to 158.87 after US core CPI held at 0.3% month on month against a 0.2% forecast.
- Markets price a 45% chance of an October Fed hike, up from 20% before the CPI release.
- A hold above 158.50 targets 159.00 to 160.00, while a close below it opens 157.00 and 155.00.
The dollar spent the Asian and European sessions boxed in against the yen and broke out the moment US inflation landed. USD/JPY rose to 158.51 during the Tokyo morning before pulling back to 158.11, then hovered near 158.48 into the New York open, up 0.09% on the day. After the September CPI release, the pair pushed through that range and traded at 158.87, up 0.36%.
That move carries more weight than its size suggests. USD/JPY has broken above its 200-day moving average after the hotter-than-expected US inflation report revived bets on further Federal Reserve hikes. The pair had spent several sessions coiling just beneath that average ahead of the data, and the CPI print supplied the catalyst, lifting Treasury yields and the dollar together.
The setup had been building for weeks. USD/JPY extended its recovery from a 152.90 low to a peak of 158.75 before stalling. On Tuesday, the pair bounced modestly from the 157.85 to 157.80 region, the weekly low, after Japanese markets reopened from a long holiday weekend. Wednesday’s break above 158.51 and 158.75 takes out the top of that range.
The yen’s broader trend is weak. Over the past month, the Japanese currency has lost 2.18% against the dollar, and it is down 4.92% over twelve months. That decline has come despite the Bank of Japan raising its policy rate twice since June, to 1.25%, the highest level in 31 years.
The thesis for this forecast is direct: everything pushing USD/JPY higher got stronger on Wednesday, and the only thing holding it back is Tokyo. US inflation re-accelerated to 3.7%, the 10-year Treasury yield rose above 5.25%, and futures priced a higher chance of another Fed hike on October 28. At the same time, Bank of Japan officials are leaning against a second straight hike on October 30, Brent crude near $106 is draining Japan’s trade balance, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s fiscal expansion is pushing up Japanese bond yields for the wrong reasons. The fundamental path points to 160.
That is exactly where the problem begins. 160.00 is a psychologically important level and the zone where Japanese authorities may step in again. Japan bought ¥11.74 trillion of yen between April 28 and May 27, and in July, Tokyo and Washington carried out their first-ever joint intervention after the yen hit its weakest level since 1986. Traders know that history, and it caps how aggressively they chase the pair.
The levels are defined. Support sits in the 158.50 to 158.75 breakout zone, then 158.11 and 157.80. Resistance stands at 159.00, then the 160.00 intervention line. A failed breakout below 158.50 would carry real weight and could send the pair toward 157.00 or even 155.00.
The CPI Print and the Fed Repricing: 45% for October, 85% for December
The yen’s slide on Wednesday was a dollar story first, and the inflation data explains why.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that consumer prices rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% year over year, up from 3.4% in August and above the 3.6% consensus. Core CPI rose 2.6% year over year, above the 2.5% forecast, while monthly core inflation held at 0.3% instead of easing to the expected 0.2%. Gasoline surged 9.1%, but price increases in recreation, used cars, education, airfares, medical care and apparel point to pressure that is broader and potentially stickier than a pure energy shock.
Rate expectations shifted sharply. Markets now see around a 45% chance of an October Fed hike, up from 20% before the data, and roughly 85% for December, with at least three 25-basis-point hikes priced over the next 12 months. That path is more aggressive than anything the Fed has signaled. New York Fed President John Williams expects only one more hike this year and none in 2027.
The Fed’s current setting adds weight to the repricing. The central bank raised its target range to 3.75% to 4% in September, its first hike since 2023, and 16 of 18 officials projected another increase. An October hike would lift the upper bound to 4.25%, widening the policy gap with Japan by another 25 basis points.
Treasury yields moved immediately. The 10-year yield rose 4 basis points to 5.25% on one measure and more than 6 basis points to 5.278% on another, putting it within 9 basis points of the October 7 high of 5.364%, the highest since 2002. Higher US yields make dollar assets more attractive relative to yen assets, and the yen once again bore the brunt.
USD/JPY is especially sensitive to US yields because the yen is a funding currency. Investors borrow in yen at low rates to buy higher-yielding assets abroad, a trade known as the carry trade. When US yields rise, the reward for that trade grows, and more capital flows out of yen.
The calendar matters. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks on Friday, and several other Fed officials have until Saturday’s quiet period to signal their views. Warsh surprised with a hawkish-leaning speech at Jackson Hole in August that triggered a broad dollar short squeeze. A repeat on Friday would push USD/JPY toward 160.
For the forecast, the Fed is now the dominant driver of USD/JPY. A market pricing three more hikes against a Fed signaling one leaves room for disappointment. But until Fed officials push back, the rate path favors the dollar.
The Yield Gap: 5.278% Treasuries Against 3.1% JGBs
The spread between US and Japanese government bond yields is the single most important structural driver of USD/JPY, and it remains wide.
The 10-year Treasury yield stands at 5.278% after Wednesday’s jump. Japan’s 10-year government bond yield traded near 3.1% in early October, after reaching 3.115% on September 25, the highest level since August 1996. That leaves a gap of roughly 218 basis points in favor of the dollar at the 10-year point.
The shorter end tells a similar story. Japan’s two-year yield fell to 1.93% at the end of September, while the Fed’s policy rate already sits at 3.75% to 4%. The policy gap between the Fed’s upper bound and the BoJ’s 1.25% rate stands at 275 basis points. Even after two BoJ hikes this year, that gap remains among the widest in the developed world.
The direction of the gap matters as much as its level. Japanese yields have risen sharply over the past year. When Takaichi took office last October, the 10-year yield stood at 1.6%. It has nearly doubled since. In theory, rising Japanese yields should narrow the gap and support the yen. In practice, US yields have risen almost as fast, keeping the differential wide.
The source of the Japanese yield rise also matters. Yields have climbed on expectations of further BoJ hikes, concerns about US tightening and market wariness toward the Takaichi government’s aggressive fiscal expansion. Part of the rise reflects a fiscal risk premium rather than a hawkish central bank. Yields rising on fiscal worries tend to weaken a currency, not strengthen it.
The carry trade depends on this gap. As long as US yields exceed Japanese yields by 200 basis points or more, investors earn a substantial return for borrowing yen and holding dollars. That return outweighs the risk of modest yen appreciation and keeps steady selling pressure on the Japanese currency.
The gap can narrow in two ways. US yields could fall if inflation eases or the Fed signals a pause. Japanese yields could rise if the BoJ accelerates its hiking pace. Neither looks likely before the end of October. The Fed is moving hawkish, and the BoJ is signaling a pause.
For the forecast, the yield gap supports a higher USD/JPY. A widening above 220 basis points, driven by Treasuries breaking 5.364%, would push the pair toward 160. A narrowing toward 200 basis points would take it back toward 157.
The Bank of Japan: 1.25%, the Fastest Tightening Since 1990, and an October Pause
The Bank of Japan has been hiking aggressively by its own standards, yet the yen keeps falling, and the October meeting is unlikely to change that.
The BoJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% on September 18 by a 7-2 vote and said it would keep raising if its outlook holds. That followed a June 16 hike from 0.75% to 1.00% by a 7-1 vote. The two increases mark the fastest tightening cycle at the BoJ since 1990, and the September move took the benchmark rate to its highest level in 31 years. Governor Kazuo Ueda said the bank had entered a new phase, shifting its focus from pushing inflation toward 2% to preventing it from overshooting that target.
The BoJ has kept the door open. Ueda said in an October 6 speech that the bank intends to continue raising its policy rate and adjusting monetary accommodation in response to developments in economic activity, prices and financial conditions. Deputy Governor Ryozo Uchida said AI is a positive demand shock adding upward pressure on activity and prices. Real wages rose 1.5% year over year in August, an eighth straight monthly gain, reinforcing the case for further tightening.
But October is likely a pause. BoJ officials are leaning toward holding rates steady at the October 30 meeting, avoiding a rare second consecutive hike, though a December increase remains on the table. Futures priced a 26% chance of an October hike in early October, and that pricing was roughly halved after the release of the September meeting summary. December move odds sit near 90%, and futures price the policy rate at 2.02% by September 2027.
The September summary of opinions included the view that there was no need to rush. Analysts read the bank as moving every three months, which means the next hike

USOIL: OPEC Supply Recovery Meets Tight U.S. Inventories
U.S. crude fundamentals are being pulled in opposite directions. The most recent OPEC report shows OPEC+ production in September at 39.07 million bpd, up 900,000 bpd from August, led by increased production by Saudi Arabia. Production in Russia, meanwhile, fell 38,000 bpd in September amid continued Ukrainian attacks on the country’s energy infrastructure. OPEC also revised its 2026 oil-demand growth estimate down to 180,000 bpd, while forecasting 2.55 million bpd of growth in 2027.
In its latest report, the EIA reported a tight balance for U.S. crude. For the week ending October 2, crude oil inventories fell 3.2 million barrels to 424.1 million barrels, with exports rising to 4.77 million bpd, and with refinery utilization rising to 92.7%.
UKOil: Hormuz Attacks Keep Shipping Risk Elevated
Brent’s main risk premium is still on the Strait of Hormuz. Vessels were hit by unknown projectiles on Tuesday. Meanwhile, Iranian officials told Reuters that Iran has changed its tactics against vessels it considers in violation of Iran’s restrictions. OPEC and non-OPEC ministers have said that shipping and insurance costs of some energy routes have climbed to more than one-third of the underlying commodity’s value, making logistics a significant constraint as Gulf production recovers.
Natural Gas: Storage Cushion Grows, but LNG Demand Expands
U.S. natural gas stocks are still comfortably padded. EIA data showed that working gas inventories were at 3,500 Bcf as of October 2, after an 85 Bcf weekly injection. Inventories are 2% above the five-year average.
Elsewhere, global LNG is still relatively tight, with around 17% of Qatar’s LNG export capacity lost to damage. Separately, President Donald Trump said Taiwan has agreed to buy 30% of the proposed Alaska LNG project’s output, although the terms were not immediately clear. The project is designed to export up to 20 million tonnes per year.

articles.title: Oil prices diverge as Brent falls below $106, WTI rises; OPEC Basket jumps 4.14% - Gulf News
articles.summary: Oil prices diverge as Brent falls below $106, WTI rises; OPEC Basket jumps 4.14%  Gulf News
articles.full_text:
Oil benchmarks show mixed trends with OPEC Basket leading gains
Global oil benchmarks moved in different directions early Wednesday, with US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rising while Brent and Abu Dhabi's Murban crude declined, according to market quotes at 7:31 a.m. Tokyo time.
WTI crude futures rose 63 cents, or 0.67%, to $94.77 a barrel. Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell 96 cents, or 0.9%, to $105.69 a barrel.
Murban crude, a key benchmark for Abu Dhabi oil, dropped $1.67, or 1.49%, to $110.57 a barrel.
The OPEC Basket recorded the strongest percentage gain among the listed benchmarks, rising $4.53, or 4.14%, to $114.03 a barrel.
The divergence suggests a mixed session across crude markets rather than a uniform move in global oil prices. The figures represent a snapshot of market quotes, and differences in benchmark pricing periods and update schedules may affect comparisons.
Oil traders are weighing competing forces: continued risks to Middle East supply routes, the prospect of additional Russian diesel supplies and concerns about global demand.
Reuters reported on October 13 that Brent settled 0.9% lower at $105.69 a barrel, while WTI rose to $94.14. The market was balancing regional security risks against the possibility of additional fuel supplies from Russia.
Shipping costs are another concern. OPEC and non-OPEC producers warned on October 12 that shipping and insurance costs for energy flows had surged to more than one-third of commodity value in some cases, adding to inflationary pressures.
OPEC's October report also showed that combined OPEC+ oil production increased by about 900,000 barrels per day in September, reaching 39.07 million bpd.
Yet higher production does not automatically resolve supply disruptions when shipping routes, insurance and delivery costs remain uncertain.

articles.title: PPI Surge Complicates Fed’s Inflation Fight, Says Apollo Chief Economist: ‘This Is The Definition Of Stagflation’ - TradingView
articles.summary: PPI Surge Complicates Fed’s Inflation Fight, Says Apollo Chief Economist: ‘This Is The Definition Of Stagflation’  TradingView
articles.full_text:
- Slok described the combination of rising prices and consumers buying less as a definition of stagflation.
- The economist pointed to pressure on interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as housing and autos.
- He expects some moderation in data center construction as expectations for AI-related earnings and revenue payoffs adjust, but said he does not expect a recession.
Apollo Global Management (APO) Chief Economist Torsten Slok stated that the Federal Reserve faces a difficult policy choice as producer prices accelerate and consumers begin pulling back on spending, raising the risk of an uncomfortable mix of persistent inflation and slowing economic growth.
“This is a definition of stagflation,” Slok said during a CNBC interview. “We have higher prices, and in response to higher prices, we buy less.”
His comments came after U.S. producer price inflation accelerated sharply in August, defying expectations for a decline. The annual producer price index (PPI) rose to 6.3%, its second-highest level in four years, higher than the expected 5.5%.
PPI Inflation Runs Hot
Monthly headline PPI climbed 1.3%, more than double the 0.6% increase economists had expected. Core PPI also exceeded expectations, with the monthly reading coming in at 0.7% against an estimate of 0.3%.
U.S. equities traded lower ahead of the PPI data release. After markets opened, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were on track to hit their worst week since June. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) was down 0.4%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) dropped 1.3%. Meanwhile, SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) stayed in the green, with gains of around 0.44%.
SPY and QQQ were among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. Retail sentiment around QQQ shifted to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ territory over the past day, while chatter increased to’high’ from ‘normal’ levels.
Fed Faces Inflation-Growth Trade-Off
According to Slok, the hotter inflation reading complicates the Fed’s efforts to balance price stability against the risk of slowing growth. Slok said policymakers must decide whether to prioritize rising inflation or signs that consumers are beginning to rein in spending.
“The challenge for the Fed is: Should they be focusing on inflation going up, or should they be focusing on the slowdown in consumers’ money and the risk of GDP growth?” he said.
Slok pointed to housing and autos as early examples of interest-rate-sensitive sectors responding to tighter financial conditions. Mortgage rates have climbed substantially from their pandemic-era lows, while financing and leasing a car have become more expensive.
“The more interest rate-sensitive parts of the economy are beginning to respond,” Slok said. “We’re seeing that in housing. We’re seeing that in autos.” He added that consumers are also showing early signs of adjusting their spending as higher prices squeeze household budgets.
AI Spending Poses A Risk To GDP Growth
Slok also warned that the U.S. economy has become increasingly dependent on AI investment, leaving growth vulnerable if companies slow spending on data centers and related infrastructure.
“GDP growth is normally two [percent], and now roughly one percentage point of GDP is coming from the AI spending boom,” he said.
A slowdown in the build-out could weigh on economic growth even without triggering a recession. The key question, Slok said, is whether the financial returns from AI investment arrive as quickly as investors expect.
“What if that payoff does not arrive with the speed that the consensus was expecting?” he said.
Slok expects some moderation in data center construction as expectations for earnings and investment returns adjust, but does not anticipate a recession. “I think the answer is that we will not get a recession, but I do think we’ll get some more dampening of the data center build-out,” he said.
With PPI inflation at its second-highest level in four years, CME FedWatch data put the odds of a Fed rate hike at 27.1% in October.

articles.title: 1 of the Stock Market's Most Reliable Recession Warnings Just Disappeared. Here's What Usually Happens Next. - The Motley Fool
articles.summary: 1 of the Stock Market's Most Reliable Recession Warnings Just Disappeared. Here's What Usually Happens Next.  The Motley Fool
articles.full_text:
History shows that the 10-year/three-month Treasury yield spread has been one of the most reliable recession indicators.
The general premise is that once this spread turns negative, which is to say that the three-month Treasury yield becomes higher than the 10-year yield, a recession is likely to come sometime in the subsequent six to 18 months.
Over the past 60-plus years, this inversion has occurred eight times. All eight times, a recession occurred shortly after this trigger fired.
The ninth time this happened was in late 2022. At its bottom, this spread went to nearly -200 basis points, the lowest reading it's ever had. But there was no recession. For the first time in well over half a century, this spread going negative did not precede a recession as it has historically.
While the recession usually arrives only after the curve has uninverted, this would be the longest lead time by far. In my opinion, the signal has disappeared.
But that doesn't mean recession risk is behind us. And it doesn't mean that the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.33%) can't experience a correction here.
Why the yield curve normalizing matters
The yield curve can steepen for a few reasons. The primary ones are rising inflation expectations, Treasury bond supply, and stronger economic growth.
The current environment features the first two with some of the third. The U.S. inflation rate has been in the 3% to 4% range for most of 2026. That's caused long-term yields to rise sharply while short-term yields, which are usually tied to what the Fed does, have moved comparatively little. This is what's called a "bear steepener" and is often a bad environment for rate-sensitive sectors.
But current U.S. economic growth is softening the blow. Corporate earnings growth has been strong, and GDP growth has, for now, remained well in positive territory. When these dynamics are in place, stock prices often have room to rise even as long-term interest rates rise.
S&P 500 Index
Key Data Points
Here's what I'd do with my portfolio
Outside of the obvious fact that it's impossible to predict the future, there's also no evidence that a recession or a market correction is imminent. I'd maintain long-term positions in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF, and similar funds.
Inflation and government debt are clearly risks. But oil prices seem to be peaking, and it's easy to see a scenario where inflation comes back down quickly with a resolution to the Iran war. If the markets can avoid a lengthy Fed hiking cycle, I think stocks will be just fine.

articles.title: U.S. Inflation Accelerates in September on Energy Shock, Complicating Fed Rate Decision - IndexBox
articles.summary: U.S. Inflation Accelerates in September on Energy Shock, Complicating Fed Rate Decision  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
U.S. consumer price growth accelerated more than expected on an annualized basis in September, according to Investing.com, highlighting the effect of an energy shock tied to the Iran war that could influence Federal Reserve interest-rate decisions for the remainder of the year.
Overall consumer prices rose 3.7% in the twelve months through September, up from 3.4% in August and above expectations of 3.6%. On a month-on-month basis, the inflation gauge increased 0.6%, compared with 0.4% previously and in line with forecasts.
Gulf supply constraints caused by an expanding conflict in the Middle East pushed energy prices higher last month, even as reports indicated supplies from the region were improving.
The energy component of the Labor Department's consumer price index rose 5.2% in September after a 2.1% gain in August. Gasoline prices climbed 9.1% and accounted for more than half of the monthly increase across all items, the Labor Department said.
Excluding volatile categories such as food and fuel, the core measure rose 0.3% month-on-month and 2.6% year-on-year. Economists had expected 0.2% and 2.5%, respectively. Shelter, used cars and trucks, airline fares, medical care and apparel all contributed to the core increase.
Analysts have raised concerns that a recent jump in diesel prices could feed into transportation costs and lift prices for a range of consumer goods.
The figures are likely to be watched closely by Fed officials, particularly with the central bank's October 27-28 meeting falling before the release of the personal consumption expenditures price index, one of policymakers' preferred inflation gauges.
Last month, the Fed raised rates by a quarter of a percentage point, citing a desire to bring inflation back toward its 2% target. It was the central bank's first rate increase since 2023.
Jeffrey Roach, Chief Economist at LPL Financial, said inflation pressures are broadening beyond energy, suggesting the final stretch back to target could remain uneven and keep interest rates elevated.
Can-Luca Koymen, Investment Strategist at Sygnum Bank, said the stronger-than-expected core CPI reading puts an October rate hike back in play.
After the CPI report, bets increased that the Fed could raise rates again this month. According to CME FedWatch, there is now a 43.7% chance of another 25-basis-point increase, versus roughly 22% a day earlier. The probability that the Fed will hold rates steady fell to around 56% from 78%.
Roach said the latest report complicates the Fed's decision this month, as the path back to price stability appears increasingly difficult to navigate.
Benchmark 10-year and rate-sensitive 2-year U.S. Treasury yields both rose. Yields tend to move inversely to bond prices. In early trading, the benchmark S&P 500 and technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite were lower.

articles.title: South Korea's Stock Market Triggers 10th Circuit Breaker of the Year as KOSPI Plunges 8% Intraday; Regulators Hold Emergency Meeting - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: South Korea's Stock Market Triggers 10th Circuit Breaker of the Year as KOSPI Plunges 8% Intraday; Regulators Hold Emergency Meeting  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
South Korea's stock market suffered a violent sell-off on October 15, with both the benchmark KOSPI and the tech-heavy KOSDAQ triggering circuit breakers intraday — the tenth time this year that South Korea's stock market has activated a circuit breaker, and the first time since July 29 that both indices halted on the same day. South Korea's Financial Services Commission (FSC) promptly convened an emergency response meeting, stating it would activate contingency plans at any time if necessary to stabilize the market.
As of press time, the KOSPI had plunged as much as 9% to 5,465.03 points, while the KOSDAQ fell more than 8%. Semiconductor heavyweights led the decline, with SK Hynix extending losses to over 12%, hitting its lowest level since April 27, and Samsung Electronics dropping more than 11%.
Korea Exchange data showed that the KOSDAQ market first triggered a Level 1 circuit breaker at 12:23 p.m. local time, followed by the KOSPI at 12:38 p.m., after falling 8% from the previous session to 5,528.05 points, halting securities trading for 20 minutes. Prior to that, program trading "sidecar" mechanisms had already been activated on both boards, but selling pressure did not ease as a result.
Foreign Investors Post Eighth Consecutive Day of Net Selling
Foreign investors were the primary drivers of this round of selling. Overseas investors net sold 2.9013 trillion won (approximately $216 million) in the KOSPI market during the morning session, marking an eighth consecutive trading day of net outflows. Retail investors and institutional investors net bought 1.2170 trillion won and 1.2701 trillion won respectively, absorbing some of the foreign selling pressure to a certain extent.
Multiple factors converged to trigger this correction. Overnight, the U.S. September Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7% year-over-year, with core CPI climbing to 2.6% — both exceeding market expectations, as energy and services prices jointly pushed inflation higher. Following the data release, market bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike in October briefly rose to 50%, while the probability of a December hike spiked above 95% at one point. U.S. Treasury yields climbed in tandem, exacerbating financing pressure on AI infrastructure companies and visibly weakening investor sentiment.
Overnight, U.S. stocks had already come under pressure. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.88%, dropping more than 510 points for its biggest single-day decline since July 23, while the S&P 500 lost 1.11%. Memory chip stocks fell broadly, with SK Hynix down more than 6%, SanDisk down over 5%, and Western Digital, Micron Technology, and Seagate Technology all down more than 4%. Japanese equities were not spared either, with the Nikkei 225 falling more than 3% on the day, while SoftBank Group and Kioxia both plunged over 8%.
Regulators Step In
South Korea's Financial Services Commission convened an emergency response meeting at 2:30 p.m. that afternoon, chaired by FSC Chairman Lee Eog-weon, to assess the sharp market decline and heightened volatility, and to discuss financial market stabilization measures. Attending regulatory officials and market experts concluded that, given the combined impact of rising global interest rate expectations, uncertainty surrounding AI semiconductor investment and earnings prospects, and elevated oil prices, the recent magnitude of declines and the pace of capital outflows in South Korea's stock market may have been excessive.
In a statement following the meeting, the FSC said authorities would closely monitor both domestic and international market developments and stand ready to act at any time if necessary. The statement did not specify the content of contingency measures, but emphasized that monitoring would cover both South Korean and overseas markets.
The agency made clear it would take strict enforcement action against market-disturbing activities, including the spread of false rumors, market manipulation, and illegal short selling. This stance extends South Korean regulators' recent hardline position on market misconduct. Illegal short selling has repeatedly been a key enforcement target for South Korean regulators, who view it as a significant factor exacerbating market volatility and undermining investor confidence.
Lee Eog-weon also sent a clear signal to financial institutions at the meeting, urging them to exercise restraint in blind credit expansion, avoid indiscriminate lending growth, and genuinely strengthen customer protection mechanisms and internal risk management systems. These remarks indicate that regulators' vigilance over potential financial risks is rising.
Household Loan Growth Slows
In contrast to stock market turbulence, South Korea's credit market showed signs of cooling. Data released by the Bank of Korea on Thursday showed that household loans increased by 600 billion won (approximately $4.5 million) in September, reaching 1,198.9 trillion won — the smallest increase since March and the slowest pace in six months.
| Indicator | September Change | Notes | 
|---|---|---|
| Total household loans | +600 billion won | Smallest increase since March | 
| Mortgage loans | +2.9 trillion won | Lowest level since April | 
| Other household loans | -2.3 trillion won | August was -600 billion won; decline widened | 
Note: Other household loans include unsecured loans and stock-backed loans.
The Bank of Korea noted that the larger decline in other household loans was primarily attributable to reduced retail stock investment, quarter-end sales declines, non-performing loan write-offs, and seasonal inflows of holiday bonuses. The slowdown in mortgage loan growth stemmed from a continued deceleration in deposit-based rental transactions and a reduced supply of newly completed housing units available for occupancy. The Bank of Korea is scheduled to make its next policy decision the following week.
Analysts believe that the high-level emergency response from regulators signals that authorities are closely monitoring the potential impact of market volatility on financial stability. Against a backdrop of rising uncertainty over the Federal Reserve's monetary policy path and renewed scrutiny of global AI investment return prospects, South Korea's stock market — as a representative of semiconductor export-driven markets — will continue to face dual pressures in the near term: shifts in external liquidity conditions and internal valuation adjustments.

articles.full_text:
Bets on an October Fed rate hike briefly spiked to nearly 50% after Wednesday’s inflation report, but have since cooled.
- Bitcoin fell below $81,000 after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data revived concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates in October.
- Markets pared the odds of an October rate increase to about 26% to 30% after initially pricing in a nearly 50% chance following the inflation report.
- Fragile institutional demand, including $150.5 million in U.S. spot bitcoin ETF outflows on Oct. 14, and broader economic uncertainty are weighing on liquidity and risk appetite.
Bitcoin  and global stocks are under pressure as Wednesday’s U.S. inflation data revived concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates this month.
The largest cryptocurrency by market value is trading 1% lower since midnight UTC. Prices dipped close to $80,000 in early Asian trading before briefly rebounding to about $81,500, but that recovery has since stalled near $81,000, CoinDesk data show. Prices are down more than 2% in the past 24 hours.
Tokens such as ether , XRP (XRP), solana (SOL) are down 3.5% to 4%. PYTH is the only top-100 cryptocurrency still up more than 7%.
Traditional markets have also turned risk-averse. Nasdaq futures were down 1% at press time, extending Wednesday’s 2% decline, while South Korea’s KOSPI plunged 8% and triggered circuit breakers.
Data released Wednesday showed consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September, up from 3.4% in August and above economists’ expectations. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, climbed 2.6%, accelerating from 2.4% the previous month.
Markets have quickly repriced the odds of a Fed move. On prediction platform Polymarket, the probability of an October rate hike briefly spiked to nearly 50% after the CPI release before easing to about 30%. CME’s FedWatch tool showed a similar pattern: odds initially jumped to almost 47% from roughly 22%, before retreating to 26% as of writing.
“Stronger U.S. inflation data has renewed concerns that interest rates will stay higher for longer,” said Vikram Subburaj, CEO of India-based exchange Giottus. “September inflation rose to 3.7% annually, increasing uncertainty over the Federal Reserve’s next move. Institutional demand also remains fragile. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $150.5 million in outflows on October 14, reversing the previous day’s $175.7 million inflow.”
Market-making firm STS Digital said the uncertainty could weigh on liquidity across markets.
“With the next FOMC a coin flip, this uncertainty is damaging liquidity and dampening risk appetite across all asset classes,” the firm’s Anderson told CoinDesk in an email.
Still, Anderson thinks the Fed will hold interest rates steady this month, which is consistent with the over 70% probability of a status quo decision priced by the CME Fed funds futures as of this writing.
“Despite recent optimism in digital assets, tokens now look increasingly sensitive to macro factors, with energy shocks, fixed-income volatility and AI valuations weighing on sentiment,” he added.

The dollar index DXY rallied to a 1.5-year high on Wednesday and finished up by +0.37%. The dollar advanced on Wednesday on the stronger-than-expected US Sep CPI report, which bolsters speculation that the Fed will keep interest rates higher for longer. The CPI report boosted the chance of a Fed rate hike at this month’s FOMC meeting to 34% from 22% before the report. Also, Wednesday’s +1% rise in WTI crude oil boosted inflation expectations and could push the Fed to keep tightening monetary policy, supporting the dollar. In addition, Wednesday’s Fed Beige Book warned of intensifying price pressures that are hawkish for Fed policy and bullish for the dollar.
Comments on Wednesday from Fed Vice Chair Michelle Bowman signaled she favors keeping Fed policy steady at this month's FOMC meeting and were negative for the dollar when she said, "We have some time to wait and see how financial conditions and the economy evolve before we decide that we need to take any more action" on interest rates.

Markets are pricing in a 34% chance of a +25 bp Fed rate hike at the next FOMC meeting on October 27-28.
EUR/USD T fell by -0.08% on Wednesday. The yen rebounded from a 2.5-week low against the dollar on Wednesday and moved higher after T-note yields fell from early highs and moved lower, sparking short covering in the yen.
The yen initially fell on Wednesday after a stronger-than-expected US Sep CPI report boosted the dollar. Also, Wednesday’s +1% increase in crude oil prices is bearish for Japan’s economy and the yen, as Japan imports more than 90% of its energy. In addition, Wednesday’s decline in the 10-year Japan JGB bond yield to a 3.5-week low of 2.997% weakened the yen’s interest rate differentials.
The yen also has negative carryover from Tuesday on a report that said BOJ officials pushed back against an interest rate hike at this month's policy meeting, saying they see little need for consecutive rate hikes in the absence of signs that upside inflation risks will increase abruptly.
Markets are pricing in a 5% chance of a +25 bp BOJ rate hike at the next policy meeting on October 30.
December COMEX gold (GCZ26) closed down -69.40 (-1.66%) on Wednesday, and December COMEX silver (SIZ26) closed down -3.648 (-6.13%).
Precious metals prices plummeted on Wednesday, with gold falling to a 1-week low and silver dropping to a 3-month low. Wednesday’s surge in the dollar index to a 1.5-year high weighed on metals. Also, Wednesday’s stronger-than-expected US Sep CPI report was hawkish for Fed policy and negative for precious metals. In addition, Wednesday’s Fed Beige Book warned of rising price pressures, which is hawkish for Fed policy and is bearish for precious metals. Finally, Wednesday’s +1% rise in crude oil prices raises inflation expectations and could persuade the world’s central banks to tighten monetary policy, a negative factor for precious metals.
Recent fund support for precious metals is bullish for prices, as long holdings in gold ETFs climbed to a 4-year high last Thursday. Long holdings in silver ETFs rose to a 6.5-month high on September 22.
Strong central bank demand for gold is supporting gold prices, after last Thursday’s news showed that bullion held in China's PBOC reserves rose by 740,000 ounces to 77.47 million troy ounces in September, the largest increase in three years and the twenty-third consecutive month the PBOC boosted its gold reserves.

articles.title: Fed may hike interest rates by 50 basis points in December as inflation fears hit Wall Street - Business Upturn
articles.summary: Fed may hike interest rates by 50 basis points in December as inflation fears hit Wall Street  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
The US Federal Reserve could be facing pressure to raise interest rates again. Traders are now betting on the possibility of a larger rate increase in December, according to a report highlighted by CNBC.
The latest development comes as fresh inflation data has raised concerns about the US economy. Investors are increasingly worried that rising prices could force the central bank to keep monetary policy tight for longer than expected.
According to First Squawk, traders are considering the possibility of a 50 basis point increase in December. That would represent a half percentage point increase in interest rates. It could also mean a more aggressive approach to controlling inflation.
However, these are market expectations, not a confirmed decision by the Federal Reserve. Policymakers will have to examine incoming economic data before deciding their next move.
The changing outlook is already drawing attention across financial markets. Higher interest rates can affect everything from stock prices and mortgage costs to business investment and consumer spending.
Why traders expect the Fed to raise interest rates again
Inflation is once again becoming a major concern for the US economy.
Consumer prices rose 3.7% in September compared with the same month last year. This was higher than the 3.4% annual increase recorded in August. It also exceeded economists' expectations of 3.6%, according to Reuters.
Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, increased 2.6% over the year. Economists had expected a smaller increase of 2.5%.
These figures have made it harder for investors to expect an early end to the Fed's interest rate increases.
The central bank uses interest rates as a tool to control inflation. When borrowing becomes more expensive, households may reduce spending and businesses may delay investments. This can help slow demand and ease pressure on prices.
However, higher rates also carry risks. They can make loans more expensive, discourage hiring and put pressure on economic growth.
The Fed therefore has to balance two important goals. It needs to bring inflation under control without slowing the economy too sharply.
The latest inflation figures have complicated that task. Traders are now reassessing how much further interest rates might need to rise.
What a 50 basis point Fed rate hike in December would mean
A basis point is a unit used to measure changes in interest rates. One basis point equals 0.01 percentage point. A 50 basis point increase would therefore raise the benchmark rate by half a percentage point.
For example, if the relevant rate stood at 4%, a 50 basis point increase would take it to 4.5%.
Such a move would be larger than a typical 25 basis point increase. It would signal a stronger effort to bring inflation down.
For American households, higher interest rates can increase the cost of borrowing. People with variable rate loans may face higher payments. Those looking to buy homes or finance large purchases could also find borrowing less affordable.
Businesses could face higher costs when borrowing money to expand operations. Some companies may delay new projects if financing becomes too expensive.
The stock market could also feel the impact. Higher interest rates can make bonds and other interest bearing investments more attractive compared with stocks. They can also reduce the estimated future value of company earnings, putting pressure on share prices.
The US dollar may receive support if higher rates make dollar denominated investments more attractive to international investors. However, currency movements also depend on what other central banks do and how much of the expected increase is already reflected in market prices.
A larger increase is not guaranteed. The Fed could choose a smaller move or leave rates unchanged if the economic data support that decision.
What investors should watch before the Fed's December decision
The next few weeks could prove important for financial markets. Investors will be watching inflation reports, employment figures and statements from Federal Reserve officials for clues about the direction of monetary policy.
The Fed's next scheduled policy meeting is on October 27 and 28. The December meeting will provide another opportunity for policymakers to reassess the economy and decide whether additional tightening is necessary.
Traders have already increased their expectations for further rate increases following the latest inflation report. However, market pricing can change quickly when new data become available.
There is also a difference between expecting a rate increase and knowing that one will happen. Traders make bets based on available information, but the Federal Reserve makes its decision after considering a wider range of economic risks.
For Wall Street, the central question is whether inflation will continue to rise or begin to ease in the coming months.
If price pressures remain strong, expectations for further rate increases could grow. If inflation cools, the pressure for a larger December move could weaken.
The next inflation and employment reports may therefore have a major influence on market expectations. Until then, the possibility of a 50 basis point increase remains a scenario investors are watching, rather than a final decision by the Federal Reserve.
