articles.title: IMF Raises Spain Growth Forecast to 2.5%, Warns of AI-Linked Stock Market Correction - finance.biggo.com
articles.summary: IMF Raises Spain Growth Forecast to 2.5%, Warns of AI-Linked Stock Market Correction  finance.biggo.com
articles.full_text:
The Spanish economy will grow 2.5% this year, four-tenths of a percentage point more than estimated in July, according to new projections released Tuesday by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on the occasion of its annual meeting in Bangkok. The upward revision positions Spain as one of the best-performing advanced economies, far above the 1.1% forecast for the Eurozone as a whole.
The World Economic Outlook report, presented by the institution's chief economist, Silvana Tenreyro, also slightly raises global growth from 3% to 3.1%, and that of the countries sharing the single European currency, which rises from 0.9% to 1.1%. The improvement is largely attributed to the resilience shown by the global economy, underpinned by massive investments in artificial intelligence, which are said to have offset the impact of higher energy and commodity prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.
Tenreyro stressed that Asia in general, and China in particular, have benefited from the deployment of AI, outpacing the global expansion rate. However, she warned that the picture is "highly uneven," with countries most dependent on hydrocarbon imports in a fragile position, often aggravated by rising financing costs.
Growth, in fact, is becoming notably concentrated. According to the report, 32 countries now account for 95% of global growth, compared with 54 in April. The United States and China concentrate more than three-quarters of net import demand for chips and other AI-related equipment.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva focused on the labor impact of this technology, which she described as "a slow-moving tsunami, but a tsunami nonetheless." According to her estimates, around 40% of jobs globally will be augmented, degraded, or eliminated over time.
Another central concern for the institution is the high level of indebtedness, which is approaching levels recorded during the pandemic. Unlike then, the IMF urges fiscal consolidation to curb the inflationary escalation, which stands at 4.7% globally, through budgetary restraint and deficit reduction.
The IMF's forecasts assume an increase of nearly 41% in oil prices this year, to an average of $96 per barrel, and contemplate that crude and gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz will resume in March. Global inflation would decline to 4.1% in 2027.
As for the major economies, U.S. growth remains stable at 2.3% for both 2026 and 2027. China, the world's second-largest economy, would expand 4.5% this year, below the 5% of 2025, in line with the government's official target. India would once again be the fastest-growing major economy, with a 7% advance, though lower than the 7.7% of the previous year.
France, by contrast, would grow an anemic 0.4% this year, with a downward revision. The slight improvement in Germany's outlook could be related to the militarization of its economy, the report notes. Emerging and developing economies most vulnerable to rising energy costs will see their growth slow to 3.7% this year, from 4.5% in 2025, before regaining momentum in 2027.
The situation is considerably worse in the Middle East and Central Asia, regions whose economies will contract this year before recovering with growth of 6.3% in 2027. Thailand, host of the joint IMF and World Bank meeting, would grow 2.1%.
Financial Risks and the AI Bubble
Immediately after the presentation of the World Economic Outlook, the Global Financial Stability Report added further doses of caution. The document warns of a possible "systemic risk" arising from a correction in securities tied to the artificial intelligence boom, the high cost of treasury bonds in major economies, and the possibility of cyberattacks, potentially made more devastating by AI itself.
The report notes that although the main companies in the AI ecosystem have generated profits so far, a correction "exacerbated by increased leverage, concentrated exposure, and circular financing arrangements" cannot be ruled out. In other words, the same AI multinationals tend to be the ones financing and investing in their own suppliers.
Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director of the IMF's Monetary and Capital Markets Department, indicated that an AI-related stock market correction is only one of the risks. Rising bond yields and cyber threats capable of disrupting financial systems are other evolving problems, he added.
These warnings coincided with heavy selling of AI-linked stocks in Asia, where South Korea's Kospi index plunged as much as 7% before closing down 5.5%.
The IMF also warns that concerns about the fiscal stability of some economies, along with the rebound in inflation, could trigger a sharp rise in sovereign debt interest rates and "unleash further market disorder." "These risks in themselves do not necessarily threaten financial stability, but could become systemic if they amplify financial vulnerabilities," the report states.
Globally, banks generally maintain solid balance sheets to weather crisis scenarios, while households have reduced their debt exposure. Despite this, a sharp correction in real estate assets could negatively impact consumption and mainly affect lower-income families, according to the document.
Outlook for 2027
Although global growth should improve by a few tenths in 2027, to 3.4%, the IMF warns that its estimates are subject to a large number of imponderables. The institution acknowledges that its projections are "held together with pins," given the geopolitical and financial uncertainty surrounding the baseline scenario.
The annual meeting in Bangkok brings together finance ministers and central bank governors from the IMF's 191 member countries, who will assess the state of the global economy and debate strategies to support financial stability and sustained growth.
Among the most notable absences from the report is any substantial reference to concern over housing prices, as well as a very nuanced mention of the destruction of mid-level jobs caused by automation. Climate change and the war in Ukraine also do not appear as highlighted priorities, issues that occupy a marginal place in the institution's concerns.
The following table summarizes the main growth projections for 2026 and 2027:
| Region or country | 2025 (estimate) | 2026 (forecast) | 2027 (forecast) | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Global economy | 3.5% | 3.1% | 3.4% | 
| Advanced economies | 2.0% | 2.1% | 1.9% | 
| Spain | — | 2.5% | — | 
| Eurozone | — | 1.1% | 1.2% | 
| United States | — | 2.3% | 2.3% | 
| China | 5.0% | 4.5% | — | 
| India | 7.7% | 7.0% | — | 
| Emerging and developing economies | 4.5% | 3.7% | 4.4% | 
| France | — | 0.4% | — | 
| Thailand | — | 2.1% | — | 
Note: 2025 figures correspond to previous IMF estimates; dashes indicate that the report does not provide a specific figure for that year or region.
The improved outlook for Spain contrasts with the sluggishness of other major European economies and reinforces the idea of an uneven recovery, in which countries with greater exposure to technology and lower external energy dependence manage to sustain growth momentum.

articles.title: Fed funds futures price an 88% chance of a December hike, the main lid on gold’s rebound above $4,200. - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: Fed funds futures price an 88% chance of a December hike, the main lid on gold’s rebound above $4,200.  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- Spot gold XAU/USD rose $16.80 to $4,187.60, defending the $4,150 floor for a second straight session.
- Fed funds futures price an 88% chance of a December hike, the main lid on gold’s rebound above $4,200.
- Central banks bought 289 tonnes of gold in the second quarter, a 62% jump from a year earlier.
Spot gold traded at $4,187.60 an ounce at 9:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, up $16.80 on the day. The session range ran from $4,150.10 to $4,201.40, and the 24-hour window stretched from a low of $4,150.52 to a high of $4,216.21. December COMEX futures traded at $4,193.60 by 10:24 a.m. ET after printing $4,210.40 in early trading, and they reached $4,209.90 in Asian hours when spot was up 0.4% at $4,185.69.
The path inside the session tells you how fragile the bid is. In the Asian morning, spot gold slipped 0.2% to $4,164.45 as the dollar held near an 18-month high. By 7:45 a.m. ET it had recovered to $4,186.89. By 8:28 a.m. ET it was $4,184.43. At 9 a.m. ET it was quoted at $4,182 on one tape and $4,179.27 on another, against $4,163 to $4,164.85 at the same hour Monday. The metal spent the whole morning grinding between $4,150 and $4,216, and every push above $4,200 got sold.
That is the shape of the market heading into Wednesday’s September CPI report at 8:30 a.m. ET. Gold closed last week at $4,194.645 on spot, a 1.47% weekly gain and its first winning week in three, with COMEX futures settling at $4,220.30. It touched a one-week high on Monday, then gave ground into the U.S. close as the dollar index rose to 102.41 and spot slipped 0.5% to roughly $4,170. Tuesday’s rebound to $4,187.60 recovers that loss, but it has not cleared Friday’s settlement.
The bigger frame is a market still digesting a crash. Gold set its all-time high at $5,597.23 on spot on January 29, 2026, with COMEX futures peaking at $5,626.80 the same day. From there the metal fell 29.7% to a 52-week low of $3,900. At $4,187.60, spot gold sits 25.2% below its record and 7.4% above its low. It is down 2.2% from $4,277 one month ago and up 2.7% from $4,078 one year ago.
The thesis for this forecast is direct: gold is pinned between a Federal Reserve that markets now expect to hike again in December and a floor built by central-bank buying, Middle East risk and an oil shock that keeps inflation hedges in demand. The $4,134 to $4,227 band holds that tension. Wednesday’s CPI decides which side breaks. A soft core print clears $4,227 and opens $4,277 to $4,300. A hot one sends gold back to test the $4,090 two-month low set last Wednesday.
Fed Funds Futures Price an 88% Chance of a December Hike
The single heaviest weight on gold is the rate path. Fed funds futures on Tuesday priced a 21% probability of a rate hike at the October 27-28 FOMC meeting and an 88% probability of a hike by December. Other readings across the morning put the October odds at 19% and the December odds at 85%. Real-money prediction markets showed 19.5% for October and 75.5% for December as of late Monday. However it is measured, the market expects another tightening move before year-end.
That is a remarkable setting for gold to be holding $4,187. The Fed hiked in September. The 10-year Treasury yield traded at 5.22% Tuesday morning, down 2 basis points from Monday’s 5.24% close, after the 10-year and 30-year reached 5.28% and 5.63% respectively last week, their highest levels since 2002. Gold pays nothing. Every basis point of yield on a risk-free Treasury raises the opportunity cost of holding bullion.
Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack sharpened the hawkish case on Monday. In a speech and interview, she said the Fed should move relatively quickly to a more restrictive stance, that inflation has become broader-based and is starting to affect firms’ pricing plans, and that demand from AI investment and wealth effects is supporting price pressures. She prefers smaller moves made sooner rather than waiting and having to make a larger correction. She kept an open mind on October.
Inflation expectations give the hawks their ammunition. The New York Fed’s one-year inflation expectation rose to 3.9% in its latest survey, the highest since May 2023, and that reading landed on October 7, the same day gold hit its two-month low. Gold fell on the inflation data because the market read it as a Fed problem, not as a hedging opportunity.
That is the crux of gold’s 2026 problem. In a normal inflation scare, gold rallies as a store of value. In this one, rising inflation expectations translate directly into higher rate-hike odds and higher real yields, and that channel overwhelms the hedge demand. The metal’s 29.7% drawdown from January was driven by the transition from a cutting cycle to a hiking cycle, and the market has not yet priced the end of that hiking cycle.
The calendar this week is dense. CPI hits Wednesday, PPI and retail sales on Thursday, and Fed officials appear at the IMF on Friday. Governor Christopher Waller, Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin and Boston Fed President Susan Collins spoke Tuesday. Each data point will move the December odds, and with 88% already priced, the asymmetry favors gold on a soft print: there is far more room for those odds to fall than to rise.
Wednesday’s CPI at 8:30 a.m. ET: The Print That Breaks the Range
September CPI is the main event, and gold’s reaction function is clear. A cooler print, especially on the core measure, would support gold through lower real yields and a weaker dollar. A hot core print would rebuild December hike risk and cap the rebound, and could trigger another dip in gold toward last week’s lows. The market is positioned for hawkishness with 88% December odds, so the bar for a positive surprise for gold is lower than the bar for a negative one.
The headline number has upside risk built in. WTI crude traded at $93.68 by 10:24 a.m. ET Tuesday after touching $91.78 in early trade, and Brent topped $105 in the prior session, with one print over $106. Gasoline prices have tied 2022’s record for the most days above $4 a gallon in a single year. Energy flows directly into headline CPI, and crude above $90 through the September survey period means the headline figure will likely run hot regardless of core.
Core is the number that matters for the Fed. Hammack’s language about inflation becoming broader-based is a statement about core goods and services, not energy. If core comes in at or below expectations, the market will look through a hot headline and start pricing out some of that December hike. If core accelerates, the October meeting comes back into play, and the 21% probability could move sharply higher.
The bank earnings released Tuesday showed how inflation and rates are already biting. JPMorgan booked $658 million in losses on investment securities, and CEO Jamie Dimon listed sticky inflation, rising interest rates, large fiscal deficits and elevated asset prices among the forces he said continue to shift under the surface. Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf named higher interest rates, higher oil prices and persistent inflation as the main risks to the economy. Two of the largest banks in the country flagged the same macro mix that is holding gold down.
The setup for gold into the print is defensive but not bearish. The metal has held $4,150 for two sessions in a row, it posted its first weekly gain in three weeks last Friday, and its intraday lows have come in Asian hours rather than U.S. hours, which suggests Western buyers are absorbing the selling. A soft CPI would hit a market that is already structurally short on rate exposure.
Timing matters here. The print lands at 8:30 a.m. ET, an hour before U.S. equity markets open, while gold futures and spot trade through it. The first 30 minutes after the release will set the tone. Watch whether spot holds $4,180 on any initial knee-jerk move lower: support levels in that area at $4,180.98 and then $4,155.31 are where buyers stepped in Monday and Tuesday.
The Dollar Near an 18-Month High Is the Second Lid on Gold
The dollar is doing the Fed’s work on gold. The dollar index closed Monday at 102.41 to 102.55 depending on the tape, with the currency holding near an 18-month high. A stronger dollar raises the cost of gold for buyers paying in euros, yen, rupees and yuan, and it historically moves inversely to bullion.
Tuesday brought some relief. A softer dollar, lower Treasury yields and a pullback in oil prices all supported metals in early U.S. trading. The 2-basis-point dip in the 10-year to 5.22% and the dollar’s easing from Monday’s highs were enough to lift gold 0.39% on the session to $4,186.90 by early U.S. hours. That is a measure of how sensitive gold is to marginal moves in the dollar right now.
The dollar’s strength is a direct product of the Fed’s turn. With U.S. rates rising while other central banks hold or ease, capital flows toward dollar assets. The September hike widened the rate gap with Europe and Japan, and an 88% probability of another hike in December keeps the gap widening. Japanese producer inflation cooled overnight, which reduces pressure on the Bank of Japan to tighten and keeps the yen weak against the dollar.
The interaction between the dollar and gold in India shows the damage. Domestic gold prices in India fell for a second straight day on Tuesday, with 24-carat gold priced at ₹1,49,670 per 10 grams in Mumbai and Bhubaneswar and ₹1,49,810 in Delhi. articles.full_text:
Gold is often described as an inflation hedge, but a hot Consumer Price Index (CPI) report does not automatically send its price higher. The September US CPI release is scheduled for October 14, 2026, and traders will compare the result with expectations for inflation and Federal Reserve policy. With gold already volatile, the report could move Treasury yields, the dollar and XAU/USD in different directions.
This guide explains how CPI affects gold prices, examines updated monthly data, and sets out what could happen if the next inflation reading surprises markets.
The US Consumer Price Index tracks changes in prices paid by consumers for a basket of goods and services. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the headline index and detailed categories each month. Traders often focus on the 12-month inflation rate, but the latest monthly change provides a more immediate indication of momentum. CPI helps shape expectations about future interest rates, which can alter gold’s appeal even before the Federal Reserve changes policy.
As of the morning of October 14, the latest published report covers August 2026: headline CPI was up 3.4% year over year and 0.4% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis. Core CPI rose 2.4% year over year and 0.3% month over month. September data had not yet been released at the time of writing.
Headline CPI includes food and energy prices. Core CPI excludes those categories to provide another view of underlying inflation. Both matter for gold. A jump in energy prices may raise the headline number and inflation concerns, while persistently firm core inflation may make traders expect restrictive monetary policy for longer.
The Fed’s formal 2% target uses the personal consumption expenditures price index, but CPI often changes expectations for its next decision. See the Fed interest rate forecast.
A release can move markets even when inflation declines. If annual CPI falls from 3.4% to 3.2%, but economists expected 3.0%, the upside surprise could lift bond yields and the dollar.
Compare headline and core CPI with both monthly and annual forecasts. The first price move can reverse as markets digest the details.

The answer to “how does CPI affect gold prices?” lies in several competing channels. Inflation may increase demand for an asset that cannot be created by a central bank, while the interest-rate response can raise the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset. The balance varies with the economic setting.
When CPI exceeds expectations, traders may anticipate higher policy rates or a delay in rate cuts. Nominal Treasury yields can rise, making interest-bearing assets more attractive than gold, which pays no interest. What matters especially is the real yield: the nominal yield adjusted for expected inflation. Rising real yields are often a headwind for gold; falling real yields can support it.
If a CPI surprise lifts inflation expectations faster than nominal yields, real yields can fall and gold may rise. One report does not determine Fed policy. Markets.com explores the wider effect of rates in how interest rates affect stocks.
Gold is commonly priced in US dollars. A stronger dollar can make it more expensive for buyers using other currencies, potentially reducing demand. A soft CPI reading may weaken the dollar if traders expect easier Fed policy, which can help XAU/USD. Dollar moves can be more influential in the first minutes after the announcement than the inflation number alone.
Persistent inflation can erode purchasing power and make gold attractive as a long-term store of value. During geopolitical stress or concerns about financial stability, buyers may seek gold even as rates rise. Central-bank purchases, investor flows and physical demand can also affect prices independently of US CPI. The World Gold Council identifies currencies, opportunity costs, risk and momentum among gold’s key drivers.
These forces explain why a “hot CPI equals higher gold” rule is unreliable. Watch the bond and currency response alongside the gold price itself.
If CPI increases, the immediate gold reaction depends on the size and composition of the surprise. A stronger reading may support gold’s inflation-hedge narrative, yet it may also lift real yields and the dollar. The table describes plausible reactions rather than predictions for the October 14 release.
| CPI outcome | Likely market interpretation | Possible gold reaction | What to check | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Above expectations; yields and dollar rise | Fed may keep policy restrictive for longer | Gold may fall initially | Real yields, core CPI and Fed-rate pricing | 
| Above expectations; real yields fall or risk aversion rises | Inflation concerns outweigh the rate effect | Gold may rise | Inflation expectations and safe-haven flows | 
| Broadly in line | Little change to the policy outlook | Initial volatility may fade | Revisions and underlying categories | 
| Below expectations; yields and dollar fall | Less pressure for tighter policy | Gold may rise | Whether the disinflation trend persists | 
| Below expectations; growth fears dominate | Inflation cools alongside weaker activity | Direction can be mixed | Equity markets, credit and safe-haven demand | 
For example, a headline CPI rise driven by energy costs could worry investors about purchasing power, while a softer core reading reduces concern about persistent inflation. Conversely, firm core services inflation could push rate expectations higher even if the headline figure looks calm. Traders should compare both readings with consensus estimates and monitor the first hour’s moves in Treasury yields and the dollar.

The chart below pairs the same calendar months: the World Bank’s monthly average London PM gold benchmark in US dollars per troy ounce and the BLS headline CPI-U 12-month change. The latest common month is August 2026. September gold data exist, but September CPI had not been released when this article was prepared, so September is excluded.
Sources: World Bank Pink Sheet, monthly commodity prices and BLS August 2026 CPI release, Table 5. Gold prices are rounded monthly averages; CPI is the unadjusted 12-month percentage change. The BLS historical table does not show an October 2025 CPI observation, so the line has a gap. Separate vertical scales have different units and do not establish causation.
The chart illustrates why comparing levels can mislead. Gold climbed from roughly $2,034 per ounce in January 2024 to about $4,309 in December 2025, even though CPI was lower at several points during that interval. Later, headline inflation accelerated to 4.2% in May 2026 while gold’s monthly average fell from its February high of about $5,020 to roughly $4,587. By August, CPI had eased to 3.4%, while the gold monthly average recovered to around $4,411.
The two lines also use different measures: gold shows a price level; CPI shows the rate of change in consumer prices. A visual crossing of the lines has no financial meaning. Monthly averages can conceal sharp announcement-day moves, so this chart describes the wider relationship rather than predicting the next CPI-day return. Readers examining the longer cycle can compare it with the gold price trend analysis.

Rising consumer prices do not guarantee that gold will keep pace over days, months or even years. The price of gold also reflects what investors expect next. If inflation has already been anticipated, the CPI release may add little new information. If it persuades traders that the Fed will maintain higher rates, yields and the dollar may climb enough to pressure gold.
Gold can also fall when investors raise cash, fund flows turn negative or geopolitical fears fade. Conversely, falling real yields, a weaker dollar or renewed risk aversion can lift gold while CPI declines.
Gold can rise in dollars while delivering a smaller gain after inflation. Assess purchasing-power protection over an appropriate holding period. For recent price context, see the gold price forecast for 2026, 2027 and 2030.
A new high after the October CPI release is possible, but the hurdle is substantial. The World Gold Council reported that spot gold briefly reached approximately $5,595 per ounce in January 2026. A Markets.com market update placed XAU/USD near $4,153 ahead of the October 14 report. These are intraday spot reference points; the chart’s $5,020 February peak is a separate monthly average and should not be treated as the same record.
From $4,153, a return to the approximately $5,595 intraday peak would require a gain of about 35%. One softer CPI print could help sentiment, but a sustained advance would likely require a broader shift in real yields, the dollar, Fed expectations or safe-haven demand.
Watch whether a post-release move lasts through the US session and subsequent Fed commentary. The Markets.com gold market update gives pre-announcement context.

articles.title: The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 5.05% while UK August GDP beat forecasts | That's TradingNEWS - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 5.05% while UK August GDP beat forecasts | That's TradingNEWS  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- GBP/USD trades at 1.3270, up 0.69%, after a session range of 1.3197 to 1.3283.
- UK GDP grew 0.1% in August against a forecast 0.1% contraction, after 0.4% in July.
- The Bank of England held Bank Rate at 3.75% in a 6–3 vote, with three members backing a hike to 4%.
Sterling is leading the majors against the dollar on Thursday. GBP/USD traded at 1.3270 at 16:16 CEST, up 0.69% from Wednesday’s close of 1.3197, with a session range of 1.3197 to 1.3283. The pound has now erased the entire post-CPI selloff and pushed back above Wednesday’s pre-release high of 1.3275.
Wednesday’s swing set the stage. The pair opened that session at 1.3255, traded near 1.3265 around midday London time, then collapsed to 1.3137 after the US inflation release, a 15-week low and the weakest level since late June. The pound fell 0.5% from the open to 1.3194 before recovering overnight to 1.3236 in early Asian trade.
The recovery came in two legs. The first came overnight as US Treasury yields slipped. The second came at 7:00 a.m. London time, when UK GDP data beat forecasts and pushed the pair to 1.3264. The US producer price data at 1:30 p.m. London time added a third push as the 10-year Treasury yield dropped sharply.
The monthly picture shows the damage the dollar rally did before Thursday. GBP/USD stood at 1.3420 on September 30 and 1.3539 on August 31. At 1.3270, the pair is down 1.1% since the end of September and 2% since the end of August. Over the past month, sterling has weakened 1.03%, and over 12 months it is down 1.42%.
The 2026 context frames the current level. GBP/USD averaged 1.3448 from January through September. The current price sits 1.3% below that average, and the October monthly average sits at 1.3151, showing how much of the month the pair spent below 1.32.
Sterling is outperforming the euro. GBP/EUR held broadly unchanged at €1.1816 while both currencies rallied against the dollar. EUR/USD gained 0.5% to 1.1217 Thursday, a similar move to the pound’s 0.69%, but the pound has held its 2026 range far better. EUR/USD has fallen 6.5% from its January peak and sits at a 17-month low; GBP/USD sits only at a 15-week low.
That relative strength is the thesis. The pound’s bounce rests on more than a weaker dollar. The Bank of England is closer to a rate hike than the European Central Bank, UK growth is beating expectations, and the gap between UK and US policy rates is narrow. Those factors give sterling a firmer floor than the euro, and they make 1.3283, Thursday’s high, the level that decides whether the recovery extends.
The Dollar Side: 18-Month High Wednesday, Reversal Thursday
The dollar remains the dominant driver. The US dollar index hit an 18-month high on Wednesday after US consumer inflation rose to 3.7% in September, above forecasts. After the CPI release, the index faded to 101.74. Heading into the week, it stood at 102.06 with a weekly high of 102.53.
Thursday extended the reversal. The dollar weakened 0.38% against sterling during the early European session, 0.48% against the euro, 0.22% against the yen and 0.59% against the Swiss franc. The pound’s gain built through the day as US data arrived.
The bond market triggered the move. The 10-year Treasury yield fell 14 basis points to 5.05% after the September producer price data, from 5.19% before the US open. Both the 10-year and 30-year yields fell more than 13 basis points, putting the 30-year on track for its biggest drop since November 25, 2024. The 10-year touched 5.36% on October 7, its highest level since 2002.
The decline came on hot data. The September Producer Price Index rose 1.3% for the month and 6.3% over 12 months, the biggest monthly increase since March 2022. Forecasts called for 0.6% and 5.5%. In a normal regime, that print would lift US yields and the dollar. Instead, investors bought Treasuries as US equities sold off on AI financing fears.
US equities explain the shift. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.05% to 26,411.88 after a 1.9% drop Wednesday, with chip stocks down for an eighth straight session and CoreWeave falling 6.89% to $61.25 on debt concerns. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 7.57% overnight. When US assets sell off on credit fears, Treasury demand rises and the dollar’s yield advantage narrows.
The dollar rally had been crowded. Four straight weekly gains built large long-dollar positions into the CPI release. When the inflation data failed to push yields higher, those positions began to unwind, which accounts for part of the pound’s 86-pip range Thursday.
The dollar index sets the near-term direction. A sustained move below 101.50 would likely push GBP/USD through 1.3283 toward 1.3350. A rebound above 102.53 would bring 1.3137 back into play within days.
Friday is the next test. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks, offering the market’s last major policy signal before the Fed’s pre-meeting blackout. His tone on the October meeting will move the dollar more than any UK data due before the end of the month.
UK GDP Beats: 0.1% Growth in August Against a Forecast Contraction
The UK data gave sterling its own support. The UK economy expanded 0.1% month-on-month in August, slowing from 0.4% growth in July but beating expectations of a 0.1% contraction. July’s 0.4% gain matched June’s growth, giving the economy three straight positive months.
The three-month view looks stronger. UK GDP grew 0.4% in the May-to-July period compared with the previous three months. With August adding 0.1%, the economy is on course for a much stronger third quarter than the Bank of England expected.
The Bank’s own forecast is the benchmark. The Bank’s latest third-quarter growth projection stands at 0.4%, itself an upgrade from an earlier expectation of 0.1%. A quarter that exceeds 0.4% would show the economy running hotter than the central bank’s models, which strengthens the case for tighter policy.
The market reaction was immediate. GBP/USD rose to 1.3264, up 0.25% from Wednesday’s close, after the release. The data reinforced expectations of a November Bank of England rate hike.
Growth matters more than usual for sterling right now. In most cycles, the UK economy’s weakness has limited how far the Bank of England can tighten. This year, energy prices from the Middle East conflict are pushing inflation higher while growth holds up. That combination gives the Bank room to raise rates without triggering a recession, which supports the pound.
The contrast with the eurozone is sharp. Eurozone growth forecasts stand at 0.9% for 2026, and the ECB has signaled patience despite 3.8% inflation. UK growth is outperforming expectations while inflation rises, which points to a more hawkish central bank and a firmer currency.
The labor market adds context. The UK unemployment rate stood at 4.9%, with the harmonized rate for the first quarter of 2026 at 5.0%, above Germany’s 3.9% and the US rate of 4.3% but below France’s 8.2%. A 4.9% unemployment rate gives the Bank some slack, which tempers the hawkish case.
Public finances remain a background risk. Public sector net debt reached 95.1% of GDP at the end of August, up from 93.8% a year earlier. Rising debt with higher interest rates raises fiscal costs, which could weigh on gilts and sterling if markets start pricing fiscal stress.
Bank of England at 3.75%: Three Votes for a Hike
The Bank of England is the pound’s main support. At its September 16 meeting, the Monetary Policy Committee voted 6–3 to maintain Bank Rate at 3.75%. Three members voted to raise the rate by 25 basis points to 4%. The split was identical to July’s.
Three dissenters in two consecutive meetings is a strong signal. The committee needs only two more votes to shift to a hike. The August GDP beat adds weight to the hawkish side, and the next meeting in November is now a live decision for markets.
The inflation outlook drives the debate. UK CPI inflation rose to 3.1% in August from 2.9% in July and is likely to rise further over coming quarters. The MPC expects inflation to reach slightly above 4% in the first quarter of 2027. Before the Middle East conflict, the Bank expected inflation to fall to 2% from April 2026 and stay there for the rest of the year.
Services inflation offers some relief. Services inflation was 3.4% in August, unchanged from July and down from 4.5% in March. The Bank watches services closely because they reflect domestic costs. A stable services rate suggests energy is driving the headline increase, not wage-driven second-round effects.
The rate path has reversed. UK interest rates rose from 0.1% in December 2021 to 5.25% in August 2023, then fell by 1.5 percentage points from August 2024 to December 2025. Bank Rate has held at 3.75% since. A November hike would mark the first increase since 2023.
The policy gap with the Fed is narrow. The Fed’s target range stands at 3.75%-4.00% after its September hike. Bank Rate at 3.75% matches the lower end of that range, leaving a gap of 0 to 25 basis points. That compares with a 125-to-150-basis-point gap between the Fed and the ECB’s 2.50% deposit rate.
That gap explains sterling’s resilience. The rate differential is the main driver of major currency pairs. A near-zero gap between the UK and US means sterling doesn’t face the same carry disadvantage the euro faces. If the Bank of England hikes in November and the Fed holds in October, the gap would flip in sterling’s favor.
The risk is a Fed move first. If the Fed hikes on October 28, its range would rise to 4.00%-4.25%, opening a 25-to-50-basis-point gap over the Bank of England until November. That would pressure sterling in the short term.
Fed Odds: October Hike Pricing Jumps From 22% to 49%
The Federal Reserve sets the other side of the pair. Before Wednesday’s CPI, futures priced a 22.1% chance of a 25-basis-point hike at the October 27-28 FOMC meeting. After the release, odds jumped above 49% before settling below 45%. December hike odds stand at 89.7%.
The US inflation data justifies the pricing. September CPI rose 3.7% annual

articles.full_text:
USD/JPY extended its pullback from the 159.00 area, a three-week high, and fell to around 157.60, a one-week low, during Thursday’s Asian session. The move came as markets weighed the risk of Japanese official intervention alongside the Bank of Japan’s gradual tightening stance after taking its policy rate to a 31-year high of 1.25% in September. In the US, the initial lift to the dollar after Wednesday’s firmer Consumer Price Index proved fleeting as expectations built that the Federal Reserve will skip an October increase, pushing Treasury yields lower and encouraging further USD profit-taking, even as pricing still implies over an 85% chance of another rise by year-end.
Attention is also on reports that the BoJ may avoid a back-to-back hike in October, a factor that could restrain JPY strength. Later on Thursday, the US Producer Price Index is due, while Friday brings a speech from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh. Technically, the pair has broken the 100-period simple moving average support on the four-hour chart and bears are watching the 23.6% Fibonacci retracement; further downside targets include 38.2% at 156.71 and then 50.0% at 155.98, with 61.8% at 155.25. Resistance sits at the 100-period SMA near 157.97, ahead of the 159.07 swing high.
Derivatives Strategies and Risk Management
We suggest derivative traders prepare for sudden swings by using protective put options or downside hedges while USD/JPY trades around the 157.60 mark. Historical data shows that actual or threatened Japanese currency interventions can push the Yen up by 300 to 500 pips in a matter of hours. Trimming leverage on long exposure is a prudent step while market intervention fears remain high.
We advise waiting for a clear breach beneath the 23.6% Fibonacci retracement before committing to new bearish derivative positions. A sustained move lower opens up clear downside targets at the 38.2% level of 156.71 and the 50.0% retracement near 155.98. Utilizing short put option spreads allows traders to profit from this technical breakdown without facing uncapped risk if the Dollar rebounds suddenly.
Opportunity Assessment and Volatility Approaches
We see compelling value in setting up bullish call options if spot prices drop closer to the strong structural support band between 155.25 and 156.00. Futures market data currently reflects over an 85% chance that the Federal Reserve will raise borrowing costs by the end of the year, keeping the broader Dollar uptrend intact. Historically, wide yield differentials between the US and Japan have reasserted themselves once initial intervention panics cool off.

Sharp shifts in volatile energy prices and policy commentary could easily trigger a rapid retest of upper resistance levels at 157.97 and 159.07. articles.full_text:
Japanese Finance Minister Kaoru Yosano warned market speculators that Japan stands ready to intervene in the foreign-exchange market again if necessary.
Zhitong Finance APP learned that Japanese Finance Minister Katsunobu Kato warned market speculators that Japan is prepared to intervene in the foreign exchange market again if necessary. Earlier, the latest U.S. inflation data came in higher than expected, pushing the yen-dollar exchange rate to a near-term low this month.
She also stated that, since the U.S. and Japan jointly intervened to support the yen in July of this year, Tokyo and Washington have maintained their respective positions on exchange-rate issues.
On Thursday morning in Bangkok, before attending the G20 summit, Satsuki Katayama told reporters: "Our stance on foreign-exchange issues is entirely consistent with the signal we sent during our joint intervention with the other country. The U.S. side is currently aligned with us, and if necessary, we will act without hesitation."
Kazuki Katayama's remarks came against the backdrop of U.S. CPI data released on Wednesday, which showed the highest inflation level in five months, further weighing on the yen. On that day, the yen fell as low as 158.95 per U.S. dollar before narrowing its losses as U.S. Treasury yields retreated.
During this visit, Sayuki Katayama will attend a series of international finance and economic conferences. Finance ministers and central bank governors from participating countries are expected to engage in discussions on a range of global issues, including rising global bond yields and the financial risks posed by cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI).
Commenting on the recent surge in global bond yields, Sayaka Katayama noted that, among the major advanced economies, Japan is one of the few countries that can credibly demonstrate fiscal sustainability. She emphasized that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and her cabinet have repeatedly and explicitly pledged to steadily reduce the debt-to-GDP ratio and keep government borrowing within a prudent range.
"Not every country can make such a clear commitment as we have," said Kozue Katayama. "We can confidently articulate our fiscal responsibility, and I hope to send that message with unwavering resolve."

articles.title: CoreWeave bond yields near 15 percent as stock sinks on AI debt fears - Startup Fortune
articles.summary: CoreWeave bond yields near 15 percent as stock sinks on AI debt fears  Startup Fortune
articles.full_text:
CoreWeave's bonds are flashing a warning the stock chart alone never could. Yields on its unsecured notes jumped toward 15% this week, and credit default swap spreads nearly doubled in a matter of days.
CoreWeave shares fell as much as 16% on October 14, and the stock's slide wasn't the real story. The real story was happening in the bond market, where CoreWeave's unsecured notes due in 2032 sank below 80 cents on the dollar, pushing their yield above 15%, according to data cited by Forbes. That's up from around 9% over the summer. A corporate borrower paying 15% to raise money isn't getting a market rate. It's getting a distress rate.
Credit default swaps told the same story from a different angle. Spreads on CoreWeave's five-year debt, the cost of insuring against the company defaulting, jumped from 368 basis points on October 6 to 643 basis points by that Friday, according to Bloomberg data. Translate that into dollars and insuring $10 million of CoreWeave debt for five years now costs roughly $643,000 a year, nearly double what it cost a week earlier. Bond traders don't move spreads like that over a routine stock dip. They move them when they start pricing real odds of not getting paid back.
Equity investors sell a stock because they think it's overvalued or because sentiment turned. Bond investors demanding 15% are saying something sharper: they think there's a real chance the company can't service what it owes. CoreWeave carried roughly $35 billion in debt and $5.5 billion in cash as of June 30, according to the company's own disclosures, and it took on more since, including a $2 billion convertible note offering in September. The business model is simple to describe and expensive to run: borrow heavily to buy Nvidia GPUs and build data centers, then lease that capacity to hyperscalers and AI labs under multi-year contracts. It works as long as lenders believe the contracts will keep paying out faster than the debt comes due.
That belief took a hit on October 8, when CoreWeave shares fell nearly 8% after a report that OpenAI's annualized revenue at the end of September came in near $50 billion, below the nearly $70 billion figure that had circulated earlier. OpenAI is one of CoreWeave's largest customers, with contracts reported to be worth up to $11.9 billion. Microsoft accounts for roughly two-thirds of CoreWeave's revenue on its own, and Meta has committed $21 billion more. When the revenue picture for your biggest tenant gets murkier, the market that actually has to get repaid, the bondholders, reacts first and reacts hardest.
Brannin McBee, CoreWeave's co-founder, told the Financial Times the firm wants insurers' capital pools, which he calls effectively unlimited, to fund its GPU buildout as CDS spreads on its debt nearly doubled in a week. - insurance companies funding AI data center expansion - CoreWeave seeks unlimited capital from insurance industry
HSBC cut its price target on CoreWeave this month, flagging high funding needs and rising debt costs, according to a note covered by Yahoo Finance. Bernstein has held an Underperform rating through the stock's swings. Not every analyst agrees the alarm is warranted: Piper Sandler has a $153 target and Truist is at $165, well above where shares trade now. That split itself is a signal. When credit markets and equity analysts disagree this sharply about the same company, it usually means the credit market is seeing something the equity story hasn't priced in yet, or that it's overreacting to a liquidity scare that passes. CoreWeave still managed to get a $2.6 billion loan oversubscribed earlier this year, even as pricing widened, which tells you lenders remain willing to show up. They just want to be paid more to do it.
None of this is isolated to one company. CoreWeave has become the clearest proxy for a question hanging over the entire AI infrastructure buildout: whether leasing contracts tied to compute demand that might shift can reliably service tens of billions in borrowed capital. Oracle has piled up its own AI-linked debt. The IMF has flagged broader concentration risk in AI financing. If CoreWeave's bonds are the canary, the mine is the whole sector's debt-funded expansion.
Frankly, a 15% bond yield on a company with $99 billion in contracted backlog is not a company nobody will lend to. It's a company the market has decided to price like a risk, not a blue chip, and that repricing has consequences for every GPU-backed loan structured the same way.

articles.title: USD/JPY Forecast: Hot US Inflation Tests Japan's Yen Defence - Exchange Rates UK
articles.summary: USD/JPY Forecast: Hot US Inflation Tests Japan's Yen Defence  Exchange Rates UK
articles.full_text:
Japanese Yen Outlook: Intervention Risk Limits Dollar Upside
MUFG sees Japanese intervention risk limiting the US Dollar against the Yen, even as firmer US inflation puts renewed pressure on the exchange rate.
Japan's resistance to a weaker Yen faces a fresh test after US inflation exceeded expectations, but MUFG doubts the Dollar can sustain a move above ¥160.
The bank's near-term USD/JPY range of 156-160 allows for renewed Dollar strength while recognising the risk that a further depreciation would draw a response from Japanese authorities.
Wednesday's US consumer-price release showed core inflation rising 0.3% in September, against the 0.2% consensus cited by MUFG before the figures.
That outcome strengthens the immediate test of its range, without establishing that intervention is imminent or that the Federal Reserve will raise rates in October.
MUFG's Tokyo head of global markets research, Teppei Ino, had identified a renewed October rate-hike debate as a potential trigger for a break above the pair's 200-day moving average.
"We expect broad dollar strength would likely push the USD/JPY above its closely watched 200-day moving average if the CPI and Chair Warsh's speech instead trigger a sharp reversal in expectations and markets once again come to expect an October hike."
The moving average was around 158.50 when the bank made that assessment.
Why Japan's warning matters at 160
Ino says: "Even then, a break above 160 is likely to prove difficult."
Ino was referring to Katayama's interviews earlier in October:
"In interviews with several media outlets last weekend, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said that USD/JPY levels above 160 ahead of the coordinated intervention at the end of July represented an extremely weak yen."
"With President Donald Trump also expressing concern about yen undervaluation, her remarks could be read as signaling that the authorities would not tolerate a sustained rise in the USD/JPY above 160."
Official resistance changes the risks facing investors selling the Yen, because a currency-buying operation can force a rapid reversal even when US interest rates favour the Dollar.
The number is nevertheless MUFG's interpretation of officials' tolerance, rather than an announced exchange-rate ceiling.
Japan's fiscal message also matters to that assessment.
Ino says: "Katayama subsequently said the government would seek to fund measures including the consumption tax cut without relying on deficit-financing bonds, through a thorough review of special tax measures, government funds and other spending, and that this would be reflected in the FY27 budget process."
He adds: "Prime Minister Takaichi also said fiscal policy would be managed while closely monitoring its impact on interest rates, exchange rates and other developments, signaling an intention to maintain confidence in the yen."
"Katayama has also stressed the importance of consistent government messaging and maintaining market confidence in relation to the Takaichi administration's economic and fiscal policies, which Treasury Secretary Bessent has cited as a factor behind yen weakness."
Ino nevertheless doubts that a consistent government message alone will trigger outright Yen buying.
Japanese rates offer a separate source of support
MUFG also sees expectations of further Bank of Japan tightening helping the currency, following the central bank's September rate increase.
Its senior currency analyst Lee Hardman says: "In the current environment of broad-based US dollar strength, we expect the yen to continue to perform better against non-US dollar crosses."
That is a more limited claim than an immediate fall in USD/JPY.
The Yen can strengthen against European currencies while making little progress against a Dollar supported by higher US yields.
Exchange Rates UK's coverage of Japanese investors' persistent overseas buying identified another obstacle to a sustained recovery: higher domestic rates have yet to produce a decisive shift away from foreign assets.
Nor does MUFG assume that every US rate increase reflected in markets will ultimately be delivered.
Before Wednesday's inflation release, its research head Derek Halpenny said: "Still, we remain sceptical that inflation pressures will continue to build and while we expect the Fed to hike again in December, we do not expect the Fed to deliver the two further rate hikes currently priced by the markets."
The firmer core CPI figure challenges that assessment at the margin, but it is one release and MUFG's argument concerned how far the full tightening cycle would extend.
The next domestic signal comes from Bank of Japan board member Junko Koeda, whose 15 October speech in Kumamoto is confirmed on the central bank's calendar.
Ino does not expect an explicit October hike signal from that appearance or the governor's post-G20 comments.
"Neither her remarks nor Governor Kazuo Ueda's press conference after the G20 is likely to signal a rate hike at this month's meeting. However, they should provide an opportunity to keep expectations of further rate hikes alive, lending support to the yen."
USD/JPY exchange rate FAQ
What range does MUFG expect for USD/JPY?
Its near-term assessment is 156-160, rather than a dated year-end target.
Does 160 guarantee Japanese intervention?
No. MUFG sees heightened resistance around that level, but officials have not announced a fixed ceiling.
What could help the Yen recover?
Further Japanese tightening and a reduction in expected US rate increases would improve its interest-rate position.

articles.title: PBOC Conducts 700 Billion Yuan Outright Reverse Repo; October Net Injection of 400 Billion Yuan Signals Easing Stance - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: PBOC Conducts 700 Billion Yuan Outright Reverse Repo; October Net Injection of 400 Billion Yuan Signals Easing Stance  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
The People's Bank of China (PBOC) announced it will conduct a 700 billion yuan (approximately $104.7 billion) six-month outright reverse repo operation on October 15. Combined with the 200 billion yuan increase already delivered via the three-month tenor this month, total net injection across both tenors in October reaches 400 billion yuan (approximately $59.8 billion), making the shift in policy stance from neutral to accommodative increasingly clear.
According to the PBOC's open market outright reverse repo tender announcement released on October 14, the central bank will conduct the 700 billion yuan operation on October 15, 2026, using a fixed-quantity, rate-tender, multiple-price auction format to maintain ample liquidity in the banking system. The tenor is six months (182 days), with maturity on April 15, 2027, subject to extension if it falls on a holiday.
With 500 billion yuan (approximately $74.8 billion) in six-month outright reverse repos maturing in October, this operation represents an increased rollover of 200 billion yuan (approximately $29.9 billion). The previous two months saw equal-amount rollovers for this tenor. Combined with the 200 billion yuan net injection from the three-month tenor on October 8, the two tenors together delivered an incremental 400 billion yuan this month, compared with equal-amount rollovers for both tenors in September.
Q4 Bond Issuance Peak Requires Liquidity Support
Wang Qing, chief macro analyst at Golden Credit Rating, told Cailian Press that two factors likely explain the increased rollover in October. First, with growth-stabilization policies being deployed intensively—particularly the additional 550 billion yuan (approximately $82.3 billion) in local government bond issuance scheduled for Q4—government bond financing volumes will rise significantly in the coming period. Combined with the continued deployment of 800 billion yuan (approximately $119.6 billion) in new-type policy-based financial instruments, all of this requires PBOC liquidity support. By injecting medium-term liquidity through both tenors of outright reverse repos, the central bank helps facilitate smooth government bond issuance and bank lending, reflecting coordination between monetary and fiscal policy.
Dong Ximiao, chief economist at Zhaolian and executive director of the Shanghai Institute of Finance and Development, believes the October increase is well-targeted. First, medium- and long-term liquidity maturing in October totals as much as 2.4 trillion yuan, comprising 1 trillion yuan in three-month outright reverse repos, 500 billion yuan in six-month outright reverse repos, and 900 billion yuan (approximately $134.6 billion) in Medium-term Lending Facility (MLF) loans—the heaviest maturity pressure of the year, requiring the PBOC to offset in advance. Second, net government bond financing is still expected to reach 1.31 trillion to 1.43 trillion yuan, concentrated in the latter half of the month. With the tax payment deadline extended to October 26–28, liquidity disturbances will cluster in the second half, and the early injection of six-month funds can effectively smooth cross-month volatility.
Following the operation, the outstanding balance of outright reverse repos will rise further in October, marginally easing pressure on banks' medium- and long-term liability positions. However, the combined window of MLF maturities and the tax period in late October will remain a key juncture for observing the PBOC's subsequent rollover intensity.
Short-term Funding Conditions Remain Loose and Stable
On the same day, the PBOC also conducted a 56 billion yuan (approximately $8.4 billion) seven-day reverse repo operation, fully meeting primary dealers' demand. According to Choice data, no reverse repos matured that day, resulting in a net injection of 56 billion yuan into the open market.
On the funding rate front, the overnight Shanghai Interbank Offered Rate (Shibor) fell 0.8 basis points to 1.288% on October 13, while the seven-day tenor declined 0.5 basis points to 1.341%. At the close, the weighted average DR007 rate rose to 1.3446%, while the Shanghai Stock Exchange's one-day government bond reverse repo rate (GC001) fell to 1.414%.
Changjiang Fixed Income noted that funding pressure this week is generally modest, and funding rates are expected to remain stable. On one hand, net government bond payments this week are relatively low; on the other, the tax filing deadline has been extended to October 26, meaning tax-period effects will likely concentrate in late October.
RRR Cut Expectations Pushed Further Back
Wang Qing noted that on September 29, the PBOC adjusted several structural monetary policy tools to strengthen support for infrastructure investment, technology financing, and small and micro enterprise lending. Combined with exports expected to maintain high growth of around 30% through year-end, the likelihood of deploying aggregate monetary policy tools such as rate cuts and RRR reductions in the near term has diminished.
He pointed out that currently and for the foreseeable future, the PBOC will primarily rely on medium-term liquidity tools such as outright reverse repos and MLF rollovers to moderately strengthen counter-cyclical adjustment. As the central bank injects medium-term liquidity at scale through these tools, RRR cuts will be postponed, reflecting a degree of substitutability between the two policy tool categories.
Zheshang Fixed Income observed that while funding conditions currently feel loose, DR001 has remained above 1.35%, presenting a pattern of "loose in quantity but not in price," which has dampened investor enthusiasm for short-dated assets. Going forward, repo rates are entering a low-volatility era, and short-dated instruments closely tied to funding conditions will also enter a "static curve."
Market attention has also focused on the relatively low core excess reserves in the commercial banking system. Analysts believe the fundamental reason is that the PBOC's medium- and long-term liquidity injection this year has been insufficient, with a preference for smoothing seasonal frictions through overnight reverse repos rather than injecting medium- and long-term liquidity through MLF, RRR cuts, or government bond trading. This "withdraw long, inject short" approach to open market operations has pushed funding conditions back into a structural shortage framework, creating loose conditions at month-end and quarter-end junctures while the "long-money shortage" at commercial banks persists.
Looking ahead, Dong Ximiao said that Federal Reserve rate hikes have reinforced external constraints, and the Loan Prime Rate (LPR) will most likely remain unchanged in the near term. Whether it declines in the future depends on domestic economic recovery, price trends, bank net interest margins, and changes in the external environment. He also emphasized that China's monetary policy toolbox is rich, and there remains room and possibility for further strengthening monetary policy implementation.
The outright reverse repo tool was officially launched in October 2024, with primary dealers in open market operations as counterparties. In principle, operations are conducted once per month, with tenors not exceeding one year. The tool was established to maintain reasonably ample liquidity in the banking system and further enrich the PBOC's monetary policy toolbox.

articles.title: Sebi proposes market cap-based SME IPO norms, seeks public comments on regulatory overhaul - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Sebi proposes market cap-based SME IPO norms, seeks public comments on regulatory overhaul  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
In its latest consultation paper, the regulator proposed that issuers with post-issue market capitalisation of up to Rs 1,000 crore be required to list on the SME platform. Those with market capitalisation above Rs 1,000 crore and up to Rs 4,000 crore could also opt for the SME platform, subject to additional financial reporting requirements.
Sebi has invited public comments on the proposed changes to the Sebi (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018, until November 4, 2026.
Market cap to replace paid-up capital
Under the existing framework, issuers with post-issue paid-up capital of up to Rs 10 crore can access the SME platform, while those with paid-up capital above Rs 10 crore and up to Rs 25 crore may also issue securities under the framework.
An issuer that initially files under the SME framework could continue with that route if its market capitalisation exceeds Rs 1,000 crore but remains at or below Rs 4,000 crore. If it exceeds Rs 4,000 crore, the issuer would have to refile under the main board framework.
Higher profitability threshold
Sebi has proposed raising the minimum operating profitability requirement for SME IPOs. Under the existing framework, an issuer must have operating profit of at least Rs 1 crore from operations in at least two of the three preceding financial years. The proposal would require average operating profit of at least Rs 3 crore a year over the preceding three financial years, based on restated consolidated financial statements.
Issuers that do not meet the profitability requirement could use an alternative eligibility route through the book-building process, subject to at least 75% of the net offer being allotted to qualified institutional buyers (QIBs). If the required allocation is not achieved, the entire subscription money would have to be refunded. This route would not exempt issuers from other SME-specific requirements relating to business track record, conversion or reorganisation, and promoter stability.
Changes to business continuity requirements
The consultation paper proposes replacing the existing requirement to complete one full financial year after converting a proprietorship concern, partnership firm, or limited liability partnership (LLP) into a company with four consecutive completed financial quarters from the conversion date or the latest effective date of a qualifying business reorganisation.
Also read: Which bank stock should you buy ahead of Q2 results - HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Yes Bank or Axis Bank?
The issuer would also have to file at least one annual audited financial statement, or part thereof, prepared after the conversion or reorganisation with the Registrar of Companies before filing the draft offer document.
The proposed framework would extend to reorganisations in which an issuer derives more than 50% of its revenue from businesses previously carried on by a proprietorship concern, partnership firm or LLP. It also proposes a one-year seasoning requirement following a complete change in promoters or an acquisition of more than 50% of the shareholding by new promoters.
Changes to application and allotment
Sebi has proposed reducing the minimum application value for SME IPOs to Rs 1 lakh, while retaining a minimum application size of four lots, each worth at least Rs 25,000.
The proposals include allowing anchor investor allocation in book-built SME issues, with up to 60% of the portion available for QIB allocation eligible to be allocated to anchor investors.
For issues using the alternative eligibility route, the proposed allocation framework would provide for at least 75% of the net offer to QIBs, not more than 15% to non-institutional investors and not more than 10% to retail individual investors.
The minimum number of allottees in an SME IPO is proposed to increase from 200 to 500. Each retail individual investor would receive at least one minimum lot, subject to availability, with remaining shares allotted proportionately without being restricted to multiples of the minimum lot.
Sebi has also proposed reducing the trading lot for SME-listed securities to one share, replacing the existing price-band-based lot-size framework.
Underwriting and market making
The regulator has proposed removing the requirement for 100% underwriting of SME IPOs and the additional requirement for lead managers to underwrite at least 15% of the issue size on their own account.
Under the proposed framework, main board underwriting provisions would apply to SME issues, except that the 75% QIB portion under the alternative eligibility route would not require underwriting.
The consultation paper also proposes a minimum subscription requirement of 90%, with a refund where that threshold is not achieved. In line with this proposal, Sebi has proposed removing the existing requirement for the registrar to confirm that at least 90% of the offer has been subscribed before the announcement of issue closure.
Sebi has proposed removing compulsory market making for SME securities. The existing framework requires market making for at least three years from listing or migration from the main board, with the market maker required to maintain inventory of at least 5% of the securities proposed to be listed as of the allotment date.
The revised one-share trading lot and removal of compulsory market making would take effect only when Sebi issues a separate circular rescinding the existing trading-lot circular. Until then, existing market-making requirements would continue to apply, including to issuers listed after notification of the revised framework but before the separate circular is issued.
Lock-in and migration to main board
Under the proposed framework, the minimum promoters' contribution would remain locked in for three years from allotment, while promoters' holdings in excess of the minimum contribution would be locked in for one year.
The lock-in period for pre-issue capital held by persons other than promoters and the promoter group is proposed to be reduced from one year to six months. Specified securities held by the promoter group would remain subject to a separate one-year lock-in.
Existing lock-in obligations for companies already listed on the SME platform when the revised framework is notified would continue until the applicable periods expire. The changes would not retrospectively extinguish or modify those obligations.

Sebi has also proposed replacing paid-up capital-based migration thresholds with market capitalisation-based criteria. Under the proposed framework, migration to the main board would be linked to market capitalisation of Rs 1,000 crore or more but below Rs 4,000 crore, while migration would be mandatory if market capitalisation exceeds Rs 4,000 crore, subject to the applicable main board eligibility requirements.
Existing SME-listed companies would continue to follow the current migration framework, including paid-up capital-based thresholds. Companies listed on the SME platform after notification of the revised framework would be governed by the proposed market capitalisation-based criteria.
The consultation paper also sets out transitional arrangements for issuers that have already filed draft offer documents. Main board IPOs filed before notification of the revised framework would continue under the existing rules. Certain issuers that have filed draft offer documents for SME IPOs but have not obtained in-principle exchange approval or filed the relevant offer document may choose between the existing and revised frameworks, subject to the prescribed conditions.
SME IPOs raise Rs 40,222 crore
A total of 1,496 entities had been listed on SME platforms since inception as of July 31, 2026, including those that subsequently migrated to the main board. Of these, 365 companies had migrated to the main board.
Funds raised through SME IPOs since inception stood at Rs 40,222 crore, while the market capitalisation of entities listed on SME platforms, including those that had migrated, stood at Rs 4,70,984 crore, according to data from the National Stock Exchange and BSE cited in the consultation paper.
Sebi said the review seeks to make the regulatory framework proportionate to the size and nature of SME issuers, reduce avoidable compliance and fund-raising costs, facilitate wider capital market participation and retain safeguards necessary for investor protection and market integrity.

articles.title: Upward shift in the long-end U.S. Treasury interest rate threshold: Market psychological adaptation to interest rate critical points has risen to 6% - Moomoo
articles.summary: Upward shift in the long-end U.S. Treasury interest rate threshold: Market psychological adaptation to interest rate critical points has risen to 6%  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
The market previously viewed a 5% yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note as a critical threshold for risk assets, a level that triggered the financial crisis in 2007. However, despite yields breaking above 5%, U.S. equities have not experienced the anticipated deep correction. In fact, institutional assessments of the interest rate pressure threshold have risen to 6%, with some perspectives even pointing to 7%. This article analyzes changes in major asset class pricing in a high long-term bond yield environment from four dimensions: shifts in market psychology, sources of equity market resilience, the profitability paradox in the banking sector, and potential risks associated with optimistic expectations.
Reshaping Perceptions of Interest Rate Thresholds: 5% Is History as Risk Thresholds Continue to Rise
Investors' assessment of the "danger zone" for U.S. Treasury yields is not static but evolves dynamically with market conditions. Historical experience from 2007 led the market to long regard the 5% yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note as a watershed moment for equity market pressure. However, after yields actually surpassed 5%, the equity market remained resilient.
A Bank of America Global Fund Manager Survey shows that 64% of fund managers believe the stock market will only face substantial impact when the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rises to 6%. Many institutions judge the pressure threshold to be even higher, with market discussions beginning to consider the possibility of "6.5% becoming the new 5%, or even 7%."
Current mainstream institutional expectations are relatively optimistic: most fund managers believe yields in this cycle will struggle to reach 6%, and long-end interest rates are likely to decline subsequently. Several prominent bond market bears have turned cautiously bullish: Pimco has reduced its underweight position in U.S. Treasuries, while Blackstone favors short-term bonds. Supporting this expectation is the market view that the hawkish panic triggered by the Jackson Hole meeting was overinterpreted, and signals from the President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York that no rate hikes are needed next year have eased tightening expectations. This shift in market expectations essentially represents an adaptive repricing by asset allocators to the macro environment of "higher for longer" interest rates. However, it must be clarified that psychological acceptance of high interest rates does not mean asset prices have fully priced in the tail risks of further rate increases. Such optimistic judgments deferring risk carry significant uncertainty.
U.S. Equity Resilience in a High-Interest-Rate Environment: Tech Earnings Serve as a Valuation Buffer
Under classic valuation frameworks, rising risk-free rates increase discount rates, suppressing growth stock valuations. However, during the current phase of rising long-term bond yields, the resilience of the U.S. stock market has been primarily supported by strong earnings in the technology sector.
Barclays estimates that the semiconductor sector accounts for nearly one-fifth of the S&P 500's market capitalization and contributes more than one-third of overall earnings growth; earnings expectations for the Bloomberg-tracked SOX Semiconductor Index continue to be revised upward. Capital expenditure intensity is the core variable determining whether this tech boom can sustain. A few leading companies continue to make substantial capital expenditures, widening the earnings gap. Capital spending in this AI industrial cycle exhibits distinct concentration among top players, with heavy investments by a few giants dominating overall industry earnings expectations. Industry prosperity is highly dependent on the sustainability of capital expenditure plans by these leading firms, presenting significant single-point risk. Fund managers' optimistic pricing is built on the assumption that the AI-driven capital expenditure cycle will continue. If capital spending slows, the suppressive effect of high long-term bond yields on stock valuations will quickly manifest.
The U.S. CPI data for September is the next key observation window. Inflation readings will directly influence Federal Reserve policy expectations and drive the direction of long-term bond yields, serving as a crucial node for validating current market logic. As a core indicator measuring the stickiness of service and goods inflation, if the reading exceeds expectations, the market will reprice the duration of the Fed's tight policy, creating the possibility for long-end U.S. Treasury yields to surge again.
Banking Sector Amid Rising Rates: Net Interest Margins Hit Record Highs as Valuation Logic Reverses
The conventional paradigm holds that rising interest rates benefit banks' net interest margins (NIM). Recent earnings reports from major U.S. banks confirm short-term gains: JPMorgan, Citi, and Wells Fargo & Co reported a combined net interest income of $56.5 billion in the third quarter, with loan-related net interest income hitting record highs for five consecutive quarters. JPMorgan’s guidance for continued growth in interest income next year indicates that credit demand remains robust in the near term.
However, the banking sector is exhibiting a paradox of "improving profitability but weakening stock prices." Despite many large banks meeting or even exceeding earnings expectations, their share prices remain under pressure. This stems from two core contradictions:
1. Deterioration of the yield curve shape. Selling pressure on long-term bonds has flattened the yield curve, compressing banks' deposit-lending spreads. A further inversion of the curve would not only signal an impending economic recession but also directly erode profits from lending activities. The business model of commercial banks inherently relies on maturity mismatch—borrowing short and lending long. A flat or inverted yield curve directly compresses the space for maturity arbitrage, undermining the core profitability model of banks. The market no longer simply assumes that high interest rates are beneficial for banks; instead, it is beginning to weigh the long-term risks that high rates pose to bank balance sheets.
2. Divergence in trading business structures. Revenues from fixed income, foreign exchange, and commodities trading generally fell short of expectations. In contrast, equity trading benefited from market volatility and AI-driven equity financing, resulting in substantial revenue growth and becoming one of the few bright spots within the sector. This divergence illustrates that rising interest rate volatility affects different trading lines asymmetrically: fixed income businesses suffer greater shocks from rising rates, while equity investment banking and stock trading benefit from market volatility and the surge in equity financing.
In short, the dividend from net interest income can no longer sustainably support bank valuations, as investors are increasingly pricing in the forward-looking risks associated with high interest rates.
The overlooked fragility behind optimistic market expectations
The current market consensus predicts that the upper limit for long-end yields is around 6%, with interest rates set to decline soon, tech earnings maintaining high growth, and the equity market steadily weathering high interest rates. However, this scenario contains significant vulnerabilities.
Interest rate tipping points exhibit non-linear characteristics. Markets can gradually digest a slow rise in yields; however, once the institutional consensus threshold of 6% is breached, asset selling may become self-reinforcing. Historical market crises have often erupted after such critical thresholds were crossed. Financial market risk thresholds are not linearly smooth; small increases in interest rates often have limited impact, but crossing key psychological barriers can trigger passive trading behaviors such as stop-loss orders and portfolio rebalancing, creating a negative feedback loop.
Optimistic expectations are heavily dependent on declining inflation. If September's CPI exceeds expectations, fears of tighter Federal Reserve policy will resurface, pushing long-term bond yields higher and placing significant pressure on growth stock valuations. Growth stocks concentrate their cash flows in the distant future, making them far more sensitive to changes in discount rates than value stocks.
Banking profit dividends are cyclical. Growth in net interest income is not sustainable indefinitely. Once credit demand declines, deposit costs rise, or the yield curve becomes deeply inverted, bank profitability will come under rapid pressure. As competition for market deposits intensifies, rising deposit rates will gradually erode net interest margins. This is a lagging variable relative to the rate-hiking cycle and constitutes the underlying logic for the market's current caution toward bank stocks.
Conclusion
The market risk threshold for the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield has shifted higher, with institutions widely regarding 6% as a critical stress level for equity markets. Currently, U.S. equities are relying on technology sector earnings to offset the impact of rising interest rates, and net interest income in the U.S. banking sector has reached record highs; however, stock prices have already priced in the risks associated with prolonged high interest rates. The prevailing market consensus bets on an imminent decline in long-term interest rates, a view that hinges heavily on inflation trends and Federal Reserve policy.
Investors should remain vigilant: the market's psychological adaptation to interest rate thresholds does not imply that assets can indefinitely withstand higher yields. A rise in long-term interest rates fundamentally represents a repricing process across all asset classes.
