articles.title: ECB says AI is weakening workers’ bargaining power as Europe falls behind - Brussels Signal
articles.summary: ECB says AI is weakening workers’ bargaining power as Europe falls behind  Brussels Signal
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank (ECB) has warned that the spread of artificial intelligence could weaken the hand of euro area workers in pay talks, even without any rise in unemployment.
Philip Lane, the ECB’s chief economist, said in remarks to the International AI Summit in Dublin on October 13 that the scope for AI to replace some types of worker might also moderate wage growth and reduce the labour share in total income.
He said the ECB did not yet see a major change in aggregate employment trends, though hiring plans were muted, which weighed in particular on the prospects of new graduates.
Its surveys showed wide variation across industries. Workers in sectors benefiting from the build-out of AI infrastructure were more optimistic than those in knowledge-intensive sectors facing a greater risk of substitution.
The net effect on jobs would also depend on the evolution of “labour costs versus token prices”, Lane said.
Adoption was already significant and growing quickly, he added. The share of workers reporting that they used AI at work had doubled in two years to 52 per cent, from 26 per cent in 2024, while firms were set to devote about 10 per cent of their total investment to AI this year.
Even so, the European AI surge was of a different order to the boom in the United States and East Asia, he said. Digital investment in the United States had grown twice as fast as in the euro area over the past two years, and American workers spent two to three times as much of the working week using AI as their counterparts in the largest euro area economies.
The Stanford AI Index counted 59 notable AI models produced in the United States and 35 in China, against one each from France, whose flagship Mistral unveiled a new model this month, and the United Kingdom. The United States hosts 75 per cent of global AI computing capacity, Lane said, and Europe just 5 per cent.
He also tied the global investment boom to the cost of money in Europe. Because the European boom was far smaller, the global rise in long-term interest rates had spilled over into the euro area bond market and amounted to a material tightening of financial conditions.
That was a relevant factor for the ECB in deciding its monetary policy stance, he said. High equity valuations at AI firms and a surge in AI-related debt also carried risks to financial stability if investor sentiment turned.
Lane closed by saying Europe had much to gain by seizing the AI opportunity, and that the ECB was committed to making sure the transformation was underpinned by price stability and financial stability.

articles.title: AI Investment Significantly Tightening Eurozone Financial Conditions, Influencing ECB Decisions, Lane Says - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: AI Investment Significantly Tightening Eurozone Financial Conditions, Influencing ECB Decisions, Lane Says  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Philip Lane, Chief Economist and Executive Board member of the European Central Bank (ECB), said in a speech in Dublin on the 13th that the expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI) by Eurozone companies may be weakening workers' wage bargaining power, and that massive AI-related investment underway globally is significantly tightening financial conditions in the Eurozone to a level that is influencing ECB policy decisions.
Against the backdrop of surging energy prices, the Eurozone inflation rate is running at nearly double the ECB's 2% target. Policymakers are watching for signs of "second-round effects" in which price increases spill over into wages and other areas, but they currently judge that no such signs have been confirmed, particularly in wage growth.
Lane explained that while AI is not fundamentally altering employment dynamics itself, subdued corporate hiring plans are limiting workers' bargaining power as they seek compensation for high inflation. He suggested that such structural factors may lie behind the sluggish wage growth amid high inflation.
"AI's potential to substitute for certain job categories could weaken workers' bargaining power, restrain wage growth, and reduce the labor share of total income," he said in the speech.
AI Investment Pushing Up Long-Term Interest Rates
While avoiding direct commentary on current monetary policy operations, Lane offered an in-depth assessment of how AI investment financing is affecting the broader financial environment. He noted that companies worldwide are borrowing heavily to fund AI investments, which in turn is pushing up borrowing costs for all borrowers. He analyzed that this dynamic is tightening financing conditions to an extent that bears on ECB policy decisions.
"The spillover to Eurozone bond markets means that rising long-term interest rates represent a significant tightening of financial conditions for the Eurozone," he said, adding, "This is an important factor in the ECB's determination of the appropriate monetary policy stance."
The remarks have drawn attention among market participants. The ECB has been raising rates to prevent inflation from becoming entrenched, but some economists point out that if the tightening of financing conditions associated with AI investment contributes to curbing prices, the scale of tightening the ECB needs to implement could be smaller.
Longer-Term Boost to Potential Growth
Lane also addressed the longer-term structural impact of AI on the Eurozone economy. He expressed the view that AI could raise potential output and trend growth, lifting the economy's potential "speed limit."
He emphasized that for Europe in particular, AI's potential to offset the economic impact of the expected decline in the working-age population would be "especially valuable."
Ahead of its next policy meeting, the ECB is in a phase of carefully assessing inflation trends and changes in financial conditions. The impact of expanding AI investment on financial conditions may affect the real economy through channels different from conventional policy rate adjustments, and it is beginning to be recognized as a new variable in future policy decisions.

articles.title: Treasury Yields Hit 24-Year High, Yet Corporate Default Risk Stays Muted - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Treasury Yields Hit 24-Year High, Yet Corporate Default Risk Stays Muted  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
A sharp climb in benchmark borrowing costs has done little to shake confidence in the balance sheets of America's biggest companies, a divergence that defies the traditional logic of credit markets.
The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note surged from a 2026 low of 3.96% in February to 5.31% on October 5, the highest level in 24 years. Normally, such a move would signal trouble for corporate borrowers. Higher interest expense, combined with an economic slowdown that pressures earnings, should make it harder for firms to generate enough cash to cover their coupon payments, pushing default risk higher.
Yet the opposite has happened. Data from ICE Indices shows that the spread on the US investment grade corporate bond index actually narrowed between February and September, falling from 86 basis points to 84. The spread represents the extra compensation investors demand for taking on default risk relative to risk-free government debt.
Marty Fridson, publisher of Income Securities Investor, argues that the apparent anomaly has a solid economic explanation. The relationship between Treasury yields and corporate spreads is inversely correlated, not proportional as many market veterans were once taught.
"The narrowest spread, 54 basis points, occurred in September 1997, when the Treasury yield was at 6.12%, near the high end of its range," Fridson wrote in a column published October 13. "By contrast, the yield was only around the middle of its range, at 2.96%, when the spread reached its maximum of 608 basis points in November 2008."
The same pattern holds across the high-yield market, though there is an important exception. Bonds in the lowest credit rating segment, CCC and below, have seen their spreads widen as borrowing costs have climbed. That suggests investors are drawing a sharper line between companies with genuine refinancing vulnerabilities and those with stronger financial positions.
Why Rising Yields Can Strengthen Credit
Fridson identifies two key sources of higher Treasury yields, both of which tend to bolster rather than weaken corporate credit quality.
First, interest rates can rise because a vibrant economy creates strong demand for debt capital. Companies borrow to finance investments in attractive business opportunities. A thriving economy should boost the earnings that enable firms to make their required interest payments.
Second, rates can climb because investors expect higher future inflation. That also benefits borrowers. If inflation turns out to be higher than the market anticipated when firms issued their bonds, they get to repay the borrowed money in cheaper dollars. Inflation can have negative impacts on corporate profitability, but as a general rule, it works in favor of debtors.
On the flip side, when the economy weakens or markets panic, credit spreads can widen even as the Federal Reserve cuts its policy rate to stabilize conditions. That is precisely what happened in November 2008, when spreads peaked at 608 basis points while Treasury yields sat at just 2.96%.
The Refinancing Cushion
Even with yields climbing, the immediate impact on corporate income statements is likely to be limited. Thoughtful corporate treasurers have structured their debt with staggered maturities, eliminating the risk of an instantaneous spike in interest payments when rates rise.
For most companies, only a small portion of their debt comes due in the near term and would need to be refinanced at higher yields. As a result, the overall borrowing costs for investment grade firms remain largely insulated from short-term rate shocks.
This explains why default risk for medium- and high-rated bonds has not risen materially despite the surge in Treasury yields. In fact, the data suggests the opposite is true.
Academic research has repeatedly confirmed the counterintuitive pattern. Numerous studies have found that spreads typically narrow as yields rise, contradicting the logical-sounding argument that higher borrowing costs must translate into greater default risk.
The current environment appears to be another chapter in that well-documented relationship. Investors are treating the rise in Treasury yields as a signal of economic strength and manageable inflation expectations, not as a warning sign for corporate credit quality. The exception remains at the lowest rungs of the credit ladder, where the combination of higher rates and weaker fundamentals has already begun to bite.
Fridson is a former CFA Institute board member and has served as an advisor to the Federal Reserve. The views expressed in his column are his own.

articles.title: Oil prices rise for fourth straight day as Saudi-Houthi clashes intensify; WTI tops $94 - BigGo Finance

articles.full_text:
International oil prices rose for a fourth consecutive trading session as military conflict in the Middle East expanded into an exchange of strikes between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi rebels. U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude settled in the $94-per-barrel range, closing in on the $95 threshold, while Brent crude maintained strength above the $100 level.
On October 13 (local time), WTI for November delivery settled at $94.14 per barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), up $0.40 (0.4%) from the previous session — approximately 130,000 won. Although profit-taking emerged intraday following the prior day's two-week high, Middle East supply concerns drew buyers back into the market.
The direct catalyst for the day's gains was the intensifying clash between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi rebels. According to Reuters, the Houthis claimed that the Saudi-led coalition attacked Yemen's capital, Sanaa. The coalition had earlier warned residents to evacuate from oil storage facilities on the outskirts of Sanaa. The Houthis attacked King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh on October 10–11, and Aramco's headquarters complex in Dhahran, eastern Saudi Arabia, was reportedly damaged during the assault.
The expansion of attack targets from crude production facilities to transportation infrastructure is heightening market concerns. In particular, as crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz face exposure to Iranian threats, some very large crude carriers (VLCCs) have reportedly abandoned entry into the Persian Gulf and rerouted. The U.S. government stated it has provided support for the transport of more than 19 million barrels of crude per day through the Strait of Hormuz.
President Donald Trump took to social media that day, accusing the Houthi rebels of "viciously attacking Saudi Arabia and deliberately driving up oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections." He stressed that the United States would confront the Houthis after the midterms and would "never forget" these actions.
Trump's remarks introduced another layer of uncertainty into the market, as observers noted that direct U.S. involvement in the Saudi-Houthi conflict could further deteriorate the Middle East situation. Michael Lynch of Strategic Energy & Economic Research said, "There is a possibility the U.S. could intervene in the Saudi-Houthi exchange, and that has raised concerns that the situation could worsen."
Oil prices have traced a steep upward trajectory this year following the outbreak of war between the United States and Iran. Brent crude has surged more than 70% year-to-date, and with attacks recently expanding beyond production facilities to shipping lanes, tensions in energy markets have intensified further.
Some analysts, however, caution against market overreaction. Pavel Molchanov, an analyst at Raymond James, noted, "New headlines emerge every day, but the overall situation in the Persian Gulf has not fundamentally changed over the past three months." He explained that tanker operators are gradually becoming accustomed to ship-to-ship crude transfers at sea to maintain exports while reducing exposure to Iranian attack risks.
Indeed, crude transport volumes through the Persian Gulf have recovered to near pre-war levels. However, concerns remain that renewed Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz could stall the normalization of supply flows.
Meanwhile, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) lowered its 2026 global oil demand forecast in its October monthly report released that day. Despite heightened vigilance over the Middle East situation, the downward demand revision had a limited impact on oil prices.
The gold market edged lower. December gold futures on the COMEX settled at $4,177.30 per troy ounce, down $13.30 (0.3%) from the previous session — approximately 5.6 million won. As the decline in long-term Treasury yields narrowed, the relative appeal of non-interest-bearing gold diminished, contributing to selling pressure.
With Middle East supply risks serving as the key near-term support for oil prices, market participants are closely watching whether the Saudi-Houthi conflict escalates further, the possibility of U.S. military intervention, and the scale of any shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. With the vulnerability of the crude supply chain once again in focus, heightened oil price volatility appears unavoidable in the near term.

articles.title: Catch up time! Oil settles mixed, Brent near $106; booms reported near Aramco HQ in Dhahran - investingLive
articles.summary: Catch up time! Oil settles mixed, Brent near $106; booms reported near Aramco HQ in Dhahran  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- Oil settled mixed, with Brent down about 1% near $106 and WTI up near $94, as hopes over a US-Russia diesel deal offset Saudi-Houthi escalation. Booms were reported near Aramco’s Dhahran HQ, while OPEC said Saudi output jumped sharply in September.
The deferred curve is carrying the bigger signal. WTI for calendar 2027 hit a record for a 12th straight session, around $84, and Brent’s 2027 strip set records on Monday near $90. That suggests the market is pricing a lasting supply deficit, not just a front-month war premium. Diesel remains the pressure point, with product strength outpacing crude and keeping refining margins elevated. With the Dhahran reports coming late in the day, the Asian open is the first real test of how much Aramco infrastructure risk gets priced back into Brent. A narrower Brent-WTI spread also points to Middle East risk being offset at the margin by the prospect of more Russian barrels.
---
I'm doing a bit of a catch up on crude if its of any use to anyone.
Earlier:
---
Oil is caught between a Russian diesel deal that promises more supply and a Saudi-Houthi war that now reaches the doorstep of Aramco’s headquarters.
Summary:
- Brent settled down nearly $1, or circa 1%, at around $106, after Monday’s highest close since mid-September; WTI rose about 40 cents to around $94, its highest close since late September
- Hopes the US-Russia diesel export deal could free up Russian supply offset Middle East risk; the Kremlin said the deal has no direct link to Ukraine peace talks
- Loud booms were reported near Saudi Aramco’s Dhahran headquarters amid an escalating Saudi-Houthi war; Aramco did not comment
- OPEC said OPEC+ output rose sharply in September, led by Saudi Arabia lifting crude production to around 8.4 million bpd from around 6.2 million in August
- OPEC cut its 2026 demand growth forecast for a sixth straight month and raised next year’s outlook, citing the need to rebuild inventories depleted by the Iran war
- Trump accused the Houthis of trying to drive up oil prices before the US midterm elections
Oil prices settled mixed on Tuesday as hopes that a US-Russia deal on diesel exports could release more supply from Moscow offset an escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis that threatens Gulf energy infrastructure.
Brent crude futures settled at around $106 a barrel, down nearly $1 or circa 1%, after closing on Monday at their highest level since mid-September. US West Texas Intermediate rose about 40 cents to settle at around $94, its strongest close since late September, Reuters reported.
The Kremlin said it saw no direct link between the diesel deal and its position on Ukraine peace talks. It was responding to a Reuters report that US President Donald Trump’s envoys had told Ukrainian officials the arrangement was part of an effort to bring Russia back to negotiations. Trump said the Russian diesel was destined for the rest of the world rather than the United States. US diesel futures still traded up circa 5%, a sign the market remains unconvinced the deal will ease tight product supply. Diesel prices have recently hit record highs in many regions after Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy sites and Iranian attacks on Middle East infrastructure.
In the Gulf, loud booms were heard on Tuesday night near Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, the centre of the kingdom’s oil industry, according to six sources cited by Reuters. One source said the building had been struck, though it was unclear whether by a direct hit or falling debris, and an evacuation order was issued, four sources said. Aramco did not comment. The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of an intercepted missile had fallen on a residential area.
Earlier, the coalition had targeted a Yemen Petroleum Company fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa, according to Houthi-run media, and the Houthis threatened Saudi oil facilities in response. The group has spent a week firing missiles and drones at Saudi targets, including Riyadh’s international airport. Trump accused the Houthis of deliberately trying to push up oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections and said he would make a decision on Iran very soon. Separately, reports said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had discussed with Trump last week the possibility of a joint operation against Iranian military and nuclear targets, a call that came before Trump said he would not strike Iran ahead of the midterms. Iranian authorities said a tanker they described as violating rules caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.
On the supply side, OPEC said OPEC+ production rose sharply in September, driven by Saudi Arabia lifting crude output to around 8.4 million barrels per day from around 6.2 million in August, despite continued disruption to Hormuz shipments. Around a fifth of global oil supply moved through the strait before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. OPEC also trimmed its 2026 demand growth forecast for a sixth consecutive month while raising its outlook for next year, citing the need to rebuild depleted inventories.
In a further sign of widening geopolitical strain, Britain’s domestic intelligence chief said Russia and Iran were stepping up hybrid warfare campaigns in the UK. With the Dhahran reports landing late in the session, traders will look to the Asian open for the first market verdict on the risk to Saudi infrastructure.

articles.title: The AI opportunity for Europe - European Central Bank
articles.summary: The AI opportunity for Europe  European Central Bank
articles.full_text:
- SPEECH
The AI opportunity for Europe
Dinner remarks by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at The International AI Summit
Dublin, 13 October 2026
AI is a general purpose technology that can improve global living standards and the global knowledge frontier by expanding access to information and raising productivity.
That said, delivering the benefits from AI depends on a host of different actors playing their part in supporting the transformation of the economy. The list is long and includes: the developers of AI frontier models (whether proprietary or open-weight); the builders of the various layers of the AI infrastructure stack; the entrepreneurs designing the customised AI products that can best unlock productivity gains in individual sectors or in relation to specialised tasks; the research and development community that can accelerate scientific discovery and compress the time lag between invention and commercial application; the operators of the energy systems that must respond to this new source of energy demand; the financial system that is required to appropriately value AI-related assets and finance AI production and AI adoption, while also incorporating AI into its own processes; the education and training sectors that must re-design instruction, learning and evaluation methods; and, finally, the managers and workers that must implement revised business processes at the sector and firm levels to maximise the benefits of AI.
This transformation also poses many challenges for political systems, civic society, policymakers and regulators at national, European and global levels in relation to the ethical, fiscal, governance and legal issues posed by AI. How these political economy issues are resolved will have a major bearing on the AI transition path, including the appropriate speed of adjustment that balances the societal benefits, costs and risks posed by AI.
Given the scale and breadth of the AI challenge, a wide range of possible timelines and outcomes can be envisaged, depending on the rate of progress along each individual dimension. The uncertainty surrounding the impact of AI – in both the short term and the long term – is compounded by the interdependencies and complementarities across these different dimensions.
For instance, the rollout of rapid progress in AI capabilities can be held back by bottlenecks in some areas, slowing the overall pace of AI adoption. In particular, how firms and labour market institutions navigate the re-orientation of the workforce is a key issue, with some occupations facing the prospect of higher demand due to complementarities with AI and others facing lower demand due to the scope for substitution by AI.[1] The net impact on employment will also depend on the evolution of labour costs versus token prices.
The European Central Bank is closely monitoring and analysing the impact of AI on the euro area economy for several reasons.[2] First, the medium-term and longer-term positive impact of AI on the level of potential output and the trend growth rate of the economy has the potential to raise the speed limit of the economy, with direct implications for the financial system and monetary policy. For Europe, the potential for AI to offset the economic impact of the projected trend decline in the working-age population is especially valuable.
Second, more immediately, AI is already a primary factor driving current activity levels in the euro area. We see this in terms of a higher rate of business investment (firms are set to devote around 10 per cent of their total investment to AI this year), an expansion in digital services sectors and the high global demand for European components and capital goods that are part of the AI supply chain. In turn, this is supported by expansion in AI-related lending, which accounts for roughly one quarter of recent credit growth to firms.
In our surveys, we are also tracking the rate at which firms and workers are adopting AI. In our Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises for the fourth quarter of 2025, most firms reported that they were using AI: 64 per cent of firms said they were using it either experimentally or moderately, while only 7 per cent of firms reported that their use was “significant”.[3]
Our survey of households indicates that the proportion of workers using AI has doubled over the last two years, with 52 per cent now reporting that they use AI at work, compared with 26 per cent in 2024.[4] In the aggregate, workers are reporting significant time savings, but these are highly concentrated in specific sectors and specialised tasks such as coding.
Taken together, these surveys suggest that AI adoption in Europe is already significant and growing rapidly, even if it is too early to detect any material impact on aggregate productivity.
In relation to the labour market, we do not yet see a major change in aggregate employment trends but hiring plans are muted, which especially affects the prospects for new graduates. The potential for AI to replace some types of workers may also weaken the bargaining power of workers, moderating wage growth and reducing the labour share in total income. In our surveys, there is significant variation across industries, with workers in sectors benefiting from the AI infrastructure buildout currently more optimistic than those in knowledge-intensive sectors that face greater AI substitution risk.
At the same time, it is also important to appreciate that the quantitative scale of the European AI surge is of a different order to the AI boom in the United States or East Asia. Over the last two years, digital investment in the United States has grown twice as fast as in the euro area, while US workers spend two to three times as much of the working week using AI as workers in the largest euro area economies.[5] In terms of the AI frontier, the Stanford AI Index calculates that the United States and China have produced 59 and 35 notable AI models, respectively, while France and the United Kingdom have produced one each. In terms of AI computing capacity, the United States hosts 75 per cent of the global aggregate, whereas Europe hosts just 5 per cent. Although international trade in AI goods and services can do much to spread the benefits of AI around the world, asymmetrical AI capacity across countries may generate a host of economic and geopolitical issues.[6]
Third, it is likely that the global AI investment boom and expectations of a future global AI-driven productivity boost at longer-term horizons are plausibly contributing to the global increase in long-term interest rates.[7] Especially since the scale of the European AI boom is not of the same order as the global AI boom, the spillover to the euro area bond market means that the increase in long-term interest rates constitutes a material tightening of financial conditions for the euro area. This is a relevant factor for the ECB in determining the appropriate monetary policy stance.
Fourth, the high equity valuations of AI firms and the global surge in AI-related debt issuance carry macroeconomic and financial stability risks in the event of even a temporary reversal in the expected rate of AI advancement or a decline in investor sentiment.[8] Accordingly, the financial stability and banking supervision functions of the ECB are closely monitoring the evolution of AI-related financial risks and, in addition, the associated cyber risks.[9]
Fifth, the ECB has an extensive internal AI adoption agenda. Given that we are a knowledge-intensive organisation, AI has great potential to improve our analytical capacity and organisational efficiency. Over the last several years, I have been very impressed by the bottom-up initiatives of ECB staff to apply AI in a wide range of applications.[10]
In closing, Europe has much to gain by seizing the AI opportunity. The ECB is committed to making sure that the AI transformation in Europe is underpinned by price stability and financial stability.
In these remarks, I have highlighted that the aggregate impact of AI depends on a multi-dimensional transformation of the economy over an extended period. This is best achieved by recognising the collective interest shared by all sectors and policymakers in ensuring a sustainable AI transformation path. To this end, this AI summit provides an important opportunity to learn from each other and listen to a wide range of perspectives on AI.
- See, for example, Garicano, L., Li, J. and Wu, Y. (2026), Messy Jobs: The Work that AI Cannot Reach, Upriver Press.
- See also Lane, P.R. (2026), “AI and the euro area economy”, speech at the ECB-SAFE-RCEA International Conference on the Climate-Macro-Finance Interface (3CMFI), 23 March.
- Among firms planning AI-related investment over the next 12 months, most expect to invest in AI-related technologies and tools, as well as in employee training, financed mostly through internal funds. 49 per cent of firms plan to invest in AI technologies and tools (e.g. software licences), 46 per cent in training employees, 40 per cent in data and infrastructure and 12 per cent in hiring AI specialists. See also: Ferrando, A., Lamboglia, S., Rariga, J. and Schmidt, M. (2026), “Adopting and investing in AI: evidence from euro area firms in the SAFE”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 2, ECB; Chaloupka, D., Lalinský, T. and Lopez-Garcia P. (2026), “What separates firms that use AI intensively from firms that don’t?”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 24 June. On how firms are financing AI, see: Cianfarani, A.S., Di Casola, P., Ramos, J. and Zander, D. (2026), “Funding the AI revolution: evidence from euro area sectors”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 6 October.
- Dias da Silva, A., Lebastard, L. and Sondermann, D. (2026), “AI adoption and the productivity promise: what workers report”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 26 August.
- Bick, A., Blandin, A., Deming, D.J., Fuchs-Schündeln, N. and Jessen, J. (2026), “Mind the Gap: AI Adoption in Europe and the U.S.”, NBER

articles.title: BlackRock Ends Six-Year Treasury Underweight, Cuts U.S. Stocks to Neutral as Yields Hit 5.25% - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: BlackRock Ends Six-Year Treasury Underweight, Cuts U.S. Stocks to Neutral as Yields Hit 5.25%  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager with more than $15.3 trillion under management, has abandoned its long-standing underweight position on U.S. government bonds, upgrading Treasuries to overweight for the first time in roughly six years. The shift, announced Tuesday in its weekly market commentary, is funded in part by cutting its stance on U.S. stocks to neutral from overweight.
The firm's strategists, led by BlackRock Investment Institute's Jean Boivin, Wei Li, and Rick Rieder, now favor shorter-duration government debt, lifting long-term Treasuries to neutral. "Yields have reset toward our long-held higher-rates view, and we want to lock in some attractive income," the firm stated.
The decision marks a decisive reversal of a portfolio "mainstay" that had defined BlackRock's positioning since October 2020, when the 10-year Treasury yield sat below 0.9%. That benchmark yield has since surged roughly 110 basis points this year to approximately 5.25%, a level not seen since 2002. The 30-year yield has likewise touched 24-year highs, driven primarily by higher real interest rates rather than escalating inflation expectations or term premiums, according to the firm's analysis.
Intensifying global competition for capital and heightened geopolitical friction in the Middle East have pushed up the neutral rate, causing markets to price in an additional 160 basis points of Federal Reserve tightening since January. BlackRock considers those hawkish expectations "overdone."
"We are upgrading shorter-term Treasuries to overweight, where we see scope for excessive Fed tightening expectations to unwind, and long-term Treasuries to neutral as higher yields now provide better compensation for interest rate risk," the firm said.
At current yield levels, BlackRock calculates that investors hold a 75-basis-point cushion against further rate increases over the next 12 months before total returns turn negative. That buffer provides substantial insulation, particularly at the short end of the yield curve where the potential for restrictive policy expectations to ease appears greatest.
Profit-Taking in Equities
The reallocation is partly financed by closing out a long-held overweight position in U.S. equities, alongside a reduction in U.S. agency mortgage-backed securities to neutral. BlackRock framed the equity downgrade as a tactical risk-management adjustment tailored to a volatile macroeconomic regime.
"We are managing near-term risk, not changing our core convictions," the firm said. "Higher yields offer an opportunity to add Treasuries, funded partly by taking profits on U.S. equities."
The pressure on stocks was already visible in recent sessions. All 30 companies in the PHLX Semiconductor Index declined during Monday's trading, while Nvidia shares fell approximately 1.7%. Concerns about returns on AI infrastructure investment have weighed on semiconductor valuations, with earlier revenue uncertainty surrounding OpenAI contributing to declines in Nvidia, AMD, and other technology companies.
Despite the near-term position reduction, BlackRock reiterated its structural conviction in the artificial intelligence transformation. Higher interest rates are widening the gap between high-performing businesses and weaker peers, favoring companies that deliver earnings above their cost of capital. The firm continues to prefer AI-focused equities, listed infrastructure, and emerging market equities, noting that S&P 500 earnings are projected to expand nearly 30% year-on-year in the third quarter.
"We remain constructive on AI and stand ready to add risk again as visibility improves and attractive entry points emerge," BlackRock said.
Market Context
The tactical reallocation comes during a period of sharp gyrations across sovereign bond markets. Global government bonds experienced pronounced volatility last week as 10- and 30-year U.S. Treasury yields touched their highest levels since 2002 before easing following solid demand at Treasury auctions. European debt markets faced similar pressure, led by French sovereign debt as fiscal governance concerns mounted.
Investors now turn their attention to Wednesday's U.S. inflation report, which will offer the first snapshot of September price pressures. With recent Federal Reserve meeting minutes confirming a cautious stance among policymakers, these inflation figures are expected to serve as the immediate catalyst shaping Fed policy expectations and Treasury yield trajectories.
Higher-than-expected inflation could increase pressure on expensive technology stocks, particularly as AI concentration leaves the S&P 500 increasingly dependent on a small group of companies. BlackRock's shift reflects these broader risks without suggesting that the AI investment cycle has ended.

articles.title: RBI’s ‘bazooka’ sees rupee rising 1.4% versus dollar in two days, but should central bank let it fall? - The Times of India
articles.summary: RBI’s ‘bazooka’ sees rupee rising 1.4% versus dollar in two days, but should central bank let it fall?  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Where is the rupee headed? The Indian currency has been in a free fall for several quarters now. At one time its one-year forward even breached the 100 mark prompting experts and economists to wonder if the rupee will cross the 100 mark versus the US dollar.
A lot has changed since then. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has stepped in to build a record foreign exchange reserves chest to arm itself with tools to intervene in the forex market. The FCNR(B) deposits scheme helped attract billions of dollars, putting India in a comfortable position on the forex reserves front.
Yet continued capital outflows, high oil prices, uncertainty on the US-Iran war front, and rising US bond yields have added pressure to the currency, pushing it to record lows of almost 97.
More recently, RBI’s measures unveiled last week have led to the rupee appreciating sharply. On Friday it closed at 96.61. Since then it has appreciated by Re 1.36 or 1.41% to 95.24.
One thought process is that the RBI should allow the market forces to let the rupee find its levels. Indeed the IMF recently said that India should allow the exchange rate to act as a shock absorber.
Interestingly, RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra believes that the rupee is actually undervalued.
A currency is said to be undervalued when it is weaker than what experts believe is its fair value based on underlying economic fundamentals.
However, an undervalued currency does not automatically mean it will strengthen soon. The currency can continue to remain weak for an extended period because of capital outflows, global uncertainty or other market pressures.
What should RBI do? How effective would its latest measures be for long-term prospects of rupee? And, should the rupee be allowed to depreciate?
RBI’s measures
Last week, RBI unveiled what SBI Research has called a bazooka to protect the rupee’s slide.
These measures were:
RBI opened a direct dollar-supply window for three state-run OMCs shifting roughly $10-12 billion per month away from the open spot market.
The daily CRR maintenance has been raised to 99% and simultaneously to tighten liquidity in the system the RBI has announced a Rs 25,000 crore OMO sales.
RBI has tightened foreign exchange derivative regulations by prohibiting the rebooking of cancelled rupee derivative contracts
It has lowered the threshold for taking FX derivative positions without underlying exposure from $100 million to $5 million across all Authorised Dealers
It has strengthened documentation requirements to prevent duplicate hedging, and introduced a Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve for larger contracts.
RBI's Rupee Defence: 4 Key Measures
Vivek Kumar, Economist at QuantEco sees RBI’s special measures as a comprehensive package for addressing both internal and external macro pressures.
“The dual focus on increasing the price of money (i.e., interest rate) and restricting its availability (i.e., draining surplus liquidity) is an appropriate policy response to the emerging inflation and currency risks,” Vivek Kumar tells TOI.
In addition, tighter regulation of rupee hedging and trading will dramatically shrink space for speculation and short-circuit the self-fulfilling expectation of currency weakness.
How long will the effect last?
The effect may however be short-term.
Interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve have historically put emerging markets under pressure through shifts in capital flows, financing conditions and exchange rates.
The Federal Reserve raised rates on September 17, marking its first increase since July 2023.
As Vivek Kumar points out: the underlying pressure on the rupee from a firm dollar, elevated energy prices, and continued portfolio outflows persists.
Brent Crude Price Trend Line
“As such, while these measures will help to stabilise the rupee, they won't engineer a reversal beyond the initial knee-jerk relief rally. Since the rupee remains exposed to the current set of adverse global factors, durable stability will be conceivable only if the global tensions ease,” he says.
“Meanwhile, the RBI could focus on maintaining an ex-ante real policy rate of 1.0-1.5% to ensure durable macroeconomic balance. This can be complemented with measures to attract foreign investment,” he adds.
Yet another important factor is the central bank’s stance that it will not target any particular level of the rupee versus dollar. Any intervention will be aimed at curbing speculative pressures and volatility.
FPI outflows
Ranen Banerjee of PwC India says that the recent measures taken by RBI will surely address the pressures on rupee caused by speculative trades.
“These measures are not towards addressing the fundamentals of demand and supply of forex but more to make the supply more orderly for the oil companies and make the demand for forex real and not speculative,” he explains.
SBI Research says that while the RBI has been taking all possible steps to thwart a seemingly difficult global playbook, there is an urgent need also by the government to address some of the long pending structural issues regarding capital inflows. For example, it recommends abolishing the long-term capital gains tax on equities. This would help deal with capital outflows more effectively.
Should RBI let the rupee depreciate?
There are the costs associated with a weaker rupee.
While exports benefit from a depreciating currency, imports become costlier. In the current scenario, with oil prices high, it acts as a double whammy when India imports higher inflation.
And, the inflationary pressures for a net importing country like India increase with a weaker rupee. The fiscal pressures also increase owing to higher energy and fertiliser costs in rupee terms.
Sujan Hajra, Chief Economist at Anand Rathi Group notes that the immediate costs are especially relevant for India, whose crude-oil import dependence reached approximately 88.7% in FY2025–26, according to PPAC data.
“Depreciation compounds an oil-price shock, raising domestic production costs and potentially inflation. It also increases the rupee burden of unhedged foreign-currency debt, reduces purchasing power and can weaken foreign investors’ dollar returns. Crucially, depreciation raises the rupee cost of imports immediately; improvement in the dollar trade balance requires a subsequent response in export and import volumes,” he explains.
What RBI governor said on rupee
Hence, experts say the aim should be to have the exchange rate closer to the real effective exchange rate and not target a particular exchange rate.
Radhika Rao, Senior Economist and Executive Director at DBS Bank cautions against the fallout of letting rupee depreciate.
“While exchange-rate flexibility is a shock absorber, policymakers will be mindful of the risk that one-way currency depreciation can become self-reinforcing. Preventing a disorderly depreciation is therefore as important as preserving flexibility,” she tells TOI.
“Beyond a point, it can become destabilsing for capital flows, price stability and sentiments, requiring an active policy response,” she adds.
Rao is of the view that the breadth of the restrictions highlight the authorities view that the USD/INR is nearing a defacto red line and that the recent bout of rupee depreciation is being viewed as disorderly rather than fundamentals driven.
Ranen Banerjee, Partner and Leader, Economic Advisory at PwC India says that the rupee should find its natural level based on the dollar forex demand and supply.
“Targeting an exchange rate is always futile as we have only limited firepower and means to address external factors that determine forex flows. Volatility owing to speculation on the rupee needs to be managed and that is what RBI is doing,” he tells TOI.
As Sujan Hajra points out: A record low against the dollar does not, by itself, establish whether the rupee is cheap or expensive.
“Valuation requires examining inflation-adjusted exchange rates against trading partners, productivity and the external balance. Equally, a fundamentally undervalued currency can weaken temporarily when dollar demand exceeds supply,” he tells TOI.
“I favour calibrated intervention to prevent self-reinforcing depreciation, alongside sufficient flexibility to accommodate persistent external pressures. The objective should be orderly adjustment and anchored inflation expectations,” he says.
Economists believe that the economy’s growth momentum, demand in the Indian economy and the opportunities for growth are being currently overshadowed by capital flows to AI centred investments, higher yields in the developed markets and higher oil prices.
“It is a cycle and we need to manage the macro through this cycle as there has been no change in the underlying fundamentals of the Indian economy as can be seen from the growth forecasts being upgraded by almost all external agencies,” Banerjee says.
IMF may favour market-driven exchange rate adjustments, but for RBI orderly currency movements assume priority.
And, as the RBI governor pointed out, the rupee is undervalued, which means the economy’s fundamentals do not warrant such sharp levels of depreciation.
DK Srivastava, Chief Policy Advisor at EY India says the US dollar remains overvalued and the rupee undervalued.
“Rising US bond yields are attracting capital flows into the US, including from India, adding pressure on the rupee and deepening its undervaluation,” he tells TOI.
“In this environment, the RBI should continue to guide the rupee along a trend consistent with inflation differentials. While inflation remains elevated in both economies, India’s CPI inflation averaged 4.8% during June-September 2026, compared with about 3.4% in the US during June-August 2026, suggesting that some depreciation may be warranted,” Srivastava adds.

articles.title: Crude Oil Rally: WTI Spikes Above $115 as Iran Conflict and Strait of Hormuz Disruption Trigger Supply Shock - Goodreturns
articles.summary: Crude Oil Rally: WTI Spikes Above $115 as Iran Conflict and Strait of Hormuz Disruption Trigger Supply Shock  Goodreturns
articles.full_text:
Global crude oil prices surged past $100 per barrel this morning as the escalating Iran conflict in West Asia disrupted oil production and shipping routes, which rattled the global energy markets, triggering a sharp rally in crude oil prices.
Benchmark crude prices climbed to their highest levels since 2022, as supply fears intensified after production cuts across several OPEC oil producers and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important oil transit routes.
WTI crude jumps above $115 per barrel
According to trading economics, WTI crude oil futures surged as much as 31% on Monday, before easing slightly to trade around $115 per barrel, which is the largest single-day gain since April 2020. The market saw a 35% rally in Crude oil prices over the last week due to escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
Benchmark Brent crude also climbed above $110 per barrel as the supply shock hit the global energy markets.
As quoted by Wall Street Journal, JPMorgan Chase analyst Natasha Kaneva said, "In the whole written history of the strait, it has never been closed, ever, To me, it was not just the worst-case scenario. It was an unthinkable scenario."
Strait of Hormuz disruption impacts oil markets
A major reason behind the crude oil price spike is the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow maritime corridor that normally carries about 20% of the world's oil supply and LNG shipments. The US-Iran conflict has severely reduced tanker traffic, with many vessels avoiding the route due to security risks.
The near-closure of the strait has forced oil exporters to slow production because crude shipments cannot leave the region easily, causing storage facilities in Gulf countries to fill rapidly.
Oil output collapses In Various Regions
As per Reuters report, "One of the biggest supply disruptions has occurred in Iraq, the second-largest producer in OPEC. Production from its major southern oilfields has fallen dramatically by nearly 70%, dropping to around 1.3 million barrels per day from roughly 4.3 million barrels per day before the conflict"
The report further stated that Oil producers in the Gulf have further tightened global oil supply and accelerated the surge in international crude oil prices. UAE & Kuwait, which is fifth-largest oil producer in OPEC, announced precautionary cuts to oil production and refinery output after warning of threats to ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
The surge in oil prices above $100 per barrel has raised concerns about global inflation, fuel costs and economic growth, particularly for major oil-importing economies such as India, China and several European countries. 
The prolonged disruptions in Middle East oil supply could push crude prices even higher and may create more economic pressures globally.

articles.title: IMF warns an AI stock correction could threaten global financial stability - Startup Fortune
articles.summary: IMF warns an AI stock correction could threaten global financial stability  Startup Fortune
articles.full_text:
The IMF's Global Financial Stability Report, out October 13, puts a hard number on the danger: seven companies now make up more than 35% of the S&P 500's value, and $1.4 trillion in future revenue is riding on deals between hyperscalers and AI firms that may not be able to pay.
The International Monetary Fund has spent most of 2026 talking about AI as a growth story. On Tuesday, in its October Global Financial Stability Report, it switched to talking about AI as a risk to the plumbing of the financial system itself. The Fund's language is specific: a correction in AI-linked equities and credit, if it comes, "could trigger a market correction" that spreads well beyond tech stocks.
Here is the number that frames everything else. The so-called Magnificent Seven, Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla, now account for more than 35% of the S&P 500's total market value, according to the IMF's report. A decade ago that figure sat around 12%. Their combined market capitalization has grown more than 50% in just the past two years. That is not a diversified index anymore. It is a bet on seven balance sheets.
What makes this different from a normal tech rally is how the money actually moves. The IMF's report tracked fourteen publicly disclosed deals since 2023 in which hyperscalers, the Microsofts and Amazons and Googles of the world, have put roughly $300 billion of equity into financially weaker AI companies, backed by another $650 billion in debt. In return, the hyperscalers have locked in $1.4 trillion in future revenue commitments, mostly through chip orders and cloud service contracts. That is the structure Kristalina Georgieva's economists are worried about: a handful of giants extending credit and equity to partners whose ability to pay depends entirely on AI demand materializing on schedule.
The IMF's own stress test offers some comfort and some new worry. Banks representing 22% of global banking assets showed weak capital levels under a severe scenario combining an AI shock, a bond market shock and an energy shock, up from 18% in the Fund's 2025 assessment. That is a one-year jump in fragility, not a collapse. The headline finding is still that the core banking sector holds up.
The IMF, BIS, and Bank of England have each warned this month that AI leverage poses a greater systemic threat than stretched valuations alone. With US margin debt at a record $1.4 trillion and leveraged ETF assets doubling in under 70 days, the risk isn't a slow correction but a forced deleveraging cascade that could move faster than 2008. - AI leverage in financial markets - central banks warning AI risk
The leverage has moved somewhere else instead. Hedge funds' combined gross equity positions and margin loans have climbed from about 10% to roughly 15% of advanced-economy GDP, the report found, and the share of single stocks packed into leveraged exchange-traded funds has jumped from 16% to 28% as retail investors chase amplified exposure to AI names. That is where a correction would actually bite first: not insured deposits, but margin calls and levered ETFs that retail money has piled into without necessarily knowing it.
Georgieva has been building to this point all year. Speaking ahead of the IMF's annual meetings, she warned that if AI earnings fall short, "hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of U.S. equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock." The Bank of England has independently reached a similar comparison, saying some U.S. stock valuation measures are close to levels seen at the peak of the dot-com bubble.
Frankly, the Fund isn't predicting a crash. It is doing something more useful: pricing the collateral damage if one happens. IMF modeling has warned that a moderate correction in AI stock valuations, combined with tighter financial conditions, could reduce global growth by 0.4 percent relative to baseline, while a faster AI-driven surge could lift global growth by about 0.3 percent in 2026-27 if productivity gains arrive sooner. That asymmetry, a modest win if AI delivers against a modest loss if it doesn't, is itself the story. It is not a coin flip with equal stakes on both sides.
What should worry StartupFortune's readers specifically is the private side of this. Many of the AI firms taking hyperscaler money and debt are not publicly listed, which means they report less, and a funding shortfall there doesn't show up on anyone's stock ticker until a hyperscaler writes it down. The IMF also flagged signs of rising defaults in private credit more broadly, warning they could cascade into concerns about corporate credit for highly leveraged borrowers facing AI-driven disruption to their own businesses, not just AI firms themselves.
None of this means the banking system is about to seize up the way it did in 2008. The IMF's stress tests still showed banks' capital buffers remaining broadly resilient in a hypothetical downturn triggered by an AI slowdown and bond-market fragility. But the Fund's own numbers show the cushion thinning, not thickening, year over year. A fifth of global banking assets now sit in institutions the IMF classifies as weak under stress. That is the kind of detail that does not make headlines the way a stock crash does, and it is exactly the kind of detail that matters more.

articles.full_text:
On October 13, 2026, News Corporation filed an 8-K with the SEC confirming it provided daily repurchase disclosures to the Australian Securities Exchange as of October 9, 2026, in compliance with ASX regulations for its ongoing stock buyback program.
Key Highlights
- Repurchase authorization: News Corporation is authorized to repurchase up to $1 billion in aggregate of its outstanding Class A and Class B common shares under its Repurchase Program.
- ASX disclosure requirement: Per ASX rules, the company must provide daily disclosures of any Repurchase Program transactions to the Australian Securities Exchange.
- Four exhibits submitted: Exhibits 99.1, 99.2, 99.3, and 99.4 include copies of information submitted to the ASX on the respective dates indicated in each exhibit.
- Two classes of shares involved: The Repurchase Program applies to both Class A common stock (par value $0.01 per share) and Class B common stock (par value $0.01 per share).
- Forward-looking statements disclosed: The filing notes that the exhibits contain forward-looking statements under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, including the company's intent to repurchase shares, which are subject to uncertainties and changing conditions.
Details on News Corporation's ASX Buyback Reporting and Program
According to the filing, News Corporation (NASDAQ:NWSA and NASDAQ:NWS) submitted this 8-K under Item 8.01 (Other Events) to fulfill its ongoing disclosure obligations related to the Repurchase Program. The company highlighted that ASX rules require daily reporting of repurchase transactions to the Australian Securities Exchange. Additionally, News Corporation reports Repurchase Program details in its quarterly and annual SEC filings.
The filing included four exhibits, each containing information provided to the ASX on the dates specified within the exhibits. Detailed transaction-level data for each day covered is contained within these exhibits and not reproduced in the main 8-K text. The filing was signed by Michael L. Bunder, Senior Vice President, Deputy General Counsel and Corporate Secretary, on October 13, 2026.
The filing described statements about the company’s intent to repurchase shares as forward-looking statements subject to risks such as "changes in the market price of the Company's stock, general market conditions, applicable securities laws and alternative investment opportunities," along with other factors detailed in the company’s regulatory filings. News Corporation disclaimed any obligation to update these statements except as required by law or regulation.
Summary of Disclosures
On October 13, 2026, News Corporation filed an 8-K reporting that it had submitted daily stock repurchase disclosures to the ASX as required, attaching four exhibits covering activity around October 9, 2026, under its $1 billion stock repurchase authorization.

articles.title: Hong Kong SFC Freezes Over HK$4.6 Billion; Chabaidao Among Three Stocks Suspended for Alleged IPO Manipulation - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Hong Kong SFC Freezes Over HK$4.6 Billion; Chabaidao Among Three Stocks Suspended for Alleged IPO Manipulation  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
The Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has taken enforcement action against two syndicates suspected of manipulating initial public offerings, freezing assets totaling more than HK$4.66 billion (approximately $593.8 million) and directing the Hong Kong Stock Exchange to suspend trading in Chabaidao (02555.HK). This represents the highest restriction amount ever issued by the SFC in a case of this kind.
Starting at 9:00 a.m. on October 13, trading in shares of Sichuan Baicha Baidao Industrial Co., Ltd. was halted on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. The exchange executed the suspension pursuant to Rule 8(1) of the Securities and Futures (Stock Market Listing) Rules, acting on the SFC's directive. Later that day, the SFC disclosed details of the action in a press release, stating that the syndicates in question are suspected of engaging in fraudulent schemes intended to create a false or misleading appearance of demand for IPO shares.
The SFC said it has serious concerns that Chabaidao's IPO may have been artificially manipulated. While the investigation is ongoing, suspending trading in the stock is necessary and appropriate to maintain an orderly and fair market and to protect the interests of the investing public.
Freeze Amount Sets Record for Cases of This Kind
The SFC disclosed that, with respect to the first suspect syndicate, it has issued restriction notices to six brokerage firms, prohibiting them from disposing of or dealing with assets held in client accounts in the names of Sun Ran and eight related companies, capped at HK$4.379 billion (approximately $558.0 million). This is the highest restriction amount ever imposed by the SFC in a case of this kind. The syndicate is suspected of involvement in fraudulent schemes related to the IPOs of Cloudbreak Pharma Inc. (02592.HK) and Chabaidao.
With respect to the second suspect syndicate, the SFC issued restriction notices to 29 brokerage firms involving assets held in client accounts in the names of Liu Haoran, The Reynold Lemkins Group (Asia) Limited, and Kaufmann & Company Pan-Asia Limited, capped at HK$285 million (approximately $36.3 million). This syndicate is suspected of involvement in a fraudulent scheme related to the IPO of Tianju Dihe (Suzhou) Technology Co., Ltd. (02479.HK).
Among the three implicated stocks, Cloudbreak Pharma has been suspended since September 10, Tianju Dihe has been suspended since April 1, 2025 for failure to publish financial results, and Chabaidao was ordered to suspend trading in this latest action.
The SFC noted that some IPO proceeds may have been diverted away from the relevant companies pursuant to undisclosed agreements between the listed companies and the suspect syndicates, purportedly for investments in so-called financial products. Such agreements may have facilitated the secret channeling of IPO proceeds back to key IPO placees or their associates.
The brokerage firms that received restriction notices are not subjects of the investigation, and the notices do not affect their operations or other clients. The SFC considers that issuing the notices to preserve the relevant assets is desirable in the interests of the investing public or the public interest. The parties involved may in due course be ordered to make compensation to affected investors through restoration proceedings.
Regulator Emphasizes Zero Tolerance
SFC Chief Executive Officer Julia Leung said that market integrity and soundness are the cornerstones of maintaining a fair capital market and genuine investor confidence. The SFC adopts a zero-tolerance policy toward any form of IPO manipulation, price rigging, or creation of a false market. She said that in practical terms, the SFC takes highly focused and appropriately calibrated regulatory action, striving to create a conducive environment that promotes a virtuous cycle of sustainable market development.
Michael Duignan, Executive Director of Enforcement, said the actions taken to date have dealt a significant blow to two suspect syndicates allegedly involved in IPO manipulation. Suspending trading in Chabaidao shares and preserving assets related to the suspected schemes are aimed at protecting investors and upholding the integrity and soundness of Hong Kong's markets, while also helping to strengthen investor confidence in the fairness and integrity of Hong Kong's IPO market.
As the investigation is ongoing, the SFC said it would not comment further.
The Divergence Between Chabaidao's Operations and Share Price
Chabaidao listed on the main board of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on April 23, 2024, with an issue price of HK$17.5 (approximately $2.2) per share, raising approximately HK$2.586 billion (approximately $329.5 million) at a listing market capitalization of HK$25.859 billion (approximately $3.3 billion), carrying the halo of being the "first franchise-based tea beverage stock." However, the stock broke issue price sharply on its debut, closing at HK$12.8 (approximately $1.6), a decline of more than 26%.
On the last trading day before suspension, Chabaidao closed at HK$4.035 (approximately $0.51), a cumulative decline of nearly 77% from the issue price, with market capitalization shrunk to approximately HK$6 billion (approximately $764.5 million).
From an operational standpoint, Chabaidao's offline business continues to grow. Full-year 2025 revenue reached CNY 5.395 billion (approximately $807.4 million), up 9.7% year-on-year; net profit was CNY 805 million (approximately $120.5 million), up more than 70% year-on-year. In the first half of 2026, revenue continued to grow to CNY 2.655 billion (approximately $397.4 million), up 6.2% year-on-year; net profit for the period was CNY 345 million (approximately $51.6 million), up 3.5% year-on-year.
In terms of store network, as of the end of June 2026, Chabaidao had 8,778 stores, a net increase of 170 from 8,608 at the end of 2025. Within the half-year period, 669 new stores were added, while 499 franchise stores ceased operations. Overseas stores increased from 38 at the end of 2025 to 72, covering 13 countries and regions.
However, changes in the revenue mix warrant attention. In the first half of 2026, revenue from merchandise and equipment sales was CNY 2.524 billion (approximately $377.7 million), accounting for 95.0% of total revenue, up 7.0% year-on-year; royalty and franchise fee revenue fell to CNY 81.02 million (approximately $12.1 million), down 19.5% year-on-year. Gross profit for the period was CNY 797 million (approximately $119.3 million), down 2.1% year-on-year, with gross margin declining from approximately 32.6% in the same period last year to approximately 30.0%. The company said the decline in gross margin was related to developing its fresh-brewed coffee business and offering certain concessions to franchisees.
| Metric | FY2025 | H1 2026 | 
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | CNY 5.395 billion | CNY 2.655 billion | 
| Revenue YoY growth | +9.7% | +6.2% | 
| Net profit | CNY 805 million | CNY 345 million | 
| Gross margin | Not disclosed | ~30.0% | 
| Total stores | 8,608 | 8,778 | 
| Royalty & franchise fee revenue | CNY 192 million | CNY 81.02 million | 
Note: Data sourced from company financial reports and interim reports
Industry-Wide Broken IPOs and the Capital Narrative Dilemma
Chabaidao's predicament is not an isolated case. Hong Kong's new-style tea beverage sector has been weakening since 2021. Nayuki (02150.HK) had an issue price of HK$19.8 (approximately $2.5) in 2021, and its share price has since fallen below HK$1 (approximately $0.13), a cumulative decline of more than 90%. Guming (01364.HK) fell 6.44% on its debut in February 2025. The only exception is Mixue Bingcheng (02097.HK), which rose more than 43% on its debut in March 2025, but its extreme scale of over 40,000 stores globally does not offer broadly applicable reference value.
The slowdown in industry growth has exacerbated valuation corrections. The growth rate of the new-style tea beverage industry fell from 19.3% in 2023 to around 5.7% in 2025, leaving high valuations without the support of a growth narrative. In 2025, China's new-style tea beverage industry saw a net reduction of approximately 39,000 stores, with a closure rate as high as 16.2%.
Chabaidao's IPO subscription data also did not show robust market demand. According to the allotment results disclosed by the company in April 2024, the Hong Kong public offering received 4,593 valid applications, with a subscription level of 0.5 times; the international offering had a subscription level of 1.11 times, with 122 placees. Due to under-subscription in the Hong Kong public offering, 7.4408 million shares were reallocated to the international offering. After deducting listing expenses, Chabaidao's net IPO proceeds amounted to approximately HK$2.463 billion (approximately $313.8 million).
Notably, Chabaidao did not introduce cornerstone investors in this IPO. In the Hong Kong market, cornerstone investors are generally viewed as a signal of institutional confidence in a company's fundamentals. The absence of cornerstone investors means the listing pricing lacked institutional endorsement and was more susceptible to short-term capital influence.
Pre-IPO dividend arrangements have also drawn attention. According to the prospectus, from 2021 to 2023, Chabaidao distributed a cumulative total of CNY 1.576 billion (approximately $235.9 million) in dividends to shareholders over the three-year period. Controlling shareholders Wang Xiaokun and Liu Weihong, a married couple, received approximately CNY 1.287 billion (approximately $192.6 million) through direct and indirect shareholdings, exceeding the company's combined net profit for 2020 and 2021.
As the regulatory investigation progresses, Chabaidao faces not only questions about the quality of growth at the operational level, but also scrutiny from the capital market over the compliance of its listing process. How this storm will ultimately resolve rema

articles.title: Hong Kong SFC Halts Trading in Chabaidao, Citing Suspected Artificial Manipulation of IPO Subscription Demand - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Hong Kong SFC Halts Trading in Chabaidao, Citing Suspected Artificial Manipulation of IPO Subscription Demand  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
The Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) announced on October 13 that it had directed the Hong Kong Stock Exchange to suspend trading in Sichuan Baicha Baidao Industrial Co., Ltd. (Chabaidao, 02555.HK) from 9:00 a.m. that day, citing heightened concerns that the company's initial public offering (IPO) may have been artificially manipulated to create a false impression of demand for its shares.
This marks a rare compulsory trading suspension by Hong Kong's securities regulator targeting the new listing process in recent years. The regulator also disclosed that it has taken action against two groups suspected of participating in fraudulent schemes, with related investigations still ongoing.
SFC Chief Executive Officer Julia Leung said in a statement: "Market integrity and robustness are the cornerstones of a fair capital market and genuine investor confidence. We adopt a zero-tolerance policy toward any form of IPO manipulation, price rigging, or creation of a false market." She emphasized that the regulatory action aims to foster an environment conducive to a virtuous cycle of sustainable market development.
The Regulatory Logic Behind the Suspension
The SFC issued the suspension directive under Section 8(1) of the Securities and Futures (Stock Market Listing) Rules. This provision empowers the SFC to direct the Hong Kong Stock Exchange to suspend trading in a stock when it deems it necessary to maintain an orderly and fair market, or to protect the interests of the investing public.
This rule has played a pivotal role multiple times in the history of Hong Kong capital market regulation. Previous cases that fell under this provision include Hanergy Thin Film Power and Hontex International — the latter was ultimately ordered by the SFC to delist after inflating financial data in its listing documents, and more than HK$1 billion (approximately $127.4 million) in raised funds was returned to investors through a restoration process.
If Chabaidao is found to have engaged in IPO manipulation, it could face penalties ranging from fines to mandatory delisting, and individuals involved in the manipulation may also bear legal liability.
The SFC simultaneously issued restriction notices to multiple brokerages, freezing assets associated with nine entities and three entities, prohibiting the relevant brokerages from disposing of or dealing with the relevant assets, or executing any instructions from these entities, without prior written consent from the SFC.
Notably, the brokerages that received restriction notices are not the subjects of the SFC's investigation. The notices do not affect the normal operations of these brokerages or their other clients. The SFC stated that issuing the notices to preserve assets is a prudent measure, as the parties involved may later be ordered through a restoration process to compensate affected investors.
The Contrast After a 70% Plunge
Chabaidao listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in April 2024 at an offer price of HK$17.5 per share. The stock broke below its issue price on the first day of trading and continued to decline thereafter. Before the suspension, the stock traded at HK$4.035, down approximately 77% from its offer price, with a total market capitalization of approximately HK$5.962 billion (approximately $759.7 million).
In stark contrast to the stock price trajectory is the company's fundamentals. Chabaidao's revenue and profits are still growing, with its business model primarily generating revenue from selling raw materials and equipment to franchisees. This contrast — decent operating performance alongside a sharply declining share price — has raised market questions about the authenticity of the subscription frenzy at the time of its listing.
Hong Kong's new stock market has seen frequent first-day breakouts in recent years, with some companies employing various tactics during the listing process to inflate subscription enthusiasm and create the appearance of robust demand. The SFC's action this time sends a clear signal: the regulator is intensifying scrutiny of the IPO process, particularly the verification of subscription demand authenticity.
The SFC emphasized that what has been disclosed so far is suspected manipulation of IPO demand, and the allegations have not yet been finally determined. The specific identities of the two groups under investigation and the details of their conduct remain to be further disclosed.
During the suspension period, the SFC will continue its investigation. The timing of resumption of trading depends on the progress of the investigation and subsequent decisions by the regulator. For investors holding Chabaidao shares, they face a liquidity freeze in the short term, and whether they can obtain compensation through a restoration process depends on the investigation results and the progress of legal proceedings.
The potential impact of this incident on Hong Kong's new stock market should not be underestimated. Companies planning to list and their sponsors may face stricter scrutiny of subscription demand, and investor enthusiasm for new stock subscriptions may also cool as a result. The SFC's intervention through a trading suspension demonstrates its firm stance in maintaining market order during the new share issuance process.

articles.title: Copper Price 2026: Record Hunt on the LME and Forecast to Year End - Steel and Stainless Steel News
articles.summary: Copper Price 2026: Record Hunt on the LME and Forecast to Year End  Steel and Stainless Steel News
articles.full_text:
13 October 2026 – Copper has made good use of the past few months: at around $14,600 per tonne, the red metal is 17 per cent above the start of the year and close to its September record. How it got there and what may still be possible by year end. Also, some hope for Europe’s SMEs: Merz, Meloni and De Wever are calling for an emergency brake on burdensome EU legislation.
Several Member States Call for a Brake on Brussels
Some positive news on SME policy for a change. It happens rarely enough to deserve a mention.
Friedrich Merz, Giorgia Meloni and Bart De Wever wrote to European Council President António Costa on Monday, according to Politico. Their demand: national capitals should be able to stop new EU legislation when it places excessive burdens on businesses and public administrations. An emergency brake on overregulation from Brussels.
Fewer Forms, Faster Approvals
The proposal also calls for faster planning and approval procedures. A new priority rule would temporarily suspend certain areas of regulation. Further simplification packages should focus first on SMEs, while reporting obligations should be reduced broadly. The reasoning hits the mark: unnecessary burdens must not lead to the permanent loss of industrial capacity.
The Catch
The EU Treaties currently provide no general emergency brake of this kind. The Commission will defend its right of initiative. Whether the letter becomes more than paper will become clearer at the EU summit starting on Thursday. Still, three heads of government from major industrial countries are not talking about new obligations, but about abolishing them and creating a stop button for legislative proposals.
One wish remains: the brake should urgently apply to CBAM and safeguard tariffs as well. Both cost small and medium sized enterprises unnecessary billions of euros every year. Whether the Merz government would support that, however, is more than doubtful. The tariffs are written into the coalition agreement and were most likely put there by the SPD.
Copper Price 2026: Record Hunt on the LME and Forecast to Year End
It is time to take another look at copper. The red metal has used the past few months well: at around $14,600 per tonne on the London Metal Exchange, LME, it is trading more than 17 per cent above the start of the year. “Doctor Copper”, the old economic diagnostician, is in excellent spirits.
January: Rocket Start
Copper entered the year at $12,423. On 29 January, it jumped above $14,500 for the first time. By spring, the price temporarily slipped below $12,500. A correction, not a change of direction.
Mid-Year: Building Momentum at High Levels
In June, copper traded between $13,500 and $14,000 per tonne, while banks became increasingly bullish. On 10 September, it reached an all-time high of $14,875.
October: Tight Supply Meets Strong Demand
A mudslide following heavy rainfall at Chile’s major El Teniente mine is fuelling concerns about further supply disruptions. Chinese inventories are thin, and importers are paying a premium of around $118 over the LME price, the highest since 2022.
Outlook: Record in Sight
Deutsche Bank believes copper could make another attempt at the record high in the near term. Goldman Sachs forecast $13,735 for year end during the summer, while Citi sees $15,000 within twelve months.
Data centres, power grids and electric vehicles need the metal, while supply growth remains limited. High prices are not a disaster, but a signal: they finance new mines and more recycling.
Washington remains the wild card. A decision on Section 232 tariffs on refined copper has been pending since June, while more than 700,000 tonnes are sitting in US exchange warehouses. That metal is missing from the rest of the world. Once the decision comes, inventories are likely to start moving again.
