articles.title: Copper hits a two-week high on a Codelco supply halt — silver slips below $61 as CPI looms - Mitrade
articles.summary: Copper hits a two-week high on a Codelco supply halt — silver slips below $61 as CPI looms  Mitrade
articles.full_text:
Mitrade Insights — Copper is doing what copper does when supply gets a scare: rallying into the teeth of a macro week. LME three-month copper rose 0.56% on Monday to $14,618.50 a tonne — a two-week high — after a landslide at Codelco's El Teniente mine in Chile killed two workers and halted part of the operation, with COMEX copper adding 1.04% to $6.7615/lb. Tuesday brought a pause: futures pushed to $6.813 in Asian hours before easing to around $6.775 (−0.6%). The divergence worth watching sits next door — silver slipped below $61 (last $59.78, −0.89%), refusing to follow copper's supply trade as precious metals mark time before Wednesday's US September CPI.
The move: copper and silver part ways
| Market | Monday move | Level (last) | 
|---|---|---|
| LME 3-month copper | +0.56% | $14,618.50/t (two-week high) | 
| COMEX copper | +1.04% | $6.775/lb | 
| Spot silver | −0.9% ~ −1.1% | $59.78/oz | 
| Spot gold | easing | $4,165 ~ $4,172/oz | 
| Iron ore | steady | ~$90.8/t | 
Two things stand out. First, copper's move is a supply story, not a demand story — the accident at El Teniente, one of the world's largest underground copper mines, lands weeks after LME copper had already probed its September record zone of $14,600–$14,875 a tonne. Second, silver's inability to hold $61 despite copper's rally tells you the precious-metals complex is trading a different tape entirely: gold is stuck in a tight $4,165–$4,172 range with the dollar at an 18-month high, and silver is simply the higher-beta expression of that patience.
Why: an accident on top of a tight balance
The news. A landslide at Codelco's El Teniente complex killed two workers and forced a partial production halt. The mine is a cornerstone of global supply, and the accident revives the same question that drove copper's September surge: can the world's mines keep up with electrification and data-centre demand when single-site disruptions move the needle?
The backdrop. Copper had already spent September grinding toward record territory — supply scares have been the year's dependable bid. Monday's price action put LME copper back within $0–$250 of its September record zone, a level where the market has previously met sellers.
The demand check arrives tomorrow. China — the world's largest copper consumer — publishes September CPI, PPI and the first three quarters of trade data on Wednesday (Oct 14). PPI is expected to rise to about 4.5% year-over-year, and export growth is seen accelerating toward 30% — both cyclically supportive for industrial metals if the prints land in line.
Flows and institutional view
UBS reiterated an overweight on miners and industrials this week, backing the data-centre, mining, energy and defence-spending themes, with copper its preferred commodity — a positioning statement that explains why a single-mine accident found such a ready bid. On the precious side, silver's buyers are waiting on the same catalyst everyone else is: the CPI print that will decide whether December's Fed hike pricing (near 88%) strengthens or fades. A hot print lifts real yields and pressures metals; a soft one re-opens the door for both gold and silver.
Levels: $6.90 caps copper, $62 caps silver
* Chart source: TradingView official chart screenshot, data source Capital.com (Copper).
Copper key levels. Resistance: $6.90 (the September–October high zone) / $7.00 (round number). Support: $6.70 (the October shelf) / $6.60 (the mid-October pullback low). The structure to respect: as long as $6.70 holds, the supply trade stays in charge, and the $6.90–$7.00 band is where a challenge to the September record begins.
* Chart source: TradingView official chart screenshot, data source OANDA (Silver/USD).
Silver key levels. Resistance: $62.00 (the October rebound cap) / $64.00 (the September breakout shelf). Support: $58.00 (round number) / $56.50–57.00 (the July low zone).
What to watch: one data day, two channels
Wednesday runs both channels at once. The US September CPI (8:30 ET, consensus 3.6%–3.7%) works through the dollar channel — a hot print lifts the dollar and real yields, pressuring both metals; a soft print does the reverse. China's CPI, PPI and trade data (Wednesday, Beijing time) work through the demand channel — the export number matters most for copper, the PPI print for the industrial complex broadly.
Scenario A — supply stays in charge. Copper holds the $6.70 shelf, a soft US CPI keeps the dollar from extending, and China's prints land in line: the metal pushes back into the $6.90–$7.00 band and LME copper rejoins its September record zone. Silver plays catch-up through $62 only if real yields stop rising.
Scenario B — macro bites back. A hot CPI lifts the dollar index further from its 18-month high and copper slips back through $6.70 toward $6.60; silver, already below $61, tests $58 and drags gold's $4,165 support line into focus.
The tell for the week: watch whether copper's supply premium survives a strong-dollar test — that is the difference between a one-mine headline and a genuine re-rating.

articles.title: WTI Oil extends its pullback to $91.00 amid US imports of Russian Diesel - www.tmgm.com
articles.summary: WTI Oil extends its pullback to $91.00 amid US imports of Russian Diesel  www.tmgm.com
articles.full_text:
Crude Oil trades lower on Tuesday, as investors ponder the impact of the US President, Donald Trump’s decision to lift the ban on Russian diesel imports. The US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) barrel has retreated to session lows at $91.05 during the European Trading session, about $2.5 below the two-week high, at the $93.50 area, hit on Monday.
Markets' expectations of a significant increase in diesel supplies from Russia entering global markets will push prices lower and offset the upside pressures stemming from the escalating Middle East conflict.
Trump affirmed on Truth Social on Monday that the decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel imports for six months “is the right choice for the American people”. A report by Goldman Sachs, however, casts doubt on the overall impact on oil prices from that decision, as it said the 6 million barrels per day expected to be delivered by Russia will only lower the price of the barrel by between $1 and $2,
Elsewhere, tensions in the Middle East are far from easing, which pressures Crude prices higher. The Saudi Arabian Security Minister, Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman, called for a serious response to last weekend’s deadly attacks on Saudi Airports by Houthi militias, which threatens to escalate the US-Israel war in Iran into a regional conflict.
Analysts at ING point out that physical supply risks are not confined to geopolitical flashpoints, noting that “hurricane activity in the Gulf of Mexico continues to disrupt offshore operations for US producers.” They highlight that companies “have shut in almost 605k b/d of oil production, which is equivalent to nearly 30% of total US production in the Gulf of Mexico, according to the Marine Minerals Administration,” adding another layer of constraint to the near-term supply picture.
WTI Oil is a type of Crude Oil sold on international markets. The WTI stands for West Texas Intermediate, one of three major types including Brent and Dubai Crude. WTI is also referred to as “light” and “sweet” because of its relatively low gravity and sulfur content respectively. It is considered a high quality Oil that is easily refined. It is sourced in the United States and distributed via the Cushing hub, which is considered “The Pipeline Crossroads of the World”. It is a benchmark for the Oil market and WTI price is frequently quoted in the media.
Like all assets, supply and demand are the key drivers of WTI Oil price. As such, global growth can be a driver of increased demand and vice versa for weak global growth. Political instability, wars, and sanctions can disrupt supply and impact prices. The decisions of OPEC, a group of major Oil-producing countries, is another key driver of price. The value of the US Dollar influences the price of WTI Crude Oil, since Oil is predominantly traded in US Dollars, thus a weaker US Dollar can make Oil more affordable and vice versa.
The weekly Oil inventory reports published by the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Energy Information Agency (EIA) impact the price of WTI Oil. Changes in inventories reflect fluctuating supply and demand. If the data shows a drop in inventories it can indicate increased demand, pushing up Oil price. Higher inventories can reflect increased supply, pushing down prices. API’s report is published every Tuesday and EIA’s the day after. Their results are usually similar, falling within 1% of each other 75% of the time. The EIA data is considered more reliable, since it is a government agency.
OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) is a group of 12 Oil-producing nations who collectively decide production quotas for member countries at twice-yearly meetings. Their decisions often impact WTI Oil prices. When OPEC decides to lower quotas, it can tighten supply, pushing up Oil prices. When OPEC increases production, it has the opposite effect. OPEC+ refers to an expanded group that includes ten extra non-OPEC members, the most notable of which is Russia.

articles.title: Mortgage hedging adds selling pressure to US Treasury market as yields surge - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Mortgage hedging adds selling pressure to US Treasury market as yields surge  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Listen to this article in summarized format
Benchmark 10-year Treasury yields have climbed about 130 basis points since late February, while 30-year yields have risen 100 basis points. The increase has been driven by a surge in oil prices following the war in the Middle East, fuelling expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates multiple times over the next 12 months, the report stated.
Also Read | Global Market: South Korea’s Kospi plunges over 7% as chip stocks tumble on CXMT concerns
The rise in bond yields has pushed 30-year mortgage rates to a nearly three-year high of 7.4%, discouraging homeowners from refinancing existing loans and keeping them locked into mortgages secured at lower rates.
This shift affects mortgage-backed securities (MBS), pools of home loans that generate cash flows through borrowers' monthly principal and interest payments. As interest rates rise and refinancing becomes less attractive, the expected life of these securities extends, increasing their sensitivity to further yield moves, Reuters reported.
Investors often respond by selling Treasury futures or entering interest rate swaps to hedge the additional exposure, a strategy known as convexity hedging. Such activity can amplify bond market declines by generating further selling pressure on Treasuries.
Also Read | Global Market: Japan bond yields diverge as investors weigh inflation, BOJ outlook
Hedging Activity Gains Attention
Signs of increased hedging have emerged across interest rate markets in recent weeks, according to Reuters.
By the first week of October, nine large-block trades had been executed in CME-listed Eris SOFR Swap Futures, each carrying exposure of at least $200,000 for a one-basis-point move in interest rates, Riddle said. The transactions indicated that investors were adjusting positions in response to changes in the yield curve.
Daily trading volume in Eris SOFR Swap Futures reached consecutive records ahead of the Federal Reserve's September 16 policy meeting, including transactions positioning for an expected rate increase. Open interest, which measures the number of outstanding contracts, rose to a record 866,768 contracts on September 21, more than doubling the level recorded a year earlier.
Convexity hedging has historically reinforced bond market selloffs, making the latest activity particularly significant as Treasury yields climb.
The underperformance of mortgage-backed securities relative to government bonds and the widening of mortgage spreads have also pointed to increased hedging activity. When mortgage securities weaken more sharply than comparable-duration Treasuries during a rapid rise in interest rates, it can indicate that investors are adjusting their hedges.
According to a recent research note from Annaly Capital Management, mortgage-backed securities underperformed Treasuries with comparable duration by 96 basis points in September, marking their weakest monthly performance since the banking turmoil of March 2023.
Mortgage spreads over Treasuries also widened about 13 basis points in September to 125 basis points, according to AGNC Investment Corp., suggesting mortgage securities faced greater selling pressure than government bonds.
Impact may ease as refinancing incentives decline
Despite the signs of increased hedging, the extent to which these flows are contributing to the broader rise in Treasury yields remains uncertain.
Analysts say the impact of convexity hedging generally diminishes as interest rates rise because a growing proportion of mortgage borrowers lose the incentive to refinance. This reduces the likelihood of early loan repayments and makes mortgage-backed securities less sensitive to changes in prepayment expectations.
Amrut Nashikkar, head of derivatives strategy at Barclays, said a growing share of mortgage-backed securities was significantly out of the money, meaning borrowers had little or no financial incentive to refinance. That reduces prepayment risk and limits the potential for further rate increases to trigger destabilising hedging flows.
Neil Sun, a portfolio manager at BlueBay Asset Management, said the bulk of the selling pressure could already have occurred if interest rates stabilise around current levels.
The size of the mortgage market is another factor limiting the potential impact on Treasuries. Analysts say the sector is considerably smaller than it was before the 2008 global financial crisis, when mortgage-related hedging played a more prominent role in amplifying bond market volatility.
James Wang, head of macro at US Bank, said the mortgage market was no longer large enough to exert the same influence on Treasury yields as it did before the financial crisis.
The mortgage portfolios of government-sponsored housing enterprises Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have contracted significantly since the crisis. Before 2008, the two institutions actively managed interest-rate risk arising from differences in the duration of their assets and liabilities, making them among the largest participants in mortgage-related hedging.
While mortgage-related hedging may be adding to the pressure on government bonds, expectations for monetary policy remain the primary driver of the latest selloff, Wang said.
The outlook for Treasury yields will therefore continue to depend largely on how oil prices, inflation expectations and the Federal Reserve's policy path evolve, even as mortgage-related trading adds another layer of volatility to the bond market, according to Reuters.

articles.title: Hong Kong investigates IPO rigging, suspends Baicha stock - Yahoo Finance Singapore
articles.summary: Hong Kong investigates IPO rigging, suspends Baicha stock  Yahoo Finance Singapore
articles.full_text:
Hong Kong's securities watchdog is investigating a suspected case of rigging an initial public offering to create a false impression of demand.
(Oct 13): Hong Kong's securities watchdog is investigating a suspected case of rigging an initial public offering (IPO) to create a false impression of demand.
The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) directed the stock exchange to suspend Sichuan Baicha Baidao Industrial Co's trading from 9am on Oct 13 in Hong Kong. The regulator said it has "serious concerns that Baicha's IPO may have been rigged", according to a statement sent Tuesday after the market closed. The company's market value is HK$5.9 billion (US$752 million or $960 million).
Baicha raised about US$330 million ($422 million) in April 2024 in what was at the time Hong Kong's biggest first-time share sale of the year. Its shares plunged 27% on their first day and never traded above the offer price. China International Capital Corp was the sole sponsor of the IPO. The retail tranche was 0.5 times subscribed, while institutional investors bid for 1.1 times the shares initially made available.
Hong Kong is in the midst of a bumper year for IPO proceeds, driven by a series of listings by Chinese companies along the artificial intelligence supply chain. As dealmaking ramped up, with hundreds of listings in the pipeline, authorities have sounded the alarm on deal quality. They've also begun to tighten scrutiny of bankers' resources and document quality.
Separately, the SFC issued restriction notices to 31 brokers, prohibiting them from dealing with or processing assets relating to two syndicates on three IPOs. The first syndicate is linked to the listing of Baicha, as well as that of Cloudbreak Pharma Inc The regulator restricted dealing in assets held in client accounts of up to HK$4.4 billion - the largest such notice in SFC history - among six brokers.
The watchdog also restricted 29 brokers to deal assets of up to HK$285 million in client accounts related to the IPO of Tianju Dihe (Suzhou) Technology Co Ltd.
"We believe that the actions taken to date have significantly disrupted two suspected syndicates which may have been involved in IPO-rigging cases," SFC's executive director of enforcement Michael Duignan said in the statement.
The brokers who received the restriction notices aren't the subjects of the SFC's investigations. The restriction notices do not affect the brokers or their other clients, the watchdog said in the statement.
The SFC said its investigations are continuing and it won't make any further comments while they are underway.

articles.title: Philippine central bank chief warns of Asian financial risks - IDNFinancials
articles.summary: Philippine central bank chief warns of Asian financial risks  IDNFinancials
articles.full_text:
BANGKOK - Philippine central bank Governor Eli Remolona has urged Asian countries to reflect on the financial crisis of the late 1990s and strengthen preventive measures to avoid a similar upheaval in the future.
According to Reuters, before the Asian financial crisis erupted in 1997, countries across the region enjoyed substantial capital inflows.
At the time, the World Bank described East Asia's economic growth as the 'East Asian miracle'.
Speaking at an International Monetary Fund (IMF) panel discussion on the outlook for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), Remolona said the massive inflows of investment had ultimately led to a crisis.
He said Asian countries needed to revisit those events and step up efforts to anticipate similar risks.
'Investment poured into Asia, but the region was subsequently hit by a crisis. So, that growth was not really a miracle,' Remolona said.
'I think we need to remember that. We must prevent a crisis like that from happening again,' he added.
He argued that efforts to anticipate such financial crises had so far been insufficient.
The remarks were made during the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank in Bangkok, Thailand. Thailand was among the countries directly affected by the 1997 Asian financial crisis.
Krishna Srinivasan, Director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, said the organisation had strengthened its ability to assess financial system vulnerabilities and the spillover effects of crises from one country to another.
'We have learnt lessons from that crisis and developed guidelines for managing volatile capital flows, including determining when intervention in foreign exchange markets is necessary,' Srinivasan said.
He added that ASEAN economies had so far proved relatively resilient amid trade tensions arising from US tariffs.
However, the region's economic growth could be constrained by some ASEAN countries' dependence on imported oil and gas.
Japan's Vice Minister of Finance for International Affairs, Atsushi Mimura, also highlighted short-term risks, including energy price spikes resulting from conflicts in the Middle East and rising inflation.
Mimura stressed that government assistance to ease the burden of higher energy prices on households and businesses should be targeted, tailored to their needs and temporary.
'Fiscal support must adhere to the three Ts: targeted, tailored and temporary,' Mimura said.
Amid growing competitive pressure from China, Mimura urged ASEAN countries to increase investment to diversify supply chains for critical minerals and energy.
Japan, he said, was ready to support these efforts.
'All ASEAN countries need to increase investment to keep pace with developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and innovation,' Mimura said.
He added that ASEAN countries held strategic positions in digitalisation supply chains because they produce critical minerals.
ASEAN comprises 11 countries: Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Timor-Leste, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. (ARF/LM)

articles.summary: AI stock selloff eases as investors buy on dips amid falling bond yields  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Data-centre operator CoreWeave remained in focus. Its shares fell 2% by midday after tumbling as much as 10% earlier in the session and plunging 15% on Wednesday. The company’s bonds traded at yields as high as 16%, while its credit-default swap spreads widened, underscoring concerns about rising financing costs. Wednesday’s hotter-than-expected US inflation report highlighted the risks that elevated borrowing costs posed to the capital-intensive AI sector.
Selling remained concentrated among heavily indebted companies and stocks that had recorded substantial gains earlier this year. AI infrastructure provider Nebius fell 5%, AI server maker Dell Technologies dropped 7%, and memory-chip company SanDisk lost 2%. Despite the declines, Nebius had gained 112% in 2026, Dell had surged 273%, and SanDisk had climbed 476%, according to LSEG data.
For live updates on US Markets, click here
Some investors said an infrastructure expansion billed as the largest ever was inevitably likely to face setbacks. They expected further volatility as interest rates rose and expectations of additional Federal Reserve tightening increased.
“While increased competition within AI, rising financing requirements and higher rates may periodically add to volatility, we view this latest bout as more of a recalibration of expectations than a fundamental break in the AI investment story,” said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, chief investment officer for the Americas and global head of equities at the UBS Chief Investment Office.
AI slowdown concerns
Concerns surrounding CoreWeave and similarly positioned companies partly reflected perceptions that growth had slowed at Anthropic and OpenAI, two major AI laboratories at the centre of the boom.
“We’re getting a whole lot of information suggesting that the largest AI companies may not be generating the earnings or revenue people anticipated, and I think that makes everyone nervous about companies like CoreWeave,” Kim Forrest, chief investment officer at Bokeh Capital Partners, told Reuters.
CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator said in an internal memo that the market was acting “irrationally” and that he remained confident in the AI cloud company, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday.
Also Read: Why are credit default swaps unnerving AI investors?
Investors nevertheless remained broadly optimistic about the sector because its largest companies, including chip designer Nvidia and hyperscalers Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon, were highly profitable and widely viewed as well-managed despite debt-related concerns.
However, higher interest rates were expected to increase borrowing and construction costs, with unprofitable and less-profitable companies likely to face the greatest pressure. US Treasury yields extended their recent decline on Thursday, with the 10-year yield briefly approaching 5% before moving higher again. Even so, elevated inflation had altered investors’ expectations for interest rates.
“I do think long rates above 5% and creeping towards 6% is a problem for the marginal borrower, I’ll call them,” said Ross Mayfield, investment strategy analyst at Baird. “It gets a lot harder for the tiers below the kind of big four hyperscalers.”
The Nasdaq was down 0.4% on Thursday afternoon, while Alphabet and most other hyperscalers were little changed. SpaceX, another major AI company, fell 3%.
“This select group of companies is driving most of the growth in the economy and the stock market, and they’re investing so, so aggressively and investors just aren’t really willing to pay for it or fully buy in to the extent that we saw in the late ’90s or whatever when investors kind of lost their minds,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management. “Investors have definitely not lost their minds. They’re being very cautious, and I think selective.”

articles.summary: Japanese Yen holds firm despite hotter-than-expected US producer inflation  www.tmgm.com
articles.full_text:
USD/JPY extends its decline on Thursday, trading around 157.85 at the time of writing, down 0.30% on the day. The pair falls to its lowest level in a week, pressured by a stronger Japanese Yen (JPY) and declining US Treasury yields. However, hotter-than-expected US producer inflation data helps the US Dollar (USD) recover some of its earlier losses.
In the United States (US), the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported on Thursday that the Producer Price Index (PPI) rose by 6.3% YoY in September, compared with 5.6% in August and market expectations of 5.3%. On a monthly basis, producer prices increased by 1.3%, well above the 0.5% forecast. Core producer inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, also exceeded expectations, rising by 0.7% MoM and 5% YoY. These figures highlight persistent inflationary pressures in the US and could complicate upcoming monetary policy decisions by the Federal Reserve (Fed).
The US Dollar reacted positively to the release, with the US Dollar Index (DXY) recovering some of its daily losses after briefly falling toward 102.00. The prospect of persistently elevated inflation could encourage the Fed to maintain a restrictive monetary policy stance for longer than previously anticipated.
Meanwhile, US labor market data released on Thursday showed a slight increase in Initial Jobless Claims to 199K for the week ending October 10, compared with 198K previously. However, the figure remained below market expectations of 200K. Continuing Jobless Claims declined by 4K to 1.710M, suggesting relative stability in the labor market.
Despite these US economic releases, the Japanese Yen retains part of its gains, supported by falling US Treasury yields. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield has dropped by more than 30 basis points from Wednesday's highs, reaching a three-week low of 5.09%. This decline reduces the appeal of the US Dollar against the Japanese currency.
In Japan, expectations of further interest rate hikes by the Bank of Japan (BoJ) also support the Japanese Yen. After raising its benchmark interest rate to 1.25% in September, its highest level in 31 years, the central bank maintains its stance toward a gradual normalization of monetary policy.
On Thursday, BoJ board member Junko Koeda emphasized the need to adjust interest rates in a timely manner, taking into account economic conditions, inflation developments and estimates of the neutral interest rate. Her comments reinforce expectations of additional monetary tightening in Japan.
The Japanese currency also benefits from speculation that authorities could intervene in the foreign exchange market to support the Japanese Yen. However, reports suggest that the BoJ may refrain from delivering another interest rate hike as early as October, preferring to assess the impact of previous policy decisions on the economy.

articles.full_text:
Mumbai, Oct. 15 -- Global investors and sovereign wealth funds, including Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, Qatar Investment Authority, GIC Pte. Ltd, Norges Bank Investment Management, and Mubadala Investment Co., are seeking allocations in the anchor book of Jio Platforms Ltd's public offering, alongside asset managers BlackRock Inc. and FMR LLC, according to four people familiar with the matter.
About 15 domestic asset managers, including HDFC Mutual Fund, SBI Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, Nippon Life India Asset Management, and Motilal Oswal Asset Management, have also submitted indications of interest for a share of Jio's Rs.8,000 crore anchor book, the people said on condition of anonymity.
The asset management arms of Goldman Sachs and Franklin Templeton are also vying for a slice of the pie, the people said.
Representatives of Jio's parent company, Reliance Industries Ltd, as well as the institutional investors and fund managers, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The telecom giant's parent filed its red herring prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Board of India on Wednesday for an initial public offering (IPO) that will raise around Rs. 30,200 crore, or about $3.2 billion, at the upper end of the 1,069-1,119 price band announced per share.
The anchor allocation window, which precedes the public subscription period, allows institutional entities to secure share allotments before the main issue opens.
Under capital market regulator rules, up to 60% of the portion reserved for qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) can be allocated to anchor investors. Half of the anchor portion is reserved for domestic mutual funds.
Final share allocations for the anchor book are scheduled to be finalized ahead of the opening of the retail and non-institutional bidding windows.
Jio operates digital services and telecommunications infrastructure across India.
Existing equity holders in Jio Platforms include Meta Platforms Inc., Alphabet Inc.'s Google, KKR & Co., Silver Lake and General Atlantic.Disclaimer Published by HT Digital Content Services with permission from MINT. articles.title: Poland’s central bank crisis exposes European hypocrisy - Yahoo
articles.summary: Poland’s central bank crisis exposes European hypocrisy  Yahoo
articles.full_text:
Independent central bankers are becoming an increasing inconvenience for heavily indebted Western governments.
With public borrowing mounting and little political appetite for spending cuts, the temptation to pressure monetary authorities into keeping interest rates low, or otherwise making government debt easier to finance, is growing.
Until now, the resulting confrontations have followed a familiar pattern: populist politicians challenging central bankers who insist on operating independently of the political cycle.
Liz Truss has blamed the Bank of England for helping to bring down her premiership, while Donald Trump's attacks on Jerome Powell because of interest rates have prompted widespread concern about political interference in the Federal Reserve.
But now, events in Poland are threatening to turn that narrative on its head in a way that could potentially destabilise the region, if not the wider eurozone.
This is because in Warsaw, it is the ostensibly more institutionally minded, pro-European administration of Donald Tusk that is pursuing a central banker associated with the nationalist Right.
And it is the European Central Bank (ECB), having defended the principle of monetary independence against political pressure elsewhere, that may soon find itself having to decide how far that principle extends when the politics are reversed.
The timing is particularly awkward. With France's fiscal and political difficulties already raising questions about the euro's resilience, the last thing Frankfurt needs is a confrontation that casts doubt on the consistency of the rules underpinning European monetary governance.
Yet that is precisely the risk emerging from Warsaw.
Last Friday, a Polish parliamentary committee voted to recommend that Adam Glapiński, the governor of the National Bank of Poland, face the state tribunal because of alleged misconduct. The matter now moves to the full parliament, where a vote could take place in early November.
Glapiński is accused of improperly financing government spending through bond purchases during the pandemic, misleading the finance ministry about the bank's profits and politicising the institution.
He rejects the allegations, arguing that his actions during the pandemic were consistent with the emergency measures adopted by central banks across the developed world.
Indeed, large-scale purchases of government bonds were a central feature of the monetary response to Covid, including at the Bank of England and the ECB. This raises an important question about where the boundary lies between legitimate scrutiny of a central bank governor and the retrospective politicisation of monetary decisions that were widely accepted elsewhere.
Nonetheless, it is true that central bank independence does not confer immunity from the law. The difficulty is that Poland's institutions are themselves divided about the legal procedures by which a governor can be held accountable.
Since coming to power in 2023, Tusk's coalition has sought to reverse judicial and institutional reforms introduced by the previous Right-wing Law and Justice government, known as PiS.
Tusk's supporters – and the EU at large – regard those reforms as an assault on the rule of law. PiS, however, argues that they were necessary to address entrenched political influence within the judiciary, stemming back to the communist era.
The dispute has left Poland with competing interpretations of constitutional authority.
That matters because the contested constitutional tribunal ruled in 2024 that referring the central bank governor to the state tribunal requires a three fifths parliamentary majority, rather than the ordinary absolute majority. It also rejected the provision under which such a referral would automatically suspend him.
The government disputes the validity of those rulings.
In practical terms, the difference could determine whether Glapiński remains in office. If parliament proceeds under the lower threshold, he could maintain that any resulting suspension is unconstitutional, while the government insists it is lawful.
The consequence could be competing claims about who is legally entitled to lead Poland's central bank.
Complicating matters further is the expiry of the bank's remaining deputy governor's term on Nov 4. Without fresh appointments, its management board could fall below the minimum membership required by law to implement monetary policy, just as the dispute surrounding Glapiński approaches its decisive stage.
The same day, the bank is scheduled to announce its next interest rate decision.
Polish policymakers have argued that monetary policy can continue without Glapiński. They may be right. But setting interest rates is only one part of central banking. Implementing decisions, authorising transactions and managing financial assets also require legally recognised authority.
If the zloty came under pressure, for example, and the bank needed to intervene in currency markets, foreign counterparties might reasonably ask whose instructions they were legally entitled to follow.
This could, theoretically, split the bank into rival authorities.
The issue is not entirely without precedent. During Venezuela's political crisis, rival claims to governmental legitimacy became entangled in litigation concerning access to gold held at the Bank of England.
Poland is obviously a very different case, even though it does also hold a significant amount of gold with the Bank. But the underlying principle is the same: a central bank's ability to control its reserves depends partly on whether other institutions recognise the authority of those acting on its behalf.
This is where the ECB's predicament becomes especially interesting.
Although Poland has retained the zloty, its central bank belongs to the European system of central banks. European law provides protections against the arbitrary dismissal of central bank governors and the ECB has previously expressed concern about the proceedings against Glapiński.
Should his suspension become contested, Frankfurt may therefore be required to take a position.
Defending him could bring the ECB into conflict with a Polish government whose efforts to restore judicial independence have enjoyed broad European support. Declining to defend him, meanwhile, could raise uncomfortable questions about why political pressure on central bankers is unacceptable in Washington but potentially permissible in Warsaw.
There are important legal distinctions between these cases. Allegations of misconduct must be distinguished from political disagreement about monetary policy. The question is whether European institutions can maintain that distinction when the domestic authorities responsible for adjudicating it disagree about which laws and judgments are binding.
For the ECB, this is more than a Polish constitutional curiosity.
Its credibility depends on the perception that monetary rules are applied consistently, particularly at a time when the fiscal strains of major eurozone economies are testing the boundaries between monetary independence and government financing.
A dispute that leaves European institutions appearing to choose between competing political authorities could weaken that perception, regardless of the legal merits.
There is no inevitability about a crisis. Parliament may delay its vote, appointments may resolve the management board problem and the legal dispute may be contained before it affects monetary operations.
But Poland exposes a vulnerability that is often overlooked in discussions of central bank independence. Legal safeguards are only as effective as the constitutional consensus that gives them force.
Western policymakers have become accustomed to treating central bank independence as a settled institutional achievement, rather than a political arrangement whose legitimacy ultimately depends on competing authorities agreeing to respect it.
The Polish case may yet demonstrate that the greatest danger is not what policymakers do not know about monetary independence, but what they have come to know for certain that just isn't so.

articles.title: Dollar Retreats From 18-Month Peak as Fed Officials Cool October Rate-Hike Bets - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Dollar Retreats From 18-Month Peak as Fed Officials Cool October Rate-Hike Bets  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
The U.S. dollar pulled back from an 18-month high on Thursday as a sharp decline in Treasury yields and cautious signals from Federal Reserve officials dampened expectations for another rate increase at the central bank's late-October meeting.
The dollar index, which tracks the greenback against six major currencies, slipped 0.2% to 102.03 after touching its strongest level in a year and a half on Wednesday. The retreat came even as U.S. consumer price data released a day earlier showed inflation running hotter than economists had forecast.
The euro recovered 0.5% from its own 18-month trough to $1.1216, putting the common currency on course for its largest single-day advance in nearly two months. Sterling also strengthened 0.5% to $1.3253, holding steady after data showed the U.K. economy unexpectedly expanded 0.1% in August.
The pullback in the dollar tracked a broader shift in sentiment across financial markets. Wednesday's CPI report initially stoked bets that the Fed would need to keep policy tighter for longer, and renewed concerns about heavy debt loads among AI companies drove investors into the safety of government bonds. The resulting rally in Treasuries pushed the benchmark 10-year yield down to 5.085% and the 30-year yield to 5.428%, both hovering near three-week lows.
Kit Juckes, chief FX strategist at Societe Generale, attributed part of the dollar's move to positioning dynamics rather than any fundamental shift. "The overall picture is I think one of a little bit of a tug of war between people who would like to look for a correction in the dollar. Because positioning's too big, we've come a long way, there's not really much new news, we've got a lot of rate hikes priced in and so on. And then the economic data, which can flip it," he said.
He added that trading would likely remain volatile until investors get through retail sales and producer price data due later in the day. "I suspect it'll be choppy and uncomfortable until we've got past the retail sales and PPI numbers," he said.
Fed officials push back on October hike
Market pricing for a rate increase at the Fed's October 27-28 meeting briefly jumped to 50% in the wake of the inflation report. U.S. consumer prices rose 3.7% year-on-year in September, accelerating from 3.4% in August and surpassing the 3.6% consensus estimate. Core prices climbed 2.6% annually, also above expectations.
But a series of remarks from senior policymakers quickly tempered those wagers. Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly both indicated the central bank could afford to wait for a clearer inflation picture before moving again.
"Despite the whole CPI number coming slightly stronger than expected, I think markets have sort of taken the view that maybe it was not hot enough to force the Fed's hand for October," said Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at ANZ. "(The) October (meeting) is also just a few days before the midterm elections as well," he added. "And that's possibly why the market doesn't want to be more aggressive in pricing in for October."
Investors will now turn their attention to remarks from Fed officials, including Chair Kevin Warsh, at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday for further guidance on the policy trajectory.
Asia-Pacific currencies diverge
Elsewhere in currency markets, the Japanese yen firmed to 157.80 per dollar, gaining 0.4% after Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama renewed warnings against excessive currency volatility. The yen's strength came despite broader dollar weakness, suggesting intervention concerns were providing support.
The Australian dollar fell 0.7% to $0.6919 after domestic employment unexpectedly declined in September. Data showed payrolls dropped by 39,300, defying forecasts for a 20,000 increase, driven largely by a 73,700 fall in part-time positions. The unemployment rate held at 4.7%, its highest level in five years.
The weak labor market figures reduced expectations of further tightening by the Reserve Bank of Australia, with markets now pricing in roughly a 90% probability that the central bank will leave its cash rate unchanged at 4.6% when it meets in November.
The South Korean won was among the biggest losers in the region, with the dollar gaining 0.8% against the currency as regional equities came under pressure. The Chinese yuan traded largely flat in both onshore and offshore markets, while the Indian rupee edged 0.1% lower and the Singapore dollar strengthened 0.2%.

Note: Changes reflect Thursday's session as of the latest available data. Levels for USD/KRW were not specified in the source material.
The dollar's retreat from its multi-month peak underscores the delicate balance markets are trying to strike between persistent inflation pressures and a Fed that appears inclined toward patience. With producer prices and retail sales still to come, along with a cluster of central bank commentary at the Bangkok meetings, currency traders are bracing for what could be a volatile end to the week.

The Fidelity India Active ETF (ASX:FIIN) represents an essential strategic allocation for Australian investors trading on the Australian Securities Exchange. In an increasingly complex macroeconomic climate shaped by volatile interest rate expectations and shifting global growth dynamics, exchange-traded funds offer unmatched liquidity, transparency, and administrative simplicity. For self-managed superannuation funds and private wealth builders alike, FIIN functions as a core portfolio building block designed to deliver targeted asset-class participation while eliminating the risks and operational friction of single-security picking. Its prominence on the ASX reflects a structural shift toward low-friction, institutional-grade portfolio construction that empowers long-term investors to compound wealth efficiently across market cycles.
| Ticker | Fund Name | Benchmark Index | Expense Ratio | 
| FIIN | Fidelity India Active ETF | MSCI India Index | 1.20% p.a. | 
Investment Objective & Fund Structure
The primary investment objective of FIIN is to provide investment results that correspond closely to the total return performance of its designated benchmark before management fees, operating costs, and fund taxes. Operating under the rigorous oversight of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission as an Australian-domiciled registered managed investment scheme, the fund provides investors with full beneficial ownership and complete physical or direct asset backing. Management expenses are maintained at highly competitive levels, protecting net investor returns from fee erosion. Unitholders enjoy the administrative convenience of standard domestic tax reporting, receiving annual consolidated tax statements that streamline end-of-year compliance without cross-border withholding complexities or unnecessary regulatory entanglements.
Underlying Benchmark & Index Relationship
At the heart of the fund’s disciplined operational model is its rules-based alignment with its underlying benchmark index. Governed by independent international index providers, the benchmark implements rigorous market-capitalisation screens, liquidity thresholds, and systematic rebalancing protocols. This transparent, formulaic methodology eliminates individual manager emotional bias, focusing instead on tight benchmark replication and low tracking error across multi-year investment horizons. Periodic rebalancings ensure the underlying portfolio accurately reflects evolving market conditions while keeping turnover and transaction expenses under strict control, preserving maximum capital for unitholders throughout economic expansions.
Portfolio Holdings & Sector Diversification
From an asset allocation standpoint, FIIN provides comprehensive diversification across premier corporate enterprises and vital economic sectors. Capital is dispersed across established industry leaders possessing resilient balance sheets, defensible commercial market shares, and robust cash-flow generation capabilities. Sector exposures are thoughtfully calibrated to prevent excessive concentration in speculative segments, balancing dynamic growth engines with defensive, recession-resilient businesses. This institutional-grade diversification mitigates single-company operational vulnerabilities, buffering investor portfolios against localized industry downturns and unexpected operational shocks.
Fees, Distributions & Performance Context
Cost efficiency is a cornerstone of FIIN, featuring an ultra-lean annual expense ratio that preserves capital for long-term compound growth. The fund distributes investment income on a regular and predictable schedule, passing through corporate dividends, interest distributions, and realized capital gains directly to unitholders. Historical distribution yields have delivered dependable cash-flow streams that appeal strongly to retirees and income-conscious wealth builders. Across multi-year market cycles, reinvested total returns have tracked broader economic expansion, demonstrating the wealth-building potency of low-cost, disciplined asset compounding across extended generational horizons without unnecessary fee drag.
Key Investment Risks & Practical Considerations
Investors must carefully assess relevant market risks before allocating capital to FIIN. Investment values fluctuate in response to broader equity sentiment, sovereign interest rate decisions, and macroeconomic monetary cycles. Investors should also evaluate whether currency movements impact unhedged global exposure or whether domestic sector concentrations expose capital to localized economic contractions. Maintaining a long-term investment horizon and pairing the fund with complementary non-correlated asset classes provides the most effective defense against short-term market volatility and structural shifts in interest rates.
What Investors Should Understand Next
Before initiating or expanding an investment in FIIN, participants should review the official Product Disclosure Statement (PDS) and Target Market Determination (TMD). Continuously monitoring fund distribution statements, underlying tracking efficiency, and broader macroeconomic indicators will assist unitholders in maintaining an optimized, resilient asset allocation aligned with their personal wealth creation and retirement goals. Maintaining a balanced perspective across broad macroeconomic market regimes enables investors to achieve durable, sustainable long-term financial security.

articles.title: Dollar-Yen Slides to Upper 157 Range as Falling U.S. Yields Spur Euro, Pound Buying - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Dollar-Yen Slides to Upper 157 Range as Falling U.S. Yields Spur Euro, Pound Buying  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
The dollar-yen pair traded weakly in the Tokyo foreign exchange market on the morning of the 15th, falling to the upper 157-yen range. Dollar selling prevailed against a backdrop of declining U.S. long-term yields, with the pair sliding from an early-morning level of 158.33 yen to 157.58 yen. As of noon, the pair was hovering around 157.66 yen, roughly 67 sen weaker for the dollar compared with the New York market close of 158.33 yen.
The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield, which had climbed above the 5.20% level the previous day, fell to a level briefly below 5.10% in after-hours trading. This reinforced the dollar-selling trend. Meanwhile, the euro and pound attracted buying interest, with European currencies generally firm across the board.
EUR/USD stood at $1.1235 as of noon, roughly 0.0078 dollars stronger for the euro compared with the New York close of $1.1157. The pair's break above the previous day's high of $1.1211 added momentum to buying, pushing it to an intraday high of $1.1241. EUR/JPY also traded at 177.13 yen as of noon, about 50 sen stronger for the euro versus the New York close of 176.63 yen, with yen-selling and euro-buying driving the pair as high as 177.23 yen.
Dollar-yen dipped to an intraday low of 157.58 yen just before 11 a.m., but found support just shy of the 157.52-yen low marked on the 8th, rebounding to around 157.79 yen at one point.
BOJ Board Member's Remarks Underpin the Yen
Bank of Japan Policy Board member Junko Koeda said on the day that prices continue to carry "upside risk for both fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027." She further stated that "Japan's inflation rate is becoming more firmly entrenched as a sustained phenomenon than before," and conveyed a hawkish view that given the considerable upside risks to prices, there is "no need to be overly cautious about rate hikes."
At the same time, she noted that "it is important to carefully assess changes in financial conditions and their impact accompanying policy rate adjustments," while also indicating that financial conditions remain accommodative. These remarks were seen as a factor supporting the yen, though they were not enough to reverse the dollar-selling trend driven by falling U.S. yields.
Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama, speaking on the possibility of currency intervention, said Japan would "act without hesitation if necessary." She stressed that the message remains "completely unchanged" from the one communicated during coordinated Japan-U.S. intervention.
Australia's Employment Data Deteriorates More Than Expected
The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported that the September unemployment rate came in at 4.7%, exceeding the market consensus of 4.6% and worsening from the previous reading of 4.6%. The result triggered selling of the Australian dollar, contributing to a shift of funds into the euro and pound.
Trading ranges for major currency pairs so far today are as follows:
| Currency Pair | Trading Range | 
|---|---|
| Dollar-yen | 157.58 - 158.35 yen | 
| EUR/USD | $1.1151 - $1.1241 | 
| EUR/JPY | 176.51 - 177.23 yen | 
Note: Ranges are reference values through noon in the Tokyo market on the 15th.
Market participants widely expect U.S. yield movements to continue dictating dollar-yen direction. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield's dip below 5.10% intensified dollar-selling pressure, but the pair showed signs of bottoming out in the mid-157-yen range, suggesting a tug-of-war around that level in the near term. While expectations of additional BOJ rate hikes underpin the yen, any retreat in the outlook for higher U.S. yields would likely cap dollar-yen upside.

articles.title: Japan 10-Year Yield Rises as BOJ Outlook Mulled - TradingView
articles.summary: Japan 10-Year Yield Rises as BOJ Outlook Mulled  TradingView
articles.full_text:
Japan’s 10-year government bond yield climbed to around 2.95% on Friday, recovering some ground after the previous session’s decline as investors assessed hawkish signals from a Bank of Japan official.
BOJ board member Junko Koeda cautioned this week against excessive hesitation in raising interest rates, reinforcing expectations that the central bank could continue tightening monetary policy in the coming months following its accelerated pace of normalization.
Earlier reports suggested that the BOJ was reluctant to deliver a rare back-to-back rate hike this month, although a potential increase in December remained under consideration.
Meanwhile, BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said policymakers would continue to monitor bond yields closely, reiterating that long-term interest rates should be determined by market forces.
His comments underscored the central bank’s measured approach as it continues to move away from its previous yield curve control framework.

articles.title: Investors see outflow and FX risks as MSCI moves to downgrade Indonesia - Bilyonaryo Business
articles.summary: Investors see outflow and FX risks as MSCI moves to downgrade Indonesia  Bilyonaryo Business
articles.full_text:
Oct 16 (Reuters) – Indonesia’s stock market is no longer worthy of “emerging market” status, MSCI said, and the index provider proposed to cut it from a suite of products tracked by global investors.
The move is a major setback likely to send money fleeing. Here is what market participants are saying:
ANGUS MACKINTOSH, ASEAN SPECIALIST, ALETHIA CAPITAL, SINGAPORE:
“The move seems heavy-handed given the moves that Indonesia has made to address issues around market visibility and free float. The problem for Indonesia is a lack of evidence of implementation and a failure to sanction those obviously involved in stock manipulation. The only way for Indonesia to remedy this situation would be to impose severe sanctions and fines on those involved in concerted share manipulation.
“This move does not reflect the health of the vast majority of listed companies or indeed the Indonesian economy, and grouping Indonesia with Lebanon, Palestine, and Argentina does not make sense.”
RADHIKA RAO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DBS BANK, SINGAPORE:
“This potential development could prove more unfavourable than a tier reclassification, as passive investors bound by mandate may also reduce exposure. Any ensuing risk-off move in the currency would likely prompt greater central bank vigilance and intervention.”
GARY TAN, PORTFOLIO MANAGER, ALLSPRING GLOBAL INVESTMENTS, SINGAPORE:
“The consultation is a surprise given the steps Indonesia has already taken to improve market accessibility, including removing the minimum share price limit. The prospect of standalone status could encourage index-linked investors to further de-risk, but for Indonesia in our view the bigger concern is less the direct impact on equities and more the potential pressure on the currency from foreign outflows.”
IRMAN FAIZ, ECONOMIST, BANK DANAMON INDONESIA:
“MSCI’s unusually strong assessment increases the incentive for institutional investors to reduce exposure ahead of the final decision, potentially extending equity volatility and weakening foreign risk appetite.
“The larger risk is structural from a reduced institutional participation, thinner liquidity, to higher equity financing costs. Large-cap banks are particularly exposed, while spillovers into sovereign bonds would depend on broader investor risk appetite rather than automatic index-related selling.”
JAYDEN VANTARAKIS, HEAD OF ASEAN EQUITY RESEARCH, MACQUARIE CAPITAL, SINGAPORE:
“The working assumption for most equity investors we’d spoken with recently had been that steps taken on free-floats and shareholder concentration disclosure would be sufficient to avert a downgrade.”
“The extension of the review from November 2026 to June 2027 also prolongs the period of uncertainty for investors.”
MSCI gets set to remove Indonesia from global indexes Read full story
(Reporting by Ankur Banerjee and Gregor Stuart Hunter in Singapore and Stefanno Sulaiman in Jakarta. Compiled by Tom Westbrook. Editing by Sonali Paul)

articles.title: BBC asks judge to force Trump to sit for deposition as part of his $10bn lawsuit
articles.summary: BBC asks US federal judge to compel Trump’s lawyers to schedule deposition after his team canceled initial sessionThe BBC is asking a federal judge in Florida to force Donald Trump to sit for a deposition as part of the president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.According to a Tuesday filing, the BBC and Trump’s legal team had agreed for him to be deposed on Friday. The BBC’s lawyers wrote to the judge that they had spent months trying to secure a location for the depos...
articles.full_text:
The BBC is asking a federal judge in Florida to force Donald Trump to sit for a deposition as part of the president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.
According to a Tuesday filing, the BBC and Trump’s legal team had agreed for him to be deposed on Friday. The BBC’s lawyers wrote to the judge that they had spent months trying to secure a location for the deposition from Trump’s team.
On 28 September, Trump’s lawyers told the BBC’s counsel that the president “is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance”.
While Trump’s lawyers said they would follow up quickly with a replacement date, they did not, ultimately suggesting that he would be available in the second or third week of January, well after the deadline to complete the discovery portion of the case. Lawyers for the BBC had pledged to keep the location of the deposition confidential.
As such, the BBC’s lawyers are now asking the judge to require Trump’s team to schedule the deposition.
“Plaintiff chose to file this lawsuit and, in doing so, he accepted the obligations of civil litigation,” the BBC’s motion reads. “The BBC therefore asks the Court to compel Plaintiff to confirm a date for his deposition, notify the BBC of a secure location where such deposition is possible and any other logistics required to ensure Plaintiff’s safety, and sit for the deposition, as the core rules of discovery require.”
Magistrate judge Enjoliqué Aytch Lett has scheduled a discovery hearing that is likely to touch on the deposition issue for 22 October.
“Nearly eight months into discovery, after seven depositions of BBC witnesses, and with only two months of discovery remaining, the BBC still has not been able to depose, and does not even have a schedule to depose, the most central figure in this case: Plaintiff himself,” lawyers for the BBC wrote in the Tuesday motion.
Trump, who has a long history of legal action against media companies, filed a lawsuit against the BBC in December 2025, accusing the network of violating Florida’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act over the edit of a Panorama documentary that edited together comments he made during a rally on 6 January 2021. The BBC has apologized for the error.
“The formerly respected and now disgraced BBC defamed President Trump by intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring his speech in a brazen attempt to interfere in the 2024 Presidential Election,” a spokesperson for Trump’s legal team said in a statement. “The BBC has a long pattern of deceiving its audience in coverage of President Trump, all in service of its own leftist political agenda. President Trump’s powerhouse lawsuit is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference just as he has held other fake news mainstream media responsible for their wrongdoing.”

articles.title: Philip R. Lane: The AI opportunity for Europe
articles.full_text:
- SPEECH
The AI opportunity for Europe
Dinner remarks by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at The International AI Summit
Dublin, 13 October 2026
AI is a general purpose technology that can improve global living standards and the global knowledge frontier by expanding access to information and raising productivity.
That said, delivering the benefits from AI depends on a host of different actors playing their part in supporting the transformation of the economy. The list is long and includes: the developers of AI frontier models (whether proprietary or open-weight); the builders of the various layers of the AI infrastructure stack; the entrepreneurs designing the customised AI products that can best unlock productivity gains in individual sectors or in relation to specialised tasks; the research and development community that can accelerate scientific discovery and compress the time lag between invention and commercial application; the operators of the energy systems that must respond to this new source of energy demand; the financial system that is required to appropriately value AI-related assets and finance AI production and AI adoption, while also incorporating AI into its own processes; the education and training sectors that must re-design instruction, learning and evaluation methods; and, finally, the managers and workers that must implement revised business processes at the sector and firm levels to maximise the benefits of AI.
This transformation also poses many challenges for political systems, civic society, policymakers and regulators at national, European and global levels in relation to the ethical, fiscal, governance and legal issues posed by AI. How these political economy issues are resolved will have a major bearing on the AI transition path, including the appropriate speed of adjustment that balances the societal benefits, costs and risks posed by AI.
Given the scale and breadth of the AI challenge, a wide range of possible timelines and outcomes can be envisaged, depending on the rate of progress along each individual dimension. The uncertainty surrounding the impact of AI – in both the short term and the long term – is compounded by the interdependencies and complementarities across these different dimensions.
For instance, the rollout of rapid progress in AI capabilities can be held back by bottlenecks in some areas, slowing the overall pace of AI adoption. In particular, how firms and labour market institutions navigate the re-orientation of the workforce is a key issue, with some occupations facing the prospect of higher demand due to complementarities with AI and others facing lower demand due to the scope for substitution by AI.[1] The net impact on employment will also depend on the evolution of labour costs versus token prices.
The European Central Bank is closely monitoring and analysing the impact of AI on the euro area economy for several reasons.[2] First, the medium-term and longer-term positive impact of AI on the level of potential output and the trend growth rate of the economy has the potential to raise the speed limit of the economy, with direct implications for the financial system and monetary policy. For Europe, the potential for AI to offset the economic impact of the projected trend decline in the working-age population is especially valuable.
Second, more immediately, AI is already a primary factor driving current activity levels in the euro area. We see this in terms of a higher rate of business investment (firms are set to devote around 10 per cent of their total investment to AI this year), an expansion in digital services sectors and the high global demand for European components and capital goods that are part of the AI supply chain. In turn, this is supported by expansion in AI-related lending, which accounts for roughly one quarter of recent credit growth to firms.
In our surveys, we are also tracking the rate at which firms and workers are adopting AI. In our Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises for the fourth quarter of 2025, most firms reported that they were using AI: 64 per cent of firms said they were using it either experimentally or moderately, while only 7 per cent of firms reported that their use was “significant”.[3]
Our survey of households indicates that the proportion of workers using AI has doubled over the last two years, with 52 per cent now reporting that they use AI at work, compared with 26 per cent in 2024.[4] In the aggregate, workers are reporting significant time savings, but these are highly concentrated in specific sectors and specialised tasks such as coding.
Taken together, these surveys suggest that AI adoption in Europe is already significant and growing rapidly, even if it is too early to detect any material impact on aggregate productivity.
In relation to the labour market, we do not yet see a major change in aggregate employment trends but hiring plans are muted, which especially affects the prospects for new graduates. The potential for AI to replace some types of workers may also weaken the bargaining power of workers, moderating wage growth and reducing the labour share in total income. In our surveys, there is significant variation across industries, with workers in sectors benefiting from the AI infrastructure buildout currently more optimistic than those in knowledge-intensive sectors that face greater AI substitution risk.
At the same time, it is also important to appreciate that the quantitative scale of the European AI surge is of a different order to the AI boom in the United States or East Asia. Over the last two years, digital investment in the United States has grown twice as fast as in the euro area, while US workers spend two to three times as much of the working week using AI as workers in the largest euro area economies.[5] In terms of the AI frontier, the Stanford AI Index calculates that the United States and China have produced 59 and 35 notable AI models, respectively, while France and the United Kingdom have produced one each. In terms of AI computing capacity, the United States hosts 75 per cent of the global aggregate, whereas Europe hosts just 5 per cent. Although international trade in AI goods and services can do much to spread the benefits of AI around the world, asymmetrical AI capacity across countries may generate a host of economic and geopolitical issues.[6]
Third, it is likely that the global AI investment boom and expectations of a future global AI-driven productivity boost at longer-term horizons are plausibly contributing to the global increase in long-term interest rates.[7] Especially since the scale of the European AI boom is not of the same order as the global AI boom, the spillover to the euro area bond market means that the increase in long-term interest rates constitutes a material tightening of financial conditions for the euro area. This is a relevant factor for the ECB in determining the appropriate monetary policy stance.
Fourth, the high equity valuations of AI firms and the global surge in AI-related debt issuance carry macroeconomic and financial stability risks in the event of even a temporary reversal in the expected rate of AI advancement or a decline in investor sentiment.[8] Accordingly, the financial stability and banking supervision functions of the ECB are closely monitoring the evolution of AI-related financial risks and, in addition, the associated cyber risks.[9]
Fifth, the ECB has an extensive internal AI adoption agenda. Given that we are a knowledge-intensive organisation, AI has great potential to improve our analytical capacity and organisational efficiency. Over the last several years, I have been very impressed by the bottom-up initiatives of ECB staff to apply AI in a wide range of applications.[10]
In closing, Europe has much to gain by seizing the AI opportunity. The ECB is committed to making sure that the AI transformation in Europe is underpinned by price stability and financial stability.
In these remarks, I have highlighted that the aggregate impact of AI depends on a multi-dimensional transformation of the economy over an extended period. This is best achieved by recognising the collective interest shared by all sectors and policymakers in ensuring a sustainable AI transformation path. To this end, this AI summit provides an important opportunity to learn from each other and listen to a wide range of perspectives on AI.
- See, for example, Garicano, L., Li, J. and Wu, Y. (2026), Messy Jobs: The Work that AI Cannot Reach, Upriver Press.
- See also Lane, P.R. (2026), “AI and the euro area economy”, speech at the ECB-SAFE-RCEA International Conference on the Climate-Macro-Finance Interface (3CMFI), 23 March.
- Among firms planning AI-related investment over the next 12 months, most expect to invest in AI-related technologies and tools, as well as in employee training, financed mostly through internal funds. 49 per cent of firms plan to invest in AI technologies and tools (e.g. software licences), 46 per cent in training employees, 40 per cent in data and infrastructure and 12 per cent in hiring AI specialists. See also: Ferrando, A., Lamboglia, S., Rariga, J. and Schmidt, M. (2026), “Adopting and investing in AI: evidence from euro area firms in the SAFE”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 2, ECB; Chaloupka, D., Lalinský, T. and Lopez-Garcia P. (2026), “What separates firms that use AI intensively from firms that don’t?”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 24 June. On how firms are financing AI, see: Cianfarani, A.S., Di Casola, P., Ramos, J. and Zander, D. (2026), “Funding the AI revolution: evidence from euro area sectors”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 6 October.
- Dias da Silva, A., Lebastard, L. and Sondermann, D. (2026), “AI adoption and the productivity promise: what workers report”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 26 August.
- Bick, A., Blandin, A., Deming, D.J., Fuchs-Schündeln, N. and Jessen, J. (2026), “Mind the Gap: AI Adoption in Europe and the U.S.”, NBER

articles.title: OpenAI’s London staff receive average of £2.3m per person annually
articles.summary: Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares last yearOpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average last year, as the ChatGPT-maker poured Premier League football salaries into its bid to dominate the global AI race.Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, ...
articles.full_text:
OpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average last year, as the ChatGPT-maker poured Premier League football salaries into its bid to dominate the global AI race.
Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, which is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1tn.
The earnings amount to 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings, according to the Office for National Statistics. An OpenAI worker on an average package could expect to take home about £1,000 an hour in salary and equity before tax.
But there is understood to be a wide discrepancy between the highest and lowest earners. The biggest compensation packages are reserved for AI researchers who help build the San Francisco company’s cutting-edge models such as Astra.
The figures relate to 2025, when there was a talent war and OpenAI’s rival, Meta, was reported to be offering multi-year packages running into several hundred million dollars.
OpenAI’s London base reflects the UK capital’s status as an important hub for AI talent with some of the brightest machine-learning experts and AI researchers coming out of universities such as Cambridge. Google DeepMind is also based in King’s Cross.
The company declined to comment on the figures, which come after a series of AI safety crises involving its models. This summer AI agents, under training, escaped and hacked into an unrelated company website, Hugging Face, while this month one of its safety leaders quit, saying that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.
OpenAI’s London office has been established as its largest international research hub but it also houses a government affairs team and sales and marketing functions – responsible for selling licences to companies and organisations. George Osborne, the former Conservative chancellor of the exchequer, joined last December as the company’s head for countries.
The earnings were a big jump on the previous year, when the average pay and equity package was £1.1m.
Booming AI salaries have already had a significant effect on housing prices in San Francisco, where the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 per month, a figure that is up more than 25% from last year and is nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.
In London, OpenAI UK Ltd recorded a more than trebling of its turnover in 2025 to £293m, on which it made a £20.3m profit.
